LABOUR DEPARTMENT 

NOTIFICATION. 

No. 6989®i«. /D/1R-3/54. — 20th December 1954. — In exercise of the 
'power conferred by section 38 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 
1947), the Governor is pleased to make the following amendments in the 
Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1947, as subsequently amended, the same 
having been previously published as required by sub-section (1) of the said 
section:-* 

w Amendments. 

4l 

1. After rule 3 of the said rules, insert the following rule, namely: — 

M 3A. Application for permission under section 33. — (1) An employer 
intending to obtain? the express permission in writing of a con- 
ciliation officer, Board or Tribunal under section 33 shall present 
an application in Form A4 in triplicate to the conciliation officer, 

4* Board or Tribunal as the case may be and shall tile along with 
the application a* many copies thereof as there are opposite 
parties. “V 

(2) Every application under sub-rule (1) shall be verified at the foot by 

the employer making it or by some other person duly authorised 
» by the employer in that behalf. Where the employer is a 

* ' * company or other body corporate or an Association of persons 

ft (whether incorporated or not) such application shall be verified by 

a Director, Manager, Secretary or a Partner or by some person 
duly authorised by him in that behalf and acquainted with the 
facts of the case. 

(3) The person verifying shall specify, by reference to the numbered 

paragraphs of the application, what he verifies of his own 
knowledge and what he verifies upon information received and 
believed to be true. 

(4) The person verifying shall sign the verification and shall state the 

date on which and the place at which the verification is signed.” 

2. After rule 4 of the said rules, insert the following rules, namely : — 

- “4A. .Xotice of hy-off .— Whenever a workman whose name is borne on 
the muster rolls of an industrial establishment is laid-off by the 

* employer, the employer shall as soon as possible rejiort in Form 

; A5 the information of such lay-off %o the Labour Commissioner. 

4B. Notice of retrenchment. — (l)Whei#m an employer finds it 
necessary to retrench any workman, he shall, at least on© ironth 
- n before the date of actual retrenchment, give notice thereof in 
Fohn A6 to the Lultour Commissioner. 

Provided that where an employer retrenches any workman with imme- 
diate effect by paying him wages in lieu of notice, such employer 
. «tor immediately ufter such retrenchment, give notice thereof 
^ to the Labour Commissioner in Form A6. 

(2) Every employer shall maintain a register called the Register of 
4 Retrenched Workmen. The Register shall contain the names, 
addresses and periods of service of the retrenched workers. 

4C. Ro~empt$frment of retrenched workers. — On the occurrence of 
vacancies after retrenchment, when an employer proposes to take 
in his employ any persons, he shall arrange for the display on a 
notice board in the premises of the industrial establishment the 
details of the vacancies to* be filed prepared as tar as

No. 5983Dis. / D/1 1L-28/54. 22nd December 1954. — Whereas under 
the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 1209Dis ./ 
D/11L-28/54, dated the 23rd March 1954, the industrial dispute between 
the New Commercial Transport, P-29, Princep Street, Calcutta-13 and their 
workers represented by Motor Transport Workers’ Union, 249B, Bowbazar 
Street, Calcutta-12, regarding the matters specified in the schedule thercio 
was referred for adjudication to the First Industrial Tribunal; 

And whereas the said First Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the 
State Government its award on the said industrial dispute; 

Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 

ANNEXURE. 

In the matter of an industrial dispute between the New Commercial 
Transport, P-29, Prinoep Street, Calcutta-13 and their workers as 
represented by Motor Transport Workers! Union, 249 B, Bowbazar 
Street, Calcutta-12. 

BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 

Pbesent : 

Suit! M. C.. BANERJI, District Judge (Retd.), Judge , First. Industrial 

Tribunal . 

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by order 
No. 12091)is. /D/ 13L-28/54, dated 23rd March 1954, referred, under sec- 
tions 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between the New Commercial Transport, P-29, Princep 
Street, Calcutta-13 and their workers as represented by Motor Transport 
Workers* Union, 249B, Bowbazar Street, Calcutta-12, regarding the matters 
specified in the following schedule to this Tribunal for adjudication. 

SCHEDULE. 

(1) Reinstatement of the following discharged workers: — 

Suleman Khan, Naimuddin and Azmeri Khan. 

(2) Fixation of working hours. 

(3) Weekly rest. 

(4) Leave and holidays. 

(5) Monthly pay system. 

Notices were issued on both parties, who filed written statements setting 
forth their respective cases. 

The Union, in its written statement, states is follows: — 

The Company is a trading concern running a number of lorries carrying 
i?ooils on contract. The workmen serving under the Company have no fived 
irking hours, weekly rest or any system of leave and ‘holidays. The 
workmen joined the Motor Transport Workers’ Union in April 1953. r Jhe 


54

Management dismissed Naimuddin, one of the workers in the employment 
of the Company, on 24th October 1953, and when the other workers took up 
the cause of Naimuddin, the latter was reinstated. On 20th October 1953 
the Union sent a charter of demands to the Company as appearing in 
Annexure A to the Union's written statement. On 2nd November 1963 the 
workmen also placed identical demands before the Management by letter 
shown in Annexure B to the written statement. Instead of conceding to the 
demands of the workers, the Company suddenly discharged three Union 
leaders Suleman Khan, Naimuddin and Azmere Khan. The workmen 
staged a strike on 17th December 1953 in protest demanding immediate 
reinstatement of the three discharged workmen. A conciliation proceeding 
was started over the matter, which was unsuccessful. The dispute was, 
therefore, referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. The workmen pray 
that Suleman, Naimuddin and Azmere Khan should be reinstated with full j 
compensation for the period of their unemployment, that the working hou vo ' 
should not exceed 48 hours a week, that all workers should get one rest ill 
with pay per week, that the workmen should get gazetted holidays, oi 
month’s yearly leave and 15 days’ medical leave per year and that tl 
workmen should be paid monthly instead of weekly. There is also a pray 
that the Company be directed to take back all the old workers with fu 
com pen sal ion for the period of unemployment. This last prayer is Hi 
covered by the order of reference and shall not be considered. 

The Company, in its written statement, states as follows: — 

The New Commercial Transport had been a concern owned by S. U 
Rashid and one Noor Mohammed. It had a fleet of 6 trucks — 4 owned h 
Rashid and 2 owned by Noor Mohammed. 2 or 3 days before 16t 
December 1953, S. M. Jaipaluddin, a brother of Rashid, who looks after \h 
business, assigned duties to Suleman and Naimuddin, who used to sleep i 
the shed attached to the garage. These two persons refused to go out, In 
as the job was emergent, Jamaluddin insisted on their taking out the truck 
on this an altercation followed in which Naimuddin and Suleman filth '1 
abused Jamaluddin. S. M. Rashid came at about 9 a.m. and heard of th 
incident. Rasliid induced them to go out for the work, but the work 
lost for the delay in execution. On 16th December 1953 at 12 noon, Rashi< 
asked the two drivers Suleman and Naimuddin and the cooly Azmere Kh;u 
to go out with the trucks to carry earth. The three persons became furiou 
and refused to go out but added that they were the leaders and would go nci 
when they liked, and that if they were forced to go, they would destroy thi 
concern altogether and teach a lesson to the proprietors. On this, S. Af 
Rashid dismissed them summarily for insubordination and insolence. Oi: 
the following day, i.e., 17th December 1953, all the drivers and coolies 
on strike. The effect of the strike was that all the transport contracts madf 
by the Company were lost. On this Noor Mohammed, who had been ;i 
partner supplying two tmcks, broke away from the partnership and took 
away the trucks, two in number. The partnership having dissolved, Rn.slm] 
was left with four tmcks, out of which one had been condemned for licemc 
and the other was immobilised by damage. Since the strike, all the dri\ei.« 
and coolies along with other men were creating great noise near the gan*. 

One of the lessors of the yard got his lease cancelled, took possession of ilie

Azmere Khan, attacked the garage of the firm as also another adjacent

Naimuddin was dismissed on 24th October 1953 for impertinence and

The issue framed for the decision of this case are the same as those men- 
tioned in the order of referenre and are as follows: — 


ISSUES. 

(1) Reinstatement of the following discharged workers: — 

Suleman Khan, Naimuddin and Azmeri Khan. 

(2) Fixation of working hours. 

(3) Weekly rest. 

(4) Leave and holidyas. 

(5) Monthly pay system. 

AWARD 

DECISIONS. 

Issue No. 1. 

The New Commercial Transport carries on the business of letting out 
rucks for carrying goods. It had six trucks in commission. The concern 
van owned by S. M. Rashid and one Noor Mohammad. Four of the truck* 
MMe owned by Rashid and two by Noor Mohammad. There were (i driver* 
mil 12 coolies in the employment of the Company. Of the three dismissed 
miployees, Suleman and Naimuddin were drivers and Azmere Khan was a 
•only The Union’s case is that they were dismissed in retaliation of theii 
[rude union activities. The Company’s ease on .the other hand is that they 
kerc dismissed for insubordination. Evidence was adduced on both sides in 
iupport of their cases. P.W. 1 Naimuddin was examined l>v the Union. 
p.P.W. 1 S. M. Jamaluddin and O.P.W. 2 S. M. Rashid were examined 
[or the Company. Documents Exts. 1 and 2 were marked for the Union and 
fcxts. A to D were marked for the Company. S. M. Jamaluddin is the 




50 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 6, 1955 [Part I 


younger brother of S. M. Rashid and according to both the parties, he need 
to look after the business as a supervisor. 

The Union’s case is that the workmen joined tho Motor Transport 
Workers’ Union in April 1953 and the Union submitted a charter of demands 
to the Company on 26th October 1963. A copy of this charter of demands 
appears as Annexure A to the Union’s written statement. On 2nd November 
1953 the workmen placed identical denmuds before the Management by a 
letter, copy of which appears as Annexure B to the Union’s written state- 
ment. The Union’s case is that as a counterblast to these demands, the 
workmen mentioned in Issue No. 1, t.e*, driver Suleman and Naimuddin and 
cooly Azmere Khan were suddenly discharged by the Company and all these 
three persons were Union leaders. The workmen stated a strike on 17th 
December 1953 in protest of the Company’s action demanding immediate 
reinstatement of the dismissed workers. The matter was taken to the Labour 
Commissioner and conciliation proceedings were started, which were un- 
successful and the dispute was referred to the Tribunal. The Company’i 
case, as has been mentioned above, is that two or three days before lutl 
December 1953, S. M. Jamaluddin assigned duties to Suleman nnc 
Naimuddin, as there was some urgent works. These workers refused to g( 
out and on this, an altercation followed in which Naimuddin and Sulemai 
abused Jamaluddin in a filthy language. On 16th December 1953 S. M 
Itashid asked the two drivers, Suleman and Naimuddin and the cobly Azmer 
Khan to go out with trucks to carry earth. They refused to go out, became 
insolent and stated that they wpuld go to work when they liked and held oui 
the treat that if they were forced to go out, they would destroy the concerr 
altogether and teach a lesson to the proprietors. On this, S. M. Rashid 
dismissed them summarily for insubordination and insolence. On and from 
17th December, all the drivers and coolies went on strike. The transport 
business of the Company was closed. On 18th January 1954. the ex- 
employees of the firm including Suleman and Azmeri Khan attacked the 
garage of the firm as also another adjacent garage and caused injuries to the 
properties and person of S. Ml Rashid and Sheikh Ibrahim, a driver. The 
police arrived and arrested 11 persons on the spot, including Suleman and 
Azmeri Khan, against whom cases under various sections of the l.P.C. were

follows by Ludwig Teller in “labour Disputes and Collective Bargaining”, 
Volume i, page 883: — • 

“The right to engage in ’peaceful primary picketing in connection with 
lawful primary stride may now bo considered as having been 
stamped with approval by the greater number of jurisdictions. 
There is almost general agreement that the statement made by 
the New Jersey Court in Bayonne Textile Corporation vs.

not be enjoined if peacefully carried on and for a peaceful

If there is physcial interference with the egress and ingress in connection

» 13J hours.

In view of the decision in Issue No. 1 to the effect that the business of

60 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 6, 1866 [Pabt I 


working day in the public motor transport in the State of West Bengal. 
It shows that the normal hours constituting a normal working day and the 
interval of rest shall be in accordance with the provisions of Section 66 of 
the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, (IV of 1939). This notification also prescribes 
over-time rates of wages for work on any day in excess of the hours consti- 
tuting the normal working day. Section 66 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, 
prescribes the hours of work of the drivers, and it lays down that “no person 
shall cause or allow any person who is employed by him for the purpose 
of driving a transport vehicle or who is subject to his control for such pur- 
pose to work — 

(a) for more than five hours before he has had an interval of rest of at 

least half an hour, or 

(b) for more than nine hours in one day, or 

(c) for more than fifty-four hours in the week.” 

These hours of work were prescribed by the Government of West Bengal by 
the Notification No. 5455Lab., dated 29th August 1951, for the categories of 
employees in the Public Motor Transport for whom minimum wages were 
fixed. Under Rule 89 of the Bengal Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940, the period 
of rest has beeu defined, and it has been stated that “any time spent by the 
driver of a vehicle on or near the vehicle when it is at rest, when he is at 
liberty to leave the vehicle for rest and refreshment although «required to 
remain within sight of the lehicle shall be deemed to be an interval of rest 
for the purpose of clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 65 of the Act.” 
These rules as to working hourfj shall be followed and this issue is accordingly 
answered.

DECISION. 

The parties have not adduced any oral evidence. The Company has, 
however, only filed the audited balance-Bheet for the year 1953 as also state- 
ments showing computation of available surplus, extract from the income- 
tax return filed for the year ending 31st March 1953, depreciation statement, 
etc. 

The Company had paid six ♦lays’ basic wages as Puja bonus in the year 

1952. The Union demands one month's wages as Puja bonus for the year 

1953. The Company resists the claim on the grounds as follow: — 

(a) The payment of bonus has never been a condition of service of 

workers. 

(b) The Company has made very inadequate profits in the past and in 

fact no bonus has ever been granted to the workers except one 
week’s basic wages as Puja bonus in 1952. 

(c) The net profit as per Company’s audited statement of accounts for 

the year ending 31st March 1953 is only Rs. 10,186. The Com- 
pany’s capital as on that date was Rs. 4,80,750. As a proprietory 
concern, the proprietor is entitled to a larger return than laid 
down by the Appellate Tribunal but even allowing 6 per cent, 
return on the capital invested the total amount to which the 
proprietor is entitled will be about Rs. 28,845. The profits of 
the year however are not sufficient to provide for even the 
minimum return to the proprietor on the capital invested by 
him. 

(d) The profits have been so meagre that it has not been possible to pro- 

vide for reserves, for rehabilitation. All the surplus profits have 
been ploughed back for investment in business and there is 
nothing available for distribution as bonus. 

(e) Income-tax for the years 1951-52 and 1952-53 has not yet been 

assessed by the Income-tax Authorities. As the surplus profits 
have been ploughed back in the business and no separate provi- 
sion has been made foT Income-tax Reserve, payment ol 
additional income-tax for the aforesaid years will mean an addi- 
tional financial burdgn on the Company, 

(f) The Proprietor of the concern has not only invested his life savings 

in the business but also his skill and energy. He is the Engineer 
of the Company but has never charged any remuneration except- 
ing a moderate withdrawal every year towards meeting his 
expenses. These drawings are far below than the minimum 
return on capital to which he is entitled.

The Union claimed Puja bonus for 1953 stating among others that the

the Durga Puja Festival. The workers appealed to the management for 
payment of this bonus when the management suddenly closed the factory, 
putting them to involuntary unemployment. They received one month ’e

The company denied its liability to pay any Puja bonus for 1953 stating 
.minng others that it paid its workers bonus in three years only; 1950 to 1952 
and not in any other years. Its financial resources were extremely limited 
and it was facing serious competition for several years. It had no work 
in mi 14th Sept ember to 31st. December 1953 when it was obliged to lay of! 
its workers. Due to the illegal activities of the workers, the company 
suffered losses. It made a nominal profit of Rs. G,500 only. It was not 
e\en sufficient to provide for the minimum return on the capital invested 
|»\ the proprietor. Accordingly, the demand for payment of 2 (two' 
months’ bonus for 1953 should be refused.

Puja bonus for 1963. 


FINDINGS. 

Dr. S. K. Bose appearing on behalf of the Union made it clear that h< 
wa* supporting a demand for Puja bonus for 1953 and not for any othei 
Umu* in that year. He was not asking any bonus to be paid out of tin 
pi oiit s of the company. lie asked for the annual festival bonus. In doinj 
he mainly relied upon the evidence of hif* witness P. W. 1 Shri Karticl 
Kr (Those and the evidence of the Manager of the Company whom In 
‘summed as a witness on his behalf. He also relied upon a letter of th< 
Manager, dated 14th October 1953. in support of his contention that the 
iiiniuiLrenient gave indications of payment of this bonus in course of discus 
Mims ior an amicable settlement of* the dispute. P. W. 1 Shri Ghose sail 




THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 6, 1955 [Part I 


that they demanded this bonus verbally before the factory was closed. He 
admitted having written a letter demanding two months’ Puja bonus (Ext, 
A). This is dated 23rd September 1953 and addressed to the Manager of the 
Company. In this letter he did not mention that he demanded the payment 
of this bonus verbally before the factory was closed. So, the closing of the 
faotory has nothing to do with this demand for payment of this bonus. 
Ext. 1, as I read it, does not contain any assurance whatsoever given by the 
management for payment of this bonus. It only suggested that instead of 
resorting to illegal activities, namoly, picketing at the gate, etc., the 
workers should be advised to put up their demands through the Labour 
Commissioner in the prescribed constitutional manner. This mean, read 
in the context of the letter in which it is used, does not give any assurance 
to the workers regarding payment of bonus. Shri Ghosh said that the 
workers .received Puja bonus for six or seven years at the rate of two to three 
weeks in the beginning and one to two months before it was stopped, 
although he admitted at the same breath that in the written statement the 
payment of three years’ bonus only was mentioned. This, in view of the 
denial given bv the company, proves the company’s case that the bonuB was 
paid only in the three years mentioned in the written statement and in no 
other years in the past. The leading case on the subject of- Puja bonus is 
“Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills, Ltd.,” decided by their lordships of the Ilon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal and reported in 1952, L.A.C., page 370. 

It is not the Union’s case tjjat there is an agreement for payment of this 
bonus. Question is whether on the facts established in this case any such 
agreement can l>e implied. The payment as the evidence shows was made 
only in three years in which the company made profits and that not at an 
uniform rate. This payment, therefore, cunnot be said to be for u sufficiently 
long period. The company according to the evidence of the Manager has 
been facing a crisis gradually due to competition in the market. At first 
it was a pioneer organisation in the country. Now it has got very strong 
rivals in the field. The competition is keenly felt since 1952. In 1949, 
a retrenchment of 50 per cent, of the workers was made. The position 
improved a bit since next year but worsened since 1952. In 1953, the 
position was the worst. The workers were laid off for over three months 
and the company suffered in many ways. It made a nominal profit but then 
it was not adequate for payment of any bonus to the workers. It hardly 
leaves any balance after meeting the prior charges including making provi- 
sion for a fair return for the proprietor’s capital invested in the business. 
The company filed its audited oalance-sheet for the year 1953 and calcula- 
tions in accordance wiih the Full Bench Formula (vide Ext. B series). 
The chart shows that according to the formula, practically an equal amount 
of net profits is the deficit balance. There is no available surplus profits for 
payment of any bonus. Unfortunately, the Union did not place any sufficient 
material before this Tribunal to justify its claim for Puja bonus for 1953. 
The evidence that it adduced proves just the contrary. Considering the 
facts and the circumstances, the Tribunal is of opinion that the workers are 
not entitled to any Puja bonus for 1953. The issue is answered accordingly. 
This is my award.

DECISION. 

The parties have adduced no evidence. They rely on the annezures to 
their respective written statements as also on different awards. 

The Indian Galvanizing Co. (1926), Ltd. (hereinafter called the Com- 
pany), is an engineering concern. This Company as also the British India 
Electric Construction Co., Ltd. and Bridge & Roof Co. (India), Ltd., are 
under the Managing Agency of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co., Ltd. The 
head offices of these throe Companies are located in Calcutta and in the Bame 
building in which the offices of its Managing Agents are located. The 
factory of the Company and the office connected with the factory are situated 
at ll/Goho Road, Ghusury, Howrah. The Managing Agents have the power 
of appointing staff of the Companies and fixing their remunerations under 
article 88 of the Articles of Association. 1 

The dispute relates to the clerical Btaff attached to the Baid factory at 
11, Goho Road, Ghusury, Howrah, and to none else. The dispute arose out 
of the facts as below which are admitted between the parties. ' 

Prior to 1947, the Company had no fixed scales of wages for their 
employees. On 14th January 1947 the Managing Agents of the Company 
introduced grades and scales of wages for the clerical staff employed both at 
the head office and at the factory as below: — 

Grade 1 — Rs. 60 — 3 — 90. 

Grade II — Rs. 70 — 5 — 120. 

Grade III — Rs. 100 — 7 A — 145. 

Grade IV— Its. 150—10—200. 

Grade V— Rs. 200—10—240. 

Grade YI— Rs. 250 and upwards. 

Prior to February 1947, the Company was paying dearness allowance at 
the rate of Rb. 20 over and above some food concessions &b dearness allowance. 
In February 1947, the Managing Agents introduced a scheme of dearness 
allowance linked to the middle class cost of living index on the lines of the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme for the clerical staff of the Company 
both at the head office and at the factory at 11, Goho Road, Ghusury, 
Howrah. Under the said scheme, dearness allowance was to he paid wholly 
in cash based on the Bengal Chamber of Commerce middle class cost of living 
index as published from rime to time from March 1947. An extract from 
that scheme was given to the workmen showing the amount that would. be 
payable when the cost of livftig index (arranged in groups of ten points) 
varied from 221 to 300. From that time on the Managing Agents issued 
monthly circulars notifying changes in the cost of living index figure as 
they occurred from time to time and fixing dearness allowance payable to 
the clerical staff of each grade and a flat rate for the subordinate staff 
according to the scheme already put into force.

After giving careful consideration to the matter, I think the contentic 
of the Union should prevail. Normally a scheme once fixed should contini 
unless some substantial change intervenes. In the present case no chanf

factor of competitive market as pleaded by the Company was there whi 
the Company deliberately gave the Bengal Chaml>er of Commerce scale 
dearness allowance as a condition of service to the employees. So there 
nothing new about it. The Company did not either plead incapacity 
pay. On the contrarv, it appears that notwithstanding introduction of 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme o* dearness allowance about 8 yen 
ago, its financial position has not deteriorated. Then again out of t 
Engineering concerns this Company is not unique in paving dearm 
allowance according to the Bengal Cham her of Commerce scheme but 
appears that Messrs. Burn & Co., Ltd., 20, Nityadhan Muklierjee Roa 
Howrah, has been pacing according to the said scale (vide award publish* 
in the Calcutta Gazette % dated 12th July 1950). A party to an award h 
no doubt statutory right to terminate it in the manner indicated in section 
of the Act, but from this it does not follow that a change is warranted. T 
party who seeks a change should justify it. The Company could show no 
so to justify. In the circumstances, I find nothing to scrap the Benfl 
Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance for the clerks at t 
factory to whom it was protected by the saving in the award of the Fit 
Engineering Tribunal as already referred to. It should, therefore, contin 
wholly. 

This cannot, however, be so held with respect to the clerks at the facto 
appointed subsequent to 3rd July 1948, the date of publication of the awa 
of the First Engineering Tribunal. It haR already been noted that short 
after publication of the award of the First Engineering Tribunal, t 
Company unequivocally expressed its intention to bring the employees 
the I uctnr\ on the same looting as those in other engineering concerns ai 
accordingly re\Ued scales of pay for the clerks employed at the factor 
The Company also fixed for the new employees dearness allowance to 
paid according to the award of the Engineering Tribunal (vide Annexu 
“A” to the Company’* written statement). These clerks, who are said 




Ften I] THE OALOTJT^vGAZETTE, JANUARY 6, 1966 77 

be 10 in number, are being gaid dearness allowance according to the awards 
of the Engineering Tribunal) since their respective appointments (vide 
Annerures “J” series to the Company’s written statement). So to them 
the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale of dearness allowance was never a 
condition of service. They cannot either claim to come within the saving 
of the award of the First Engineering Tribunal. Their case is to be deter- 
mined bv the terms and conditions of their employment as specified in their 
letters of appointment. When they are being paid according to the awards 
of the Engineering Tribunals, it cannot be said that the dearness allowance 
which they have been receiving is not fair and equitable. The Company 
may have capacity to pay but it has been held in the case of Buckingham 
and Carnatic Co., Ltd., that the capacity to pay must be assessed not on 
the unit- wise basis but on industry-cu7/t-region basis, as is the recommenda- 
tion of the Fpir Wages Committee. The dearness allowance which these 
clerks are receiving may be lesser than the one which their compeers 
appointed before 3rd July <1948 are receiving, but this cannot be a ground to 
increase their dearness allowance in line with others when they have been 
appointed on different terms and conditions. Section 18(d) ot the Industrial 
lJisputes Act upon which reliance is placed by the Union for claiming 
benefit of the awards respectively of the First Engineering Tribunal and of 
the Appellate Tribunal, dated 18th October 1952, can liave no application 
to them when they were appointed specifically on different terms and condi- 
tions of service. Only those who were appointed prior to 3rd July 1948 
and who had the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale of dearness allowance 
as condition of service were protected by the saving of the award of the 
First Engineering Tribunal. Those who ‘were appointed subsequent to 3rd 
July 1948 on different terms and conditions, it is obvious, cannot come 
within the saving of the said award. The Hon’hle Appellate Tribunal 
dealt only with the cases of the clerks for whom the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce scheme of dearness allowance was condition of service and gave 
benefit of the same to them only. So to be precise, and to conclude, I find 
that the Company is to continue payment of dearness allowance according 
to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme to the clerks of the factory 
appointed prior to 3rd July 1948 and according to the award of the 
Engineer Tribunal to the clerks of the factory appointed subsequent to 3rd 
J uly 1948. 

As regards the preliminary objection raised by the Union that when the 
Managing Agents have the power to appoint staff and fix their wages and 
other emoluments and they actually did so. termination of the award under 
section 19(6) by the Company was not valid. 1 find no substance in it. The 
Company which is the principal has always such right. 

I award accordingly. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
J. MAITRA,

7295W.T. — 26th December 1954. — In exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage 
Act, 1919 (Bengal Act I of 1919), the Governor is pleased to make the 
following by-laws for the Barruckpore Municipality in the district of 
24-i'arganas, namely: — 


BY-LAWS. 

j Appointment and duties of the Registering Officer.— Every rickshaw 
in the Barruckpore Municipality shall be annually registered by the 
Registering Officer appointed for registering hackney-carriages. 

£. Qualifications of the bearers.— Every person applying for a bearer's 
licence shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer— 

(i) that he knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and is in all 

respects a tit person for such employment; 

(ii) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 

places in and around the town of Barrack pore ; 

( iii) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and 

distances prepared by the Commissioners of the municipality; 

(iv) that he knows the rules of the road and siguals used by the bearers 

and drivers of vehicles and by the traffic police; 

(v) that he is not less than 18 years of age. 

8. Contents Of license.— There shall be attached to each license, issued 
to a rickshaw bearer — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 

(b) a photograph of the bearer, to bt supplied by him; and 

(c) a printed table of fares and distances prepared by the Commis- 

sioners, for which no charge shall be paid by the bearer. 


4. Production Of licenses, — Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carry with 
him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so by the traffic 

S >lice, any Commissioner or other person authorised by the Commissioners. 

e ahull exhibit the table of fares and distances on a prominent part of the 
vehicle. 


5. Prohibition Of smoking, etc.— No bearer shall smoke while driving 
nor shall he muffle up his face .and head in "such a manner as to endanger 
the proper driving of his vehicle. 

. 6. Condition Of the riokshaufs.— (a) The body of the rickshaw shall be 
sound and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. 



(b> The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by properly 
plash boards. ^ 

The spring and axles shall be of good metal, strong and properly 
and free from rust. # 

tit The iron supports at the hgpk shall he properly curved and securely m 
m it each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

ft; The hood, apron and cushion shull be made of and covered with 
good < loth, canvas or other materials approved by the Commissioners at a 
meetup. 


The staffs shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and furnished 
at the ? ore-ends with a ring-shaj>ed metal support and connected by a 
COUiah r» guard . 4 

) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water* 

Every rickshaw shall «have two good lamps, one facing the front 
• in the rear. 

Each lamp shall have a fed glass window in the back and shall be so 
that the light from the window is risible from a point ten yards 
rear of the centre of the vehicle. 

Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the across bars or handle 
the cycle and it shall fee so constructed that if on be operated by

act of victimisation and is, therefore, liable to be set aside.

a slow worker, that the Company repeatedly asked him to improve the

1. By order No. 1216Dis. /D/9L-6(A)/64, dated the 2lth Kerch 1954,tbe 

Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under Jeo- 
tion 10 of the IndustrialDiaputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute hnlirsen 
Messrs. Goenka & Co., 5, Clive Bow, Calcutta and their worker. Shri Sushil 
Kumar Das Gupta, 7, Raj Chandra Sen Lane, post office r Amherst Street, 
Calcutta-9, represented by himself regarding the matters specified in the 
schedule, to the Third Industrial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 592Dis./D/12L-6/62, dated 
the 23rd February 1953, for adjudication. ' 

2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed ifcetfr 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on I5th March 1964, The 
parties were thereafter directed to file their list of documents. 

3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of refer- 
ence are as follows: — 

(1) Is the dismissal of Shri Sushil Kumar Das Gupta justified f 

What relief, if any, he is entitled toP 

(2) Is any sum payable to him on account of earned wages, Provides! 

Fund money, and leave payP * 

DECISION. * 

The parties have filed a joint petition of compromise on 18th December 
1954 and prayed for an award in terms thereof. The workman Shri Sushil 
Kumar Das Gupta, has been paid his dues in terms of the settlement in full 
and final settlement of all his claims. The terms of settlement are accordingly 
given effect to, and in terms thereof I make my award. The petition of 
compromise is made part of my award. 

Dictated and corrected by me.

No. 104F./F/1S-62/54. — 11th January 1955.— 
In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso 
to article 309 of the Constitution of India, read 
with article 372 of the said Constitution and para- 
graph 19 of the Adaptation of Laws Ofder, 1950, 
the Governor is pleased to make the following 
amendment in the rules regulating the conditions r 
of service of members of the State and Subordinate 
services and of officers holding specialist posts 
(unless there is anything to the contrary in the 
contract of any officer) in respect of applications 
for private employment aud the transfer of services 
to other departments of this Government or to any 
other Government, published with the Home 
(Appointment) Department notification No. 3764A., 
dated 7th September 1942, namely: — 


Amendment. 

For rule 3 of the said rules, substitute the follow- 
ing rule: — 

“ Bar to candidature for direct appointment in 
rases of eligibility fur promotion . — 3. A 
Government servant having a lieu or a 
conditional lien on a permanent post, who 
is eligible for appointment by promotion 
to an> other service or post shall not, 
unless otherwise provided in the recruit- 
ment rules relating to such other service 
or post, be eligible for appointment by 
direct recruitment thereto except where 
he obtains, under rule 5, the previous 
permission of the State Government to 
appear at a competitive examination for 
such direct recruitment. M

powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution of Imli.i, 
the Governor is pleased to make the following rules regulating the condi- 
tions of medical attendance and treatment of injuries of all Governim nt 
servants other than those to whom the Secretary of State’s Services (Medical 
Attendance) Rules, 1938, or the Central Services (Medical Attendance) Rules, 
1944, apply : — 


Rules. 

1. These rules may he called the West Bengal Services (Medical 
Attendance and Treatment ot Injury) Rules, 1954. 

2. in these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 
context, —

/ (l \ “fjcatinent ’ means the use of all medical and surgical facilities 
V available at the State hospital in which a Government servant is

(ii) the supply of such medicines, vaccines, sera or other therapeutic

(iii) the supply of such medicines, vaccines, sera or other therapeutic 

substances not ordinarily so available as the authorised medical 
attendant may cert if \ in * riling to be essential for the recovery, 
or tor the prevention o! serious deterioration m the condition of 
the Government servant; • 

(iv) providing such accommodation as is ordinal ily provided in the

the hospital being regarded as suitable for inferior Government 
servants) ; 

(v) such nursing as is ordinarily provided to in-patients by the 

hospital to which a Government servant is admitted; 

(vi) such special nursing as the authorised medical attendant, with 

the approval of the Director oi Health Services, West .Bengal, 
nun certify in writing to be essential lor the recovery or tor the

but does not include diet, or provision at the request ot the 
Government servant of accommodation superior to that des- 
cribed in sub-clause (iv); 

(d) “Government” unless specifically otherwise stated means the 
Government ol West Bengal ; 


(c) “Government servant' * means all persons in the employ oi the Gov- 
ernment of West Bengal excepting those to whom the Secretary 
of State’s Services (Medical Attendance) Rules, 19*18, or the 
Central Services (Medical Attendance) Rules. 1944, apply.

4. Subject to the conditions and in the manner provided in these rules 
a Government servant involved in an accident, whether within or without

entitled to treatment in the neurest available hospital which can, m il„.

Provided that other factors remaining euual a State hospital shall hr 
preferred in the matter of the treatment of the Government servant. 

5. In case a Government servant is involved in an accident outside i| K , 
State of West Bengal and no suitable accommodation is available foi linn in 
a hospital, the Government servant may receive treatment, at his residence iu 
at the chamber of tbe authorised medical attendant. 


6. If the authorised medical attendant is of opinion that owing to tin* 
absence or remoteness of suitable hospital accommodation or to the severity ot 
the illness a Government servant cannot be given treatment in a hospital as 
provided in rule 4, the Government servant may receive treatment at his 
residence or at the chamber of the authorised medical attendant. 


7. (a) The cost of treatment shall be borne by Government up to a 

limit of two-thirds of the total cost, the balance being borne by the Govern- 
ment servant. Where a Government, servant is entitled under rules fi and 
(i to treatment at his residence or at the chamber of the authorised medical 
attendant, any amount puid by him on account of such tieutmcnt shall he 
re-imbursed to him to the extent of two-thirds of the total cost which would 
have been incurred had he been treated in a suitable State hospital. 

(b) No fee shall be charged by a medical officer under the employment 
of the Government for services rendered under these rules. 


S. All claims for re-imbursement of the cost incurred by a Govern- 
ment servant on account of his treatment in a hospital or at his residence 
or at the chamber of the authorised medical attendant and admissible under 
sub-rule (a) of rule 7 shall be accompanied by a certificate in wrifiug by 
the authorised medical attendant, stating— 

(a) it the Government servant is treated in a hospital— 

(i) the total cost incurred by the Government servant on account 
of the treatment with necessary details, 

tii) the cost admissible under the rules, or 


(b) if the Government sen-ant receives treatment at his residence or at 
the chamber of the authorised medical attendant— 

(i) the total cost of the treatment excluding the fees paid to private 

medical practitioners, if any, which should he shown 
separately, 

(ii) the reason for his opinion referred to in rule G, 

(iii) tlie cost thut would have been incurred had the Government 

servant been treated in a suitable State hospital, 

(iv) the cost admissible under the rules.

(d) A “Probationer” is a workman who is provisionally employed to

(e) A “Badli” is a workman who is appointed in the post ot a

which is of an essentially temporary character, or who is 
engaged temporarily as an additional workman in connection 
with work of a permanent character; provided he has not 
been in continuous employment for more than six months. 

tg) A “Casual” workman is a workman whose employment is of a 
casual nature. 

(li) An ‘‘Apprentice” is a learner who may or may not he paid an 
allowance during the period of his training. The period of 
unpaid apprenticeship will not exceed six months. 

d. Scrricr records and tickets. — (a) The establishment shall

it, or surrender it to any body authorised by the Manager, 
on his behalf. 

(e) Loss of t lie departmental ticket shall immediately he notified to 
the Manager. A duplicate shall be issued on payment oi a

If aa a result of discontinuance of shift working, any 
permanent or probationer or apprentice workmen are to be 
discharged, they shall be discharged having regard to the

establishment, those with the longest term of service being 
re-employed first. 


8 Attendance and late, coming— All workmen shall be at work at 
the establishment at the time fixed and notified under 
paragraph 4 of these Orders. W orkmen attending late will 
be liable to the deduction provided for in the Payment of 
Wages Act, 193(i. No workman will be allowed access inside 
the Workshop after the expiry of half an hour from the 
scheduled time for starting work, except, in the cases where 
the Manager allows it. A period of five minutes may be 
allowed as Grace Period for attendance, subject to a maximum 
of 1ft (fifteen) minutes per week. Any workman who after 
checking in is found to be absent from his proper place of 
work during working hours without permission or without 
sufficient reason, shall be liable to be treated as absent without 
leave. 


<). Lease ami holidays.— Leave.— (1) Holidays with pay will be 
allowed as provided for the Factories Act (Amended), 1948, 
and other holidays in accordance with law, contract, custom 
and usage. 

Other holidays, for example, Festival Holidays will be allowed in 
accordance with law, contract, custom and usage. The list 
of festival holidays should be published at the beginning of 
each year, after consultation with the workmen concerned. 

(2) A workman who desires to obtain leave of absence shall apply to 
the Manager, who shall issue orders on the application within 
a week of its submission or two days’ prior to the commence- 
ment of the leave applied for, whichever is earlier, provided 
that if the leave applied for is to commence on the date of 
application, or within three days thereof, the orders shall be 
given on the same day. If the leave asked for is granted, a 
leave pass shall be issued to the worker. If the leave ia 
refused or postponed, the fact of such refusal or postponement 
and the reasons thereof shall be recorded in writing in a 
register maintained for the purjiose, and if the worker so 
desires, a copy of the entry in the register shall be supplied 
to him. If the workman after proceeding on leave desires an 
extension thereof he shall apply to the Manager who shall 
send u written reply either granting or refusing the extension 
of lesiye to the workman if his address is available and if such 
reply is likely to reach him before the expiry of the leave 
originally granted to him.

(3) If the workman remains absent beyond the period of leave 

originally granted or subsequently extended, he ahull lose his 
lien on his appointment unless (a) he returns withiu 8 duvB 
of the expiry of the leave and (b) explains to the satisfaction 
of the Manager his inability to return home before the expiry 
of his leave. In case the workman loses the lien on ),u 
appointment, he shall be entitled to lie kept on the “hadli” 
list. 

(4) A workman may be granted casual leave of absence with or 

without pay, not exceeding 10 days in the aggregate m a 
calendar year. Such leave shall nol bo for more than three 
days at a time, except in the case of sickness. Ordinarily the 
previous permission of the head of the department in the 
establishment, shall be obtained before such leave is taken; 
lmt when this is not possible, the head of the department 
shall, as soon as may be practicable, lie inhumed in writing 
of the absence from duty and tlie probable duration of such 
absence. 

10. lt&quircmcnts for entering premises by certain gates and 
liability to search . — All workmen shall* enter or leave the 
factory premises by the gate or gates specified for this 
purpose. During working hours the Factory Gates may be 
closed at the discretion of the Manager. The workmen shall 
not be permitted to leave the Factory premises during working 
hours without the special permission of the Manage] . The 
workmen are liable to be searched at the time of entering and 
leaving the Factory, and at other time whilst on duty hy any 
person authorised by the Company, provided that, * such 
searches shall be conduct ed in the presence of witnesses, 
where practicable. No female worker shall be searched except 
by a woman, and where practicable, in the presence of another 
woman. 


11. Payment of wages and avert ime. — (1) Any wages due to the 
workman but not paid on the usual pay day on account of 
their being unclaimed, shall be paid by the employer on an 
unclaimed wage pay day in each week, which shall be 
notified on the notice .boards. 

If tlie workman is unable to present himself the employer shall send 
his pay by Money Order at his cost, if requested by him to 
do so. 

(2) AVages due shall be paid daily, weekly or monthly in 
accordance with the provisions of the Payment of AVages Act, 

vm. 

(*\) Wages for overtime shall be regulated in accordance with flic 
provisions of the Factories Act, 1948, where the employee 
concerned is governed by the said Act. Tn other eases the 
overtime wages shall be admissible at the rate of JA times the 
normal wages. 


12. Slapwq e of w**.-(l) The employer may. at any time, in the 
even! of fire, catastrophe, breakdown ol machinery or 
stoppage of power supply, epidemics, civil commotion or 
. other cause beyond his control, stop any section or sections of 
the establishment, wholly or partially for any period or 
periods withoul notice.

(b) A workman may bo suspended for a period not exceeding four 
days at a time, or dismissed without notice or any compensa-

(e) The following acts and omissions shull be treated as mis- 
conduct : — 


(i) Wilful insubordination or disobedience, whether alone or in 
combination with others, to any lawful or reasonable order 
of a superior, 

(ii) theft, fraud or dishonesty in connection with the employer’s 

business or property, 

(iii) wilful damage to or loss of the employer’s goods or property, 

(iv) talcing, giving, offering or asking for bribes or any illegal 

gratifications whatsoever, 

<\) habitual absence without leave or absence without leave for 
more than ten days, 

\\\) habitual late attendance, 

^ \ i i > habitual breach of any law applicable to the establishment, 


(vm) drunkenness, intoxication, rintoim or disorde?J,\ behaviour 
during working hours at the establishment or any act 
subversive of discipline, 


(ix) habitual negligence or neglect of work, 

{\) frequent repetition of any act or omission for which a fine pay

(xi) striking work or inciting others to strike work in contraven- 
tion of the provisions of any law o?- rule having the force of 
law or of any contract, 


f v xii) engaging in trade within the factory premises without the

(xiii) habitual breach of rules or instructions for the maintenance

(xiv) allowing an unauthorised person to operate his machine, 

(xv) collection of money within the factory premises during

(xx) sleeping in the course of duty, 

(xj&j) participation in slow-down strike or wilful go-slow tactics in

(d) Without prejudice to the foregoing, it shall always be optional 

to the management to impose a fine in accordance with the 
provisions of Payment of Wages Act instead of dismissing. 

(e) No order of dismissal shall be made unless the workman 

concerned is informed in writing of the alleged misconduct * 

and is given an opportunity to explain the circumstances 
alleged against him, and to adduce evidence, if any, in his 
favour. The approval of the Manager of the establishment 
and, where there is no Manager, of the employer, is required 
in every case of dismissal, and when circumstances appear to 
warrant it, the Manager oi the employer may, whether an 
appeal has or has not been preferred, institute independent 
enquiries before dealing with the charges against a workman. 


(0 An order of suspension shall be in writing and may take effect, 
immediately on delivery to the workman. Such order shall 
set out in detail the alleged misconduct and the workman shall 
be given an opportunity of explaining the circumstances 
alleged against him. If on an enquiry tin* order is confirmed, 
the workman shall be deemed to have been absent for the 
period of suspension and shall not be entitled to any 
remuneration for the period. If, however, the order is 
rescinded, the workman shall be deemed to have been on duty 
during the period of suspension and shall be entitled to the 
same wages as he would have received if he had not been 
suspended. 

(g) In awarding punishment under this Standing Order, the 
manager Bhall take into account the gravity of the mis- 
conduct, the previous record, if any, of the workman and any 
other extenuating or aggravating circumstances that may 
exifit. A copy of the order passed by the Manager shall be 
supplied to the workman concerned. 

15. Complaints .— All complaints # arising out of employment 

including those relating to unfair treatment or wrongful 
exaction on the part of the employer or his agent, shall be 
submitted to the Manager or other person specified in this 
behalf with the right of appeal to the employer.

of opinion, as the result oi an enquiry held into

(Registered No. 39/ Cal. of 1948), in the district 
of Calcutta, under sub-section (1) of section 84 oi 
the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940, that 
the Society ought to be wound up.

ferred by sub-section (1) of section 89 of flic

DECISION. 

Issue No. 1. 

In support of his case Shri Mihir Kumar Bhattaeharjee had deposed 
before this Tribunal besides proving the correspondences between him 
and the Company and the Labour Directorate [Exts. 1, 1(a), 2 to 2(g)]. 
The Company, on the other hand, has examined its Accountant, D.W. 1, 
Shri Narayan Chandra Das, who is the Secretary of the Union since 27th 
March 1954; its Head Accountant, D.W. 2, Shri P. C. Banerjee, who is 
the President of the Union, and its Agent, D.W. 3, Sliri J. N. Mogm 
besides proving documents, Exts. PI, F2, G, H, HI, I, J and J 1. 

Before entering into the controversies, it is better to state the facts as 
are either admitted or established in evidence as this will be of help to 
appreciate the evidence. 

Messrs. Goenka & Co., was primarily dealing in tea. It was Managing 
Agents of (1) Atal Tea Co. (1943), Ltd. (Atal Tea Estate at Teraib 

(2) Singtom Tea Co. (1946), Ltd. (Singtom Tea Estate at Kurseong/ 

(3) Pandam Tea Co., Ltd. (Pandam Tea Estate at Darjeeling), (4) Bloom- 
field Tea Co., Ltd. (Bloomfield Tea Estate at Darjeeling) and Secretaries 
>f Monteviot Tea Estate at Kurseong. Shri N. C. Goenka was the sole 
proprietor of Messrs. Goenka & Co. He died on 4th April 1950, leaving 
vidow Sm. llama Sundari Devi. On his death the management came in 
he hands of Shri It. N. Agarwalla, one of the Directors of all the concerns 
mder Goenka’s management. He did the management for some time. 
Thereafter the present management, Shri Gyaniamm and Dlianoolali 
hirimar, on the basis of Power of Attorney from the widow' of late 
V. C. Goenka, took over the management from latter part ot September 
951. 

At Darjeeling the Company had an office. The said office was truns- 
erred to Calcutta and amalgamated w'ith the Calcutta office in September, 
951. The three witnesses (D. W. 1 to D. W. 3) examined on the side of 
he Company as also Shri B. K. Mitra were employees of the Company at 
)arjeeling. When the Darjeeling office was removed to Calcutta, they 
rere posted to Calcutta in September 1951. They have beeu serving in 
aieutta ever since. 

Sliri B. K. Mitra was a superintendent (below the rank of an officer) 
t Darjeeling. About 1A months after transfer of the Darjeeling office and 
u suspension of the operation of the Provident Fund, Goenka & Company 
lead Office Staff Union wms formed with Shri B. K. Mitra as Secretary 
ml D. W. 2, Shri P. C. Banerjee as President. The Union raised various 
isputes with the present management. After unsuccessful conciliation 
ln se were referred by the Government by order, dated 29th July 1952/ to 

0 llic Fourth Industrial Tribunal presided over by Shri S. C. Mukhcrjee 

01 adjudication. During pendency of the dispute betoie the said Tribunal, 
lie Company made an application under section 33 of the Act seeking perniis- 
ioii from the Tribunal to dismiss the Union Secretary, Shri B. K. Mitra, 
in mi nous charges including one of misappropriation of Company’s fund. 
\11 these matters were subsequently amicably settled and Shri S. C. 
Mukhcrjee made an award in terms of the settlement. J I is award was 
mhlished in the Calcutta Gazette on 24th February 1953. Besides coming 
o amicable settlement regarding the issues, the Company stipulated as 
olhw s : — 

“(a) The Company and/or management will not take any action against 
the existing employees which may amount to victimisation under 
the Labour Act.

THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1966 [Pakt :

Now*, let us consider behind this background, whether tlie dismissal of 
^liri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee w’as justified. In the ease of Buckingham 
& Carnatic Co., Ltd., it has been held that the decision of the management 



198 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1965 [Piet I 


with regard to a charge ofi misconduct against an employee will not pre- 
vail, if — 

(i) there is want of bona fides ; or 

{i\) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation of 
the principles of natural justice; or 

(iii) there is a basic error of facts; or 

(h) there has lieen a perverse finding on the materials. 

Though there lias been no want of bona fide*, it appears that the Company 
took action wholly on suspicion in the present case. There is no evidence 
whatever In support, the action of the Management. As to the first charge 
regarding the sealed cover received from Brokers, Carritt Moran & Co., Ltd., 
the workman, Sliri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee stated that he had placed 
the said cover along with other articles which he had received, on the table 
of the then Offiee-in-charge, Shri Maithel as was the practice then. That 
such was the practice at the time is admitted by Shri Maithel in his 
endorsement Ext. 11. It being so, it cannot be said for certain that the 
cover was not mislaid or lost from the table of Shri Maithel. The enquiry 
against Shri S. I\. Das Gupta was being held confidentially and there is 
nothing to show that Shri Mihir Kumar Bkattacharjee was aware of it. 
Then, the cover came in sealed condition and there is nothing io show that 
Shri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee was aware of its contents. There is also 
nothing to show that he was in league with Shri S. K. Das Gupta against 
whom enquiry was then being held confidentially. In the circumstances, 
Sliri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee cannot be made responsible for the loss 
of the said cover. In any case, his evidence that he had in normal course 
of business and practice placed the said cover along with other? on the table 
of Shri Maithel remains lin rebutted. It also appears that from the very 
beginning Shri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee asserted that he had placed 
that letter on the table of Shri Maithel. The management, it also appears, 
was satisfied with his explanation when it allowed the matter to 
rest after explanation was submitted. After having ' done so, 
it was really not proper and fair to revive the same subsequently and to 
make grievance about it as was done while issuing the order of suspension 
on 4th September ]9M. Be that as it may, the first charge cannot, there- 
fore, be said to have any foundation in fact but it rested wholly on suspicion. 

As regards the second charge about not, making report regarding non- 
receipt of tea samples, this was likewise without any foundation. It might 
have been within the duty of Shri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee to receive 
tea samples but from this, it does not follow that it was his duty to make 
report about what he had not been receiving. If he did not receive the 1e;i 
samples, there is nothing to show that he was to make report about them 
to anybody. Then when the tea samples ceased to come altogether since 
September it was not unnatural for him to take it to be normal feature 
Tt appears from the letter of Carritt Moran & Co., Ltd., with enclosures 
(Ext. I) that the present management came to know as early as May 19VI 
about Shri S. K. Das Gupta having been receiving tea samples from the 
said Brokers since September 1951. So, when on 2Sth August 19JVJ the 
management made query about the tea samples from Shri Mihir Kunutr 
Bhattacharjee, it cannot be said to be bona fide query. The second charge 
cannot, therefore, be said to have boon brought home against the workman, 
but it rested on suspicion. 

Requirements of natural justice, it also appears, were not fulfilled. Nh 
intimation was admittedly given to tin- workman regarding date and place 
of enquiry nor was the alleged enquiry held in his presence (vide D.W. '»)■ 


Paut I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1955 


199 


There is no written reoord ol any enquiry. D. W. 3, Shri J. N. Mogra, 
who claims to have held the enquiry, said that he made verbal queries 
from the Manager, Shri R. M. Sarkar, Shri Maithel, Shri P. C. Banerjee, 
President of the union, and Shri B. E. Mitra. But none of them has been 
examined except 1). W. 2, Shri P. C. Banerjlee before this Tribunal. 
There has been contradiction between D. W. 3 and D. W. 2. D.W. 3 said 
that D.W. 2 had personal knowledge regarding the charges while D.W. 2 
said here that he had none. D.W. 2 did not also say that there* was any 
enquiry and that he was examined in it. 1 am, therefore, unable to accept 
that any enquiry was held. 

Then the facts and circumstances of which reference had already been 
made no doubt support the allegation of the workman that the Union Secre- 
tary, Shri B. K. Mitra and the President, Shri P. C. Banerjee were gained 
over by the Company soon after the settlement as embodied in the award 
and that the Union as a result ceased to be the real representative organisa- 
tion of the workers at the relevant time, but nonetheless, it does not appear 
to me that the action taken against Shri M. K. Bhattacharjee was actuated 
for his Union activities. He was admittedly not even a member of the 
executive committee but an ordinary member of the Union. The fact that a 
relation of Shri B. K. Mitra was appointed in place of Shri Mihir Kumar 
Bhattacharjee after dismissal does not improve the case of the workman, 
more so wfien it appears that he too w r as discharged soon after (rule Ext. F). 
It rather appears to me in the context of the charge brought against Shri 
S. K. Das Gupta that Shri Mihir Kumar Bhattacharjee was proceeded with 
merely on suspicion as the important letter which lie had received was 
missing and as he had failed to make report about non-receipt of tea samples 
since September 1951. It has already been seen that the charges have 
not been proved and that the Management proceeded merely on suspicion. 

As the management proceeded merely on suspicion, the dismissal must 
be held to be unjustified although there was no lack of bona fide on the 
pari of the management. If there be reasonable grounds for suspicion, the 
proper course in that case would be to discharge the workman after paying 
him off his legitimate dues. I think, this is a case where the workman 
should have been discharged and not dismissed. I, therefore, do nol direct 
reinstatement of the workman. He should, however, get the following 
reliefs under heads as below: — 

(a) Earned wages . — There can be no dispute that the workman should 

get his salary up to 2nd September 1953. 

(b) Wages in lieu of earned leave io his credit . — The workman claimed 

wages for GO days on this head. The Company filed a petition 
stating that it had no objection if wages for GO days on account 
of earned leave be granted. The workman would, therefore, get 
wages for GO days in lieu of earned leave. 

(e) Pmvidcnt Eund money, including Coni fumy's contribution, if any . — 
As this was not a fit case for dismissal but discharge*, it is obvious 
that the workman is entitled to be paid ll)« Provident lund 
money including Company’s contribution up to the date of 
discharge. 

(d) Puja bonus payable in — I find nothing to resist tin* claim of 

the workman for a proportionate bouiis. The workman is 
accordingly allowed proportionate bonus under this head. 

In addition to these, when the workman did not merit dismissal but dis- 
f, h.iigi. 1 think, he should get. three months’ salary including d«*ainess allow- 
ance art compensation having regard to the length of service lu* put in and

other factors. The Company should make the aforesaid payments Within 
a month from the date the award becomes enforceable.

been made horui fide. The retrenched persons cannot be taken back to 
employment. There has been no unfair labour practice or victimisation of 
any workman. In the circumstances, the claim of the Union should be 
rejected.

FINDINGS. 

Issue No. 1. 

By a notice dated 27tli February 1954 (K\i. ])), Shri Gopal Chandra 
Saha, Managing Director of the Company, closed the factory for an in- 
definite period from 1st March next for slackness of business. The notice 
required the "workers to leave their addresses with the ^ factory supervisor 
or Managing Director for future reference. The Union’s cose is that thh 
jras done all on a sudden and without any justification whatsoever. 27th 
was Saturday. 1st March was Monday. So, practical ly, the work was stopped 
from 1st March next. Admittedly, the factory remains closed till to-day. 
Shri Gopal Saha, the Managing Director, said in his deposition before this 
Tribunal that he was not in a position to carry on the business due to its bad 
financial position and had no intention of carrying on the business in future. 
The Company’s case, however, is that the workers were laid off with effect 
from 1st March due to dearth of work but as it succeeded in securing some 
urgent orders, it immediately recalled the workers through Jamuna Shaw, 
one of its employees, and that the workers attended but refused to resume 
their duties. The Company lost its orders and it decided to close the factor}' 
and discharged its workers on fith March next. Shri Patit Puban Pathak, 
on behalf of the Union, contends that this lockout is wholly unjustified 
and that the workers are entitled to reasonable compensation for the period 
of lockout, that is to say, for a period of five days with effect from 1st March 
last. Gopal Babu has deposed to say that he had no work at his disposal on 
27th February last when he was obliged to lay off the workers. He secured 
some orders on the 28th and at once recalled the workers through Jamuna 
Shaw and also by a notice on the Notice Board. The workers came on the 
3rd but refused to do any work unless all the workers attended and were 
paid the unpaid wages for the absence for the previous period. He also 
said that the financial position of the Company was very bad and he was not 
in a position to carry on the business. The Balance Sheets for the previous 
two years have been submitted (Exts. A1 and A2). They show recurring 
losses of Rs. 3,3394-9 in 1359 B.S. and Rs. 15,068-13-6 in 1360 B.R. .He 
• produced some orders, dated 28th February 1954 (Ext. E series), obtained 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1966 


213 


from some of his customers to show that he had received orders only after 
the notice of laying off the, workers was issued. Against this, Shri Jamuna 
Shaw, an employee in service of this Company, said that the financial posi- 
tion was good and the order position was satisfactory; that the Company 
was , executing orders by getting the work done outside, sometimes doing 
work at night. The Union of course could not produce any better evidence, 
for obvious reasons, to show what the financial position of the Company was 
on the day of the lay off. Neither, it could show definitely or with certainty 
what the order position was at the time when the factory was closed. 
The fact remains that admittedly the work was stopped now and then and 
the workers were, on more than one occasion previous to this, laid off without 
payment. That shows that the company had no work for the full employ- 
ment of the workers and that the workers were not fully employed. There 
is no good reason why Gopal Babu all on a sudden would declare a lockout 
if he had sufficient work at his disposal, to carry on his business. The forma- 
tion of the Union is not a novel phenomenon which can strike terror into 
the hearts of an employer. In fact, Shri Gopal Saha admitted in his evi- 
dence that he had dealt with the Union and came across with its officials 
in the matter of settlement of the dispute over the dismissal of Subodli 
Mukherjee. On a consideration of all these, the Tribunal finds that the lay 
off on 27th February last was justified. 


Question now is whether the workers are entitled to compensation for 
this period of lay off; only for live days as mentioned by Sliri I’ulhak and 
not for any single prolonged indefinite period. In paragraph 2 of the 
Union’s written statement, it said that the Company employed nearly 50 
workmen. The Company denies this. In cross-examination, Sliri huinma 
Shaw, the only witness on the side of the Union, said that about .‘M or ;J5 
men used to work in this factory. He said that besides 28 workers, whose 
cases have been referred to this Tribunal, there were more than five persons 
who were also dismissed by the Company. They are also without any em- 
ployment. Shri Jamuna Shaw, who is the Assistant Secretary of the 
Union, did not move for their reinstatement. No reason has been given 
why he did not do so. It is not reasonable to believe that there* were so many 
men actually in service of the Company at the time when it laid off its 
workers. Be that as it may, the number employed was less than 50 accord- 
ing to the Union’s own evidence. Compensation for lay off is now codified 
in Chapter VA, section 25(C) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Section 25(A) 
says: Section 26(C) to 25(E) inclusive shall not apply — (a) to industrial 
establishments in which less than 50 workers on an average per working day 
have been employed in the preceding calendar month. It seems that under 
the present Act, the question of compensation for lay off arises only in indus- 
trial establishments in which 50 or more workmen are employed. In this 
particular ruse, the provisions of Section 25(C) of the Act do not apply. 
Accordingly, the workers are not entitled to any compensation for any lay 
oft’ for this period. It had been contended by Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate 
lor the Company, that the workers w r erc laid off now and then and that 
without any payment and accordingly, the company was under no obligation 
I to pay anv compensation for this lay off which was justified. As the law 
| stands today, the workers are not entitled to any compensation for lay off 
under section 25(C) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Under proviso of 
section 25(J), the right of a workman under any award in operation or any 
contract with the employer remains unaffected by the provisions of this Act. 
The Union did not claim any compensation for lay off under any such award 
or contract made with the employer. Accordingly, the workmen are not 
entitled to any compensation for this lay off. 




214 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1955 [Paet i 


Issue No. 2. 

28 workers mentioned in the order of reference were not dismissed as ii 
stated in the order hut were discharged. Question now is whether thii 
discharge is justified. The management justifies its action by saying thal 
these workers were recalled to duty, attended but refused to do any worl 
over a demand for payment of bark wages. They were accordingly charge* 
sheeted and discharged on 6th March 1954. It would appear from Ext. D, 
a notice, dated 27 th February lust, that the Company (dosed the factory foi 
indefinite period from 1st March due to slackness of business. The notice 
required all factory hands to leave their addresses either with the super- 
visor or with the Managing Director. The next notice dated, 1st March 
(Ext. Dl) informed all workers that the factory would reopen on the 3rd March 
and everybody was asked to report to duty without fail. Jamuna Shaw also 
informed them. Notice dated 3rd March, says that the workers attended 
but refused to join though asked to do so. They were asked to show reasons 
for that (vide Ext. D2). Ext. D3, dated 4th March, says that the workers 
attended at 8 in the morning but did not join their duties. Accordingly, the 
workers were asked to show cause why they should not be discharged. This 
refers to 36 workers. Ext. D4, dated 5th March, refers to two other workers 
Sumsh Ch. (those and Nagendranath Samantu. They were also asked to 
show cause why they did not joint duty after attending the factory. By 
Ext. 1)5, these 28 workers were discharged for not joining thei# duty. Shri 
Gopal Chandra Saha, the Mg. Director, said that he duly informed all the 
workers through Jamuna Shaw and the workers attended but they refused 
to do any work. He secured some urgent orders on condition of executing 
them by the 5th which lie could not execute due to this intransigent conduct 
of these workers. The orders are mentioned in several letters (Ext. E. 
series), which letters ha\e been challenged as spurious documents by the 
Union. Shri Jamuna Shaw, as already stated above, the only witness on 
the side of the Union, said in his deposition that he was never asked by the 
Managing Director to inform the workers and in fad, he did not inform 
any of them. Neither he was informed regarding the opening of the factory. 
He gives a categorical denial to the company 1 * allegations. He has suffi- 
cientl\ contradicted the evidence of Shri Gopal Saha. The workers were 
laid off for an indefinite period by a notice, dated 27th February with effect, 
from 1st March next. They were asked to leave their addresses with the 
supervisor or the Managing Director which they did. Gopal Balm did not 
inform any of the workers individually by any letter. lie said he posted 
a notice recalling the workers to join on t lie Notice Board and walled up 
another on the outer wall of the factory. He sent intimation individually 
through Jamuna Shaw. AH these have been denied. After a lay off for an 
indefinite period, the workers are likely In leave their place of work; either 
for their nati\e village or elsewhere in search of work. They are not j 
expected to conic and set 1 the notice on the Notice Board. In view of ' 
Jamuna Shaw’s evidence, it cannot be said that the workers were recalled 
to duty and they were under any obligation to conic on 3rd March. Then* h 
no independent evidence in this case to show I hat they all attended and 
refused to do any work. After all, it is an admitted fact that the workers 
did not make any demand verbally for pavment of back wages. It is, there- 
fore not known why they should at all take up an unrealistic attitude in the 
matter. Whv tlrny should attend at all and refuse to do work and earn a 
living? In this 'dale of evidence, the tribunal thinks that the workers were 
not recalled 1o duty and did not attend and refuse to work. Admittedly, 
these workers were not chnrgesheefed individually. It may be that one 
such notice as proved hi this ease by Gopal Halm was put up in the Notice 
Board. But it is not enough There was no enquiry; even the discharge 
order was not communicated to the workers individually. One curious fact 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JAN CART 20, 1955 215 


is that the management knew the existence of the Union and in fact Gopal 
Babu himself had previous occasion to have dealings with the Union officials. 
The management, strangely enough, did not communicate the order laying 
off the workers calling them to duty and discharging them by way of punish- 
ment for failing to do work. In any event, tho discharge cannot be said to 
be justified on the facts and in the circumstances of the case. If it is a dis- 
charge following the closure of the business, nothing can possibly be 
said regarding it. But the management says otherwise. The discharge was 
made by wav of punishment. Since principles of natural justice were 
violated in discharging these workmen, the order of discharge cannot be 
said to be legal ana therefore cannot stand. 

It has been urged by Shri S. C. Sen that the management was obliged 
under compulsion of events following some incidents since the formation of 
the Union to close the business for good. Tho closure is now an established 
and settled fact. The factory is not working since it was closed on 1st March, 
1954. But this is important only in deciding the question of relief. The 
Tribunal thinks that these 28 workmen were discharged without any justi- 
fiable ground. That does not mean that the closure of business is either 
mala fide or not justified. The compnny was running heavy losses in its 
business, at least for two years before the closure and there was reduction 
in the position orders as well. Accordingly, the question of reinstatement 
of these workers does not arise. In both events, viz., whether the discharge 
is justified or not — my finding is that there has not been any discharge on 
valid grounds — the workers are entitled to some relief by way of 
compensation. 

Next question is who are entitled to it and to what amount? The claim 
us it stands is not based on any award in nperntinn or on any contract with 
the employer. It is founded on section 25(F) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Naturally, the question of length and nature of service becomes important, 
lor the said section provides for payment of compensation etc. only to work- 
men who have put m continuous service for not less than one year under 
an employer. The Union relied upon the length of service as given in the 
order of reference against each worker, and did not furnish any independent 
evidence on this point. The only witness on its side Sliri Jarnuna Sliaw, 
Assistant Secretary of the Union, did not say anything on this point. On the 
contrary, Shri Gopal Saha said that this company was registered under the 
Indian Companies Act on 22nd February 1950. lie has prepaved a list show- 
ing the* length of service of the workers concerned in Ext. B, with refeience 
to the Attendance Registers (Exts. I< and FI). Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate 
fur ihe company, challenges the correctness and the propriety of the list 
jin cm in the order of reference. In the written statement, the Company 
availed the correctness of the length ot service given in the order of reference. 

i* rather unusual tor the Government to menliou the length of sen ice of 

li- workers in the order of reference. No such thing came to my nolico 

|»Te\ it hi s to this. The Government, can only mention ihe points of dispute 
h'i adjudication in the order of reference. It is improper to mcrilnm in the 
unler of reference any evidence related to that dispute when it is not agreed 
between the purties. In any case, this unifier lias got to he decided on 

mdeiice on record. As I have already stated above, iIm* Union lias not 

add iif<M 1 any evidence on this point. The Company relies on tin* Altemlanco 
lc* ” leii (Exts. F and FI) and the list prepared irom it (E_\f. J>) The 
1 uuui of course does not admit the accuracy of the list and sa\s thai all 
dn attendance registers have not been filed. There im no rwdenn- J .o sub- 
"huitiaie this contention. The Tribunal, therefore, accepts the li^t (bxt. B)
