not adduced any evidence in this case to show that the service of any of 
these workers was previously terminated. 

Shri S. C. Sen contends that a workman must put in at least one year 
of completed continuous service under an employer m order to qualify him- 
self for retrenchment relief under section 25(F) of the Act. EL© lays 
special emphasis on the first part of Section 25(F) which says: “No work- 
man employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not 
less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer 

until he has been paid compensation which shall be equivalent 

to 15 days* average pay for every completed year of service or any part there- 
of in excess of six months.” He relies on section 25(B) for the definition 
of one year of continuous service mentioned in section 25(C) and 26(F) of 
the Act and also on section 2, sub-section 2(eee) of the Act. Section 25(B) 
says: “For the purpose of section 25(C) and 25(F) a workman who during 
a period of 12 calendar months has actually worked in any industry for not 
less than 240 days shall be deemed to have completed one year of continuous 
service in the industry.” In the explanation it says how in computing the 
number of days, the da>s on which a workman was laid off or on leave with 
full wages, shall lie included. Shri Sen says that according to this defini- 
tion, a workman must have at leusl one continuous year of service to his 
credit to qualify for the relief and he gets 15 days’ average pay for every 
completed and continuous year of service, that is to say, a workman who has 
put in less than 240 days in a year, is not entitled to get any relief at all. 
A workman with such service is entitled to get only 15 days’ average pay 
for every year of such service and no compensation for putting less than 
240 days in a year. 

Shri Pathak does not accept that contention as correct. A workman must 
put in 240 days during a period of 12 calendar months for completing one 
year of continuous service. This of course includes the period of absence 
during lay off and authorised earned leave. He is not entitled to any retrench- 
ment relief under section 25(F) of the Act unless he establishes that in the 
case. But it is not necessary for him to prove that he worked for 240 days 
in each year before he gets any compensation for those years for section 26(F) 
(B) does not say “for every completed continuous year of service”. It only 
says “for every completed year of service or any part thereof in excess of 
six months”. The idea probably is to exclude casual workers from getting 
any compensation on account of retrenchment from service. Accepting this 
interpretation of section 25(F) and taking into consideration the further fact 
that the definition of continuous service includes leave with full ages earned 
in the previous years which means at least 14 days under the Factories 
Act, and the further fact that the company has not shown by evidence that 
the services of any of these men excepting Nos. 22 and 23 were interrupter 
in any way, the Tribunal finds that only 14 out of 28 workers are entitlec 
to retrenchment relief under section 25(F) of the Act. They will get — 

(i) notice pay for one month lor none of them was given any notice of 
discharge ; 

(ii) compensation equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for years noted 
against their names. 

The following are entitled to the above:

of that daft to the Chief Inspector of Factories, Ext. H6. 

Let us now consider whether Company's action in closing the factory on 
17th August 1954 was in effect a lock-out. When the closure was directed 
in consequence of the strike on the pre\ious day and when relationship of 
employer and employee did not admittedly cease between the parties, there 
can be no doubt that it was a lock-out within the meaning of section. 2(1) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act. What amounts to a lock-out was considered by 
the Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of the Presidency Jute 
Mills Co., Ltd. and their workmen reported in 1952, L.A.C., 62. In that 
case it was pointed out “lock-out presupposes the continuance of the relation- 
ship between the employer and the employee. Therefore, (1) anv act of the 
employer which terminates the services of workmen would not amount to 
lock-out; and (2) refusal to give work to workmen would not amount to lock- 
out, unless the said refusal wuh based on grounds connected with some dispute 
between the employer and his workmen.” In the present case none of the 
parties says that relationship of the employer and the employee lwtwoen the 
parties has ceased. Then it has already been seen that the closure was 
directed in consequence of the strike. So, there can Ik* no doubt that this 
was a lock-out. 


> 

i 


The next question which arises for determination is, whether the lock- 
out since 17th August 1954 is justified. In the present case both the* parties 
admit that neither the strike nor the lock-out is hit by sections 22 and 22 of 
the Act and as such none of them is illegal under section 24. A strike or 
lock-out, though not illegal, may be unjustified. Besides, a strike, though 
not illegal under section 24, would be so if i< is a “stay-in-strike”. A stay- 
in-strike is illegal because it contains an element of illegality, namely, 
criminal trespass. Sub-section (2) of section 24 lays down that a lock-out 
declared in consequence of an illegal strike shall not he illegal Jn the 
present case the occasion for the strike cannot be said to be unjustified, but 
the manner in which the strike was effected, made it a stay-in-strike, which 
wns illegal. The evidence show’s that the workmen enlered the factory at 
8 a.m. and continued there till 5 p.m. without doing any work md their 
demand was for immediate payment of the outstanding wages for July 1954- 
The evidence also shows that while so continuing inside the factory, they off 




230 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1966 [Paw 1 


and on passed objectionable remarks against the management while some 
assumed violent attitude. These in effect amounted to a stay-in-strike. 
Mr. Ludwig Teller in his book, "Labour Disputes and Collective Bargain- 
ing' 1 described a stay-in-strike as employees’ unfair laliour practice. It has 
been hold by a Tribunal on the basis of his observations: 44 A workman has 
no rigid to stay in the factory premises during the continuance of the strike. 
The permit of entry and to stay is for the employee to work. When that 
intention is absent/ and the relationship of the employer and the employee 
remains in a slate of suspended animation, the working man haB no right to 
?tav there.” Stay-in-strike has in it an element of trespass. It is accord- 
ingly illegal. So the lock-out which has been declared in consequence of 
the illegal strike would not be illegal in view of 9 ub-section (3) of section 24. 
Apart from this, the evidence shows that on l?ih August 1954 the workmen 
coming to duly demanded both wages and work together and were not will- 
ing to do work without immediate payment of wages. In the circumstances 
when the demands for work and wages were inseparable and when the Com- 
pany was not in a position <o meet the demand for payment of wages forth- 
with, it win inevitable on their part to declare lock-out as it did. There is 
nothing to show that the workmen subsequently expressed their willingness 
to resume duty without immediate payment of wages. In the circums- 
tances, when the demand for work and wages went together and there was 
no deviation from that position subsequently, I am of opinion that the lock- 
out since 17th August 1954 is justified. In the circumstances, it follows 
that the workmen are not entitled to wages for the period of lock-out. 1 
award accordingly.

AWARD. 

Messrs. Grant Advertising Incorporated, Calcutta, proposed to retrench 
32 (thirty-two) employees as per list given in the schedule to the order of 
reference and the issue is “whether the proposed retrenchment is justified”. 
The second issue is “what relief are they entitled* * P. Obviously if the 
retrenchment materialises, the second issue, viz., the question of relief would 
become relevant, otherwise not. 

The contention of the workers is that they were previously workmen of 
Messrs. Imperial Tobacco Company in its publicity department and that in 
course of time the said publicity department was transformed into Messrs. 
General Advertising Agency (India), Ltd., and the employees were also 
transferred to that concern and that Provident Fund also was similarly 
transferred without any break up. Subsequently the General Advertising 
Agency (India), Limited, ceased to function the publicity business and that 
business was taken up by Grant Advertising Incorporated and the Provident 
Fund was transferred to the new concern, viz., Grant Advertising Incor- 
porated. 

The workers further contend that Grant Advertising Incorporated “is 
sow on sound financial footing and the results of the first months of the year 
diow that trading position is satisfactory”. With regard to the question of 
relief the workers contend “the Company has no jurisdiction or right to ter- 
minate the nervines of persons who were originally appointed bv Messrs. 
Imperial Tobacco Company and by General Advertising Agency (India), 
Limited. Presumably the service having been lent, the security of their 
services ought to have been maintained by sending them back to their parent 
firm”. In this state of things the Grant Advertising Incorporated made an 
ipplication on the 2'lrd September 1 9o4 , stating the hope “that there will bo 
i substantial improvement in the company's trading position within the next 
,ix months, the Company (management) has decided not to implement the 
■imposed retrenchment of thirty-two persons mentioned in the list attached to 
:bc order of reference” and the Company prays that a “no dispute” award 
may be passed by the Tribunal and the Company also states that a notice, 
copy of which is attached to the application of date 22nd November 1954, 
marked Annexure “A” was affixed on the Notice Board on the 2<‘trd Septem- 
ber 1954. The workers however want to have an adjudication of the dispute 
as given ill the reference and their contention is that they should he given 
idiot by way of transfer back to Messrs. Imperial Tobacco Limited, irres- 
pective of the question whether the first, part of the dispute, viz., “whether 
the proposed retrenchment is justified is decided or not”. I think that would 
be simply, putting the cart before the horse. When the Company which 
proposed to retrench these workers and for which the dispute arose, wants 
to abandon the retrenchment, I do not. think the workers have any right to 
1 insist, that they should be retrenched and then by way of relief they should 
transferred back to Messrs. Imperial Tobacco Co., Limited. If they 
iave any such idea in their mind to go back to Imperiul Tobacco Company 
Limited, they are quite free to raise a fresh dispute over it so that the 
internment, if it thinks it expedient, may refer such dispute to the Indus- 
trial Tribunal, but in the present case the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
give award with regard to the relief although the proposed retrenchment 
has been given up by the employer, i.c., although the cause of action for 
which relief was relevant has ceased to exist. It may Ik* that Imperial 
Tobacco Co. (Limited) took counsel with Messrs. Grant Advertising In- 
corporated and as a result thereof the proposed retrenchment which might 
urea to complication involving Messrs. Imperial Tobacco Company Limited 
financially, has been finally given up. It is the Grant Advertising In- 
corporated which made the proposal to retrench the workmen and it is the 



284 


TI1E CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1866 [Paw I 


said employer which subsequently abandoned the said proposal, therefore the 
logical conclusion is that at present there is no dispute at all whicls can be 
adjudicated by the Tribunal. The representation made by the Company 
that, it ha h given up retrenchment idea is accepted and I also find thatthe 
Company has given effect to it by giving notice Ext. A. Therefore a "no 
dispute’* is hereby passed. The Annexure A of the Company is marked 
Appendix A to the Award. 

MOTILAL CHAKRA VATTI, District Judge,

In the hope that there ^ ill be a substantia] improvement in the Company's 
trading position within the next six months, the management has decided 
not to implement the proposed retrenchment of thirty-two persons. 

The necessity for hard work and rigid economy in all departments, how- 
ever continues and the management trusts that all concerned will in their 
own as well as the Company’s interests do their utmost to co-opetate in these 
respects. 

The management hopes that its decision regarding the proposed retrench- 
ment. will contribute towards a new spirit of co-operation between the Corn- 
pany and the Staff so that mutual aspirations may be given a chance of ful- 
filment in the forseeable future. 

For GRANT ADVERTISING, INC. 

MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, 
Judge , Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 

By order of the Governor, 

D. S. P. MTJKHERJEE. Jt. Sm 


ORDER. 

No. 1 ‘UDis. / I) 1 1L-154 /54. — 13th January 1955.— Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 2-42Dis. /])/ 
11L-1 8*1/52, dated the 25th August 1952, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. J. & R. Hutchison, Limited (Manufacturing Chemists), 10, Cine 
Row, Calcutta (factory at 90, Dum Dum Road) and their workmen 
represented by J. & R. Hutchison Workers' Union, IJ5/B, Wellington 
Street, Calcutta, regarding the matters specified in the schedule thereto was 
referred for adjudication to the Sixth Industrial Tribunal; 

And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal 
a complaint in writing was made by Sliri Satish Chandra Das, a workman 
of the said Company, liefore the said Tribunal, against the said Company 
alleging that the said Company had punished the said workman concerned in 
such dispute; 

And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudi- 
cated upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State 
Government; 




Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 20, 1955 


235 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 

ANNEXURE. 

In the matter of a oomplaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) 
Act, 1950, made by Shri Satish Chandra Das, a workman of Messrs. 
J. A R. Hutchison Ltd., 10, Olive Row, Calcutta, represented by 
J. A R- Hutchison Workers’ Union, 26/Sp Dum Dum RoafL Calcutta, 
against the aforesaid Company (Case No. 148/33A/53). 

BEFORE TIIE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, NEW SECRE- 
TARIAT BUILDING, WEST BENGAL, CALCUTTA. 

Present : 

^Shri MOTILAL CHAKRAVATT1, District Judge , 

Judge , Sixth Industrial Tribunal . 


Appearances . 

For the Company : Shri N. M. Das Gupta, Advocate. 
For the workman: None. 


The original reference out of which the present proceedings has arisen 
was made under Government order Nos. 2342Dis./D/llL-l 83/52, dated 
25th August 1952. 


AWARD. 

On behalf of the Company its lawyer appears and states that the petitioner 
Jjuh already compromised with the Company and that he (lawyer) has no 
further instruction. 

None appears on behalf of the petitioner. 1 have read the petition under 
section 33A and also the written statement hied by the Company. There is 
no material before me to think that the suspension order was unjust or un- 
reasonable or without sufficient cause although no formal cliargeshcet was 
made over to petitioner. So the application is rejected. 


MOTILAL CHAKRA YATTI, District Judge, 

Judge , Sixth Industrial Tribunal.

NOTIFICATION. 

No. 354W.T. — 19th January 1955. — In exercise 
of the power conferred by sub-section (1) and, in 
particular, by clause (a) of sub-section (2), of Bec- 
^tion 68 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (IV of 
1939), the Governor is pleased to make the follow- 
ing amendment in the Bengal Motor Vehicles 
Rules, 1940, published under notification 
No. 1930P1., dated the 21st September 1940, at 
pages 2656-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta Gazette 
of tlm 10th October 1940, as subsequently amended, 
namely : — 

Amendment. 

, In sub-rule (i) of rule 54 of the said rules for 
the words “Secretary-Member power to grant con- 
tract carriage or private carrier's permits; provided 
that the power so delegated shall not extend to the 
refusal to grant any permit, or to the grant of a 
jftrmit for contract carriages when any representa- 
tion may have been made by any person under the 
Provisions of section 50 of the Act, unless the 
Secretary-Member has by a resolution of the 
/* Authority been authorised to refuse a permit or to 
£ranx such a permit in any particular case, 
provided that when the Secretary has refused a 
permit such refusal shall be subject to the approval 
of the Authority at. its next meeting'’, substitute 
the following words, namely: — 

, ^“Secretary power to grant contract carriage or 
private carrier’s permits or temporary 
' permits under clauses (b) and (c) of sec- 
tion 62, so, however, that the power so 
delegated shall not extend to the refusal 
to grant any permit, or to the grant of a 
permit for contract carriage when 
representation may have been made by 
any person under the provisions of sec- 
tion 50 unless the Secretary has, by a 
resolution of the Authority, been 
authorised to refuse a permit or to grant 
such a permit in a particular case; 
provided that when the vSecretary has 
refused a permit such refusal or 

w r hen he has granted a temporary 
permit under the provisions of clause (h) 
or clause (c) of section 62, the grant ot 
such a permit shall be subject to the 
approval of the Authority at its next 
^ meeting”.

J. N. TALUKDAR, Secy.

By order No. 91)is. /])/ UL-192(A)/5‘1, dated Calcutta, the 4th J uiiun 
1954, the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, referml i 
abovementioued dispute to me for adjudication regarding the matters speciti 
in the schedule to the said order. 

Schedule. 

(1) Bonus for J95-J. 

AWARD. 

The content ion oi the Union i> that since 1941. the Company lias b 
paying bonus cvciy \ear in two instalment*, viz., Duja Bonus ii/thc mu. 
of Sc]dcTiil)cr and Christmas Bonus in the month of December and il is i; 
the contention of the Union that tin* bonus is payable irrespective ol pr 
or loss in anv year and that the payment ol bonus is an implied eoiitr 
between the Company and tLe employees. The Union contends that 1 
Company in order to victimise the Union members huve stopped payment 
bonus since 1952 and tin* non-payment is unjustified, arbitrary and mala jit 

The Company, however, contends that bonus was paid all along on t. 
basis of there being a profit and that since 1952 the Company traded at 


►art I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 27, 1955 




oss and “their economy has been seriously affected by adverse trading condi- 
jons” m a result of which the company has applied for permission to retrench 
1 3 of their workmen on the grounds of rationalisation owing to the 
ompany's financial losses. It is, therefore, urged that bonus was never 
n implied contract between the company and its workmen and that the non- 
ayment of bonus was not unjustified nor arbitrary nor illegal. From the 
tatement produced by the company (Ext. A), it appears that bonus was 
aid all along since 1941 up to 1951 and that bonus was paid in 1940 also 
{though in that year the company traded at a loss. Such loss happened in 
:j 52 and 1958. In 1952 Puja Bonus was paid to the Indian workmen and 
liristmas bonus was paid to the European officers and in 1958 no bonus was 
uid to anybody. From the solitary payment of bonus in the year of loss 
illing in 1940, it cannot be predicated that bonus used to be paid inospee- 
ve of profit or loss in Hny year. That would be a “generalisation on 
tuple enumeration” which is illogical. There ih no express contract 
j pay bonus to the workmen. Ordinarily, bonus is payable only in the 
tsc of profit, unless there be any contract express or implied to pay bonus 
i the year of losses as well. The practice of payment of bonus is*a piece 
C circumstantial evidence to prove such implied contract. Therefore, 1 ho 
rcumstantial evidence must be such as to be incompatible with any other 
vpothesis than that of bonus being payable irrespective of profit or loss, 
n this case there is no such circumstantial evidence from which it can be 
included or reasonably inferred that bonus was payable in case of loss also, 
licit* fore, the Company is not obliged to pay any bonus for the year 1958.

Schedule. 

,!i Wliether the termination of services of Shri Keshabdas Bo«e is

,;>) To what relief is Shri Keshabdas Bose entitled. 


AWARD. 

Eeslhihdas Bose was admittedly an employee of Messrs Bajaj & Co., a 
iNiitu ( tiiiijumy, the business of which was taken up by M sr- Chemical 
jimiU I j 1 1 1 1 1 1 od which came into existence in March HMd (see L\t. C). From 
e t*\ uU'uct* of Shri Keshabdas Bose it appears that (in np'i Dliar and 



THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 27, 1966 [Pa*t I 


Mahadeo Bajaj were tlie sole proprietors of Bajaj & Co., whereas Ganga 
Dhar Das, Mahadeo Bajaj and M. L. Khaitan are the entire body of share- 
holders of Messrs. Chemical Agents, Limited. There is no record to show 
that the services of Keshabdas Bose under Messrs. Bajaj' & Co., continued 
upto Ihe iormntkm of the limited Company as aforesaid and that this conti- 
nuity was without any break. On the other hand, I find that there were

to the workmen of Messrs Bajaj & Co. , for the period before the date ni t 
which the said limited company came into existence. 

Shri Keshabdas Bose contends that he rendered service to Messrs . 
Chemical Ageuts, Limited, up to 81st December 1952, and on that dm,, 
the management abruptly and wrongfully and without any notice, verba I h

General Motors (India), Ltd., reported in 1953 (II) L.L.J., 840 and 841 1. 
It is, therefore, clear that the discharge of Ranjit Kumar Porel during the 
pendency of the proceedings before the Tribunal between the municipality 
and its workmen was in contravention of section 33 of the Act and the, 
complaint under section 33A by the complainant was, therefore, competent, i

There is no fixed standard by which the adequacy or otherwise of the 
vl sic emoluments of a worker can be judged. There is at present no law 
,n the subject and the minimum wages have been fixed from time to time 
ndustrywise by different Tribunals within this State. But there are some 
rrv sound principles laid down by the Labour Appellate Tribunal .ml 
1 ifferent State Tribunals which guide us in this matter. The principles 
n ve been very elaborately stated at nage 509 in the case of Buckingham 
'* Carnatic Co., Ltd., decided by the Labour Appellate Tribunal and 
•epurted in 1952 L.A.C. p. 490. The Fair Wages Committee in dealing 
uth the question of wages came to the conclusion that the wages of an 
nil list r hi 1 worker must be such as would enable him to have not merely Ihe 
nviiris for bare subsistence for life but also for the preservation of hi*, 
.{liricncy as a worker. For this purpose, he must have means to provide 
ur some measure of education, medical requirements and amenities. This 
, minimum which he must have irrespective of the capacity of the 
ndijsl ry or of his employer to pay. Thus the floor level of wages is to be 
.vtcrmtned keeping in view of those considerations. The upper limit of 
vajre*' must be set by what may be called the capacity of the industry to 
,;iC, not of a particular unit thereof but ou the industry-a/m-region basis, 
tvtuern these limits, the fair wage will depend according to tilt* Fair Wage, 
n, in it tee's Beport upon the following factors: — 

(1) The productivity of labour, 

prevailing rates of wages in the same or similar occupation, in 
the same or neighbouring localities, 

(.1) the level of national income and its distribution, and 

(1) the place of industry' in the economy of the country. Their 
lordships said that in their opinion, the question of wages lus 
to be approached in the manner indicated above. 

The quest ion of fixation of basic wages has got to be answered in the light 
oi tin* observations made above.

-VHien direction of the General Manager of the Company at Bombay to 
dose down the factory was communicated to the local management by Ext. 
G3 dated 19th August 1953, the latter, it has already been noted/ tried 
to transfer as many people as could be to ease the situation (vide Ext. G4, 
tc ) Getting scent about management’s intention to close the factory, 
j^more probable as stated in Ext. G8 that the workmen became restive 
nd under instigation of some outsiders they were bent upon to create 
lischief. So, in view of the evidence and circumstances, Company's ease 
”1 living acted bona fide rather than Union's case of the Company' huving 
closed the* factory as a retaliatory measure because of the formation of 
Union and presentation of charter of demands seems to me mine probable 
.1 natural. The subsequent correspondences with the Labour Diieetorale 
E x t 13, dated 3rd September 1953, Ext. 12, dated 3th September 
Ext. II, dated Kith September 1953), all point in support of 

’ompany’s case. 

The progress reports. Ext. J series, relating to Calcutta me, a shows 
l it the Company had no much outstanding work to do b\ Juiv l'i.ri. (it 
I . two works tiiev had then, the evidence shows, one was completed u. 

m „„th and the other work which was relating to Drainage W.itw 
i thll Channel needed no machinery except one pump and one eonciete 
tixiure machine. The work at Belur which was one ol sheet piling h,i 
Protection of Belur Math from erosion, it appears, needed likewise no 
nriclnnorv requiring repair in the workshop. As regards wmk at .Mokama 
tli.it the evidence shows that the said work has been taken not by this 
('oinpanv alone but as a joint venture bv this Company abrnir with* two 
otht'i companies under the name and style of Ganga Barrage Construction 
(’o Regarding works in Sindri, Mvthon and Assam Link, these ot course 
•re not completed, hut the evidence shows that these required no major 
pair of any machinery employed in them since July 1953. In the 
reuiii stances, it is obvious, that the closure was a bona fi<h closure for 
iiirtage' of work. The correspondences with the Factory Inspector ami 
tutistiral Department which took place long before the lorm.ition of the 
iiion it bus already been pointed, showed in unmistakable terms that the 
.orkshop was established ns a temporary measure for requirements ol 
'ninnany’s works in Calcutta and neighbouring areas. So when the 
'valence shows that those works were completed and the Com pa in had no 
wssilulity in the near future to get further work, it was oloiou- that they 
■auhl not but close the factory for trade reasons. 

Alter closure, it appears that there had been no wotk m the workshop 
except one connected with packing and despatch. The cxidcmv on the 


j nu CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUABY 27, 1966 [Pam I 


side of the Union to the contrary is inoonvinoing. When 1 visited the 
workshop, 1 found carpenters forking for packing. Had the Union’s case 
of closure having been directed to victimise the workmen been true, it would 
have amounted to conduct of one cutting his nose to spite others. Nobody 
usually takes such action against his own interest. So the action of the 
Company in closing the workshop and the Lorry Department was quite 

bona fide . 


As a person cannot be compelled to carry on business any more than 
he can be compelled to acquire property there can be no direction to 
re-open the factory in any case (vide 1952, L.L.J., Volume I, page 364). 
Likewise when the employer has the right to close his business, no ques- 
tion of reinstatement would have arisen in any view of the matter (vuU 
1954 LLJ Volume I, page 188). So, only relief which the workmen 
are entitled'on account of loss of their employment following closure 
would be compensation. Though Company s initial offer as in Ext. H 
was not adequate, their latest offer as embodied in their letter dated 16th 
September 1953 (Ext. II) seems to me to lie fair and reasonable. The 
said offer is more or less in accord with the amendment of the Industrial 
Disputes Act which has been operative since 21st October 1954. The 
Company is accordingly directed to pay to the discharged workmen, - 

(a) wages for 1st and 2nd September 1953, 

(b) 15 days’ wages in lieu of notice, 

(c) wages in lieu of leave and 

(d) compensation at the rate of 15 days’ wages per completed year n| 

service, 


in accordance with their offer as contained in their letter. Ext. II du*- 1 
j 9th September 3953. The payments should he made within a month tr 
the date the award becomes enforceable.

of the workmen and when the disputes raised thereby are iliseparal 
connected, it is obvious that it would amount to an industrial dispute. T 
point is accordingly a warded against the Company.

In view of the findings under issues 2 and 4, the disputes raised urn; 
this issue do not require adjudication.

RESOLUTION No. 42ZW.T. 

Calcutta , the 24th January 1965 . 

The question of re-organising the Pub 
Vehicles Department in Culcutta has been uni 
consideration of Government for some time a 
an investigation into its working has been carr 
out by a body of experts in organisation a 
methods. After considering their report Gove 
ment have decided that the Police in Calcu 
should be relieved of the non-police duties in r 
neclion with the administration of the Pul 
Vehicles Department and that it should be pla 
under a Director who should be a high powe 
civilian officer. 

2. In pursuance of the above decision Shri 
K. Ray, I.C.S., has been appointed as Adiliti 
Transport Commissioner to take up the worl 
re-organisation of the Public Vehicles Departr 
and relieve the Commissioner of Police of 
functions which do not normally form part oj 
police work. Shri Ray will also act as Repi 
Transport Authority, Calcutta, and 80 long as 
re-organisation of the Public Vehicles Depart 
i> not completed, the Deputy Com miss 
of Police, Public Vehicles Depart 
and other police personnel will continue m 
present posts under the overall control of Sh 
K. Ra\, but in disciplinary and service m 
they will be subject to the control of the 
missioner of Police, Calcutta. 

3. It has further been decided that the

loom Organisation sanctioned in terms of Govern- 
ment order No. 26Co-op.. dated the 6th January 
1955. 

No. 1 23Co-op. / 8A -2 / 55. — 20th January 1955.— 
In exercise of the power conferred by section 24 
of the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940, the 
Governor is pleused to depute Shri S. It. Bhatta- 
charyya, Assistant ltegistrar of Co-operative 
Societies, now acting as Officer on Special Duty

fishermen in the Sunderban area on Co-operative 
basis to the service of the West Bengal Central 
Co-operative Weavers Marketing Society Limited, 
Calcutta, to act as its Executive Officer exclusively 
with effect from the 6th January 1955 until further 
orders.

In July 1950, Sliri Neogi was ill and underwent medical treatment. T1 
company uwlcr the rules was to pay all medical expenses but refused whci 
Shri Neogi asked for payment. This led to a controversy for which tlj 
management placed him under suspension with effect from 1st Septembt

Tribunal Imiud that Shri Neogi became an eye-sore to the management, for hi, 
Union activities and was victimised on false allegations. The Tribunal 
directed his reinstatement iu his former post or any post equivalent to it j fl 
pay and prospect and also for paymeut of compensation. The managcm^ 
transferred Sliri Neogi to Simla to a certain post in its Simla brunch purporj. 
iu*,, net iu term* of the aforesaid award. Shri Neogi protested Ulu | 
asked for a post in tin* company’s Calcutta offices. The company turned a 
deaf car to his request and after an exchange of some letters, dismissed 
Hence this case. 

The company in reply said that the award of Sliri G. Palit was duly 
legally implemented and as such the question of justification or not in t} K . 
matter of reinstatement did not arise. It cannot be the subject matter n \ 
further adjudication and the present reference was misconceived and bad i n 
law. The company further stated that all benefits under the award u CT(l 
given to Shri Neogi in usual course and that the award thereby was fully 
exhausted. The matter of non-implementation wap referred to Shri (I. p„ij t 
under section 20 of the Industrial Disputes Act and the learned Tnhiin;,] 
held on 22nd January 1953 as follows: “The post which the company offered 
at Simla was an equivalent post with additional amenities. This oiler won 
repeated several times but Sliri Neogi did not choose to accept it. So, the 
company terminated his service by a letter, dated 24th September 19', |. ] 
cannot say that the letter of the award was violated.” Thereafter, Shri 
Neoiri was offered provident fund money and he received it in full and final 
satisfaction nt his accounts. Since then, the relation of employer and 
employee totally ceased to exist and Shri Neogi could not raise any further 
industrial dispute. 

The issues are — 

(1) Whether the company was justified in offering reinstatement in service 

to Shri S. C. Neogi at their Simla Office in pursuance of the order 
of reinstatement given in the award of Shri G. Palit as publish'd 
under this Government order No. 3o32Lab., dated the Till .1 uue 
1951 and whether the company was justified in treating Sliri 
Neogi’s services as terminated for his failing to join in Simla ! 
Office in pursuance of the company’s direction? 

(2) If not, what redress and/or relief Shri Neogi is entitled to? 

FINDINGS. 

Issues Nos. 1 and 2. 

Shri S. C. Neogi was dismissed from service for alleged misconduct. On 
9 relerencc of the dispute arising over it, Sliri G. Palit of the Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal held that the order of dismissal was had and directed i *‘ iii-1nie- 
menf. Tin* directions given in his award are: “lie must he reinstated within 
one month of the award coining into operation either in his formci post oi 
in any post equivalent in pay and prospects.” Shri Neogi mimic ressfullj 
contested before Shri G. Palit, in an application under section 20 of llie

lustrial Disputes Act, that these directions in his award were not imple 
n ied: In his application (Ext. A7), he asked for certain payments 
ounting to Rs. 3,310-15 on different accounts, The learned Tribunul 
an order, dated 22ud January 1953, directed that the petitioner was 
;itled to Its. 170 only on account of bonus. In disposing of the claim for 
ears of wages he said, ‘‘under rules of transfer obtaining in the coiu- 
ly and re-affirmed in this award, the employees were liable to transfer 
where. The award directed that either ho should be reinstated m hi* 
[nor po&t or P 08 ^ equivalent to it in pay and prospects. The post which 
company offered at Simla Brunch was an equivalent post A\ith addi- 
ial amenities. This offer was repeated several times but the petitioner

letter, dated 24th September 1951. I cannot say that the letter of the 
3 rd was violated the claim for arrear of wages thus is untenable. ” 

The i^e No. 1 relates to the justification of this order of the manage- 
u t ior reinstatement in Simla Office and for termination of Sliri Nona's 
wees for failing to comply with that order. “ r ’ 

Shri Dus Gupto, Advocate for the company, contends that this reference 
,a (1 in law, as the present dispute is not an industrial dispute, and as the 
tlei of dispute had already been disposed of by Shri G. Dalit under section 
of the Industrial Disputes Act against the employee. He said that this 
hunal is not competent to sit on judgment over the previous award. 

I think this contention is not sound and shall fail. In the first place, 

, Tribunal is not competent to question the propriety of the order of 
•u are (1952, II, L.L.J., page (JOS). Neither it can quash the pro- 
lings, on the ground of validity of the reference. It has been held by 
Supremo Court of India in 1953, I, L.L.J., page 174 that it is tor 
appropriate Government to decide about the factual existence of the 
>ute and the necessity of the reference. A Tribunal is not ordinarily 
ipelent to quash the proceedings before it if it holds a different view. On 
i these grounds the Tribunal finds that the objection regarding the

Regarding the first point, it will appear from the compromise petite

Amended Industrial Disputes Act, ns whether the previous service render,,,]

appears that the parties are at one that the amount of compensation shio/

to that portion of the question. Regarding the period of service rea^J 
under the earlier concern, it is clear from the Company's own docim,,,^ 
that the continuity of service was accepted by it under the present limjy 
Company. 1 refer to the Ext. E of the Company’s document, filed in a 
case before me, under Government order No. 146Lab., dated 8th ,lanu ;i L 
19)], In that exhibit the Company has shown the dates of appointing 
in one column, dating long before the incorporation of this limited OoTn|, Jlnv

Regai ding the legal objection which the Company has raised, rr , jj t J 
the limited company is not bound to recognise the services rendei.-ij to f 
pre-existing concern, no matter whether that was merged in ii or Jl0 | j 
has been displaced hv the judgment of Mr. Justice Tendulkar of II m,!^ 
Iligh Couit. in Bombay Garage case, reported in 1953, L.L.J. \ 
page 14 . I quote below the relevant extract from His Lordships ( ■:.!jiik*ti 
“ in any case therefore where there i9 continuity of service. i)u> n e 
employer is bound to take into account the services rendered by tin- w f»rke 

to his predecessors in title ” This is also in agreemenl viih t 

Appellate Tribunal’s decision in the case of Lalubhai Amin Chain!, lepoil 
in 1953, L.A.(\, page 388. The contrary decision reported in 19V). L A I 
page 557, is clearly distinguishable, because that was a case of It an* 
of business from one man to another. So, both in law and in hid t 
Company cannot deprive tin* workers of the benefit of the period of 
rendered to Juggilal Kamlapat Hosiery Factory as against the )m*s 
limited concern. Besides, if other matters are taken into fonsidcrati 
we reach the same conclusion that the previous Company merged in 
present limited concern. The site of the business is the same. The ;»re* 
limited concern is a private limited company where the bulk of the slm 
if not all, is owned by the family of the previous owners. So ii is i 
difficult to put the present limited concern as a completely separate ent 
totally divorced from its context, viz., the previous concern. In that i 
also the workmen can press their claim legitimately against the pre 
limited concern, so far as their antecedent service is concerned Ike 
in which this matter has been worded in the compromise petition will 
confirm the above conclusion, viz ., that the Juggilal Kamlapd Ho f

’actory was taken over by the present Company. So, in the result, I award

{ service rendered under the present limited Company. Regarding the 
uantum, the parties are bound by the settlement made in the compromise 
etition. 

Regarding the notice pay, I am asked to decide whether the workmen 
hould get notice pay as. contemplated under section 25F of the Act. T 
, lUB t answer it in the negative. These men were retrenched long before 
his amended Act of section 25F came into force (vide the retrenchment 
otice). As this Act is not retrospective these workmen cannot have the

Notice pay under the old law. I can grant that relief under the order of 
eferenee of the Government. I grant them relief in the shape of notice 
>ay to the extent of 15 days' basic salary last drawn by them, less any 
Kiymcnt already made on this head.

-10/54, dated 12th July 1954 and 3537J)is./D/7L-47/54, dated 21st July

■iigal ineluding the Nuddea Jute Mills Co., Ltd. and their workmen to 
is Tribunal for adjudication. The proceedings arising out of this 
feronce are still pending. 


On 21 Hh August 1954 Shri Bhajahari Ghosh, a pin bov of the Nuddea 
lie Mills Co.. Ltd., filed a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial 
isputes Act stating as follows : — 


That the petitioner Bhajahari Ghosh had been working as a pin boy 
i the South Mill Mechanic Department as a temporary workman und the 
rtitioner was informed on the 20th July 1954 that his service would 
vnimnte on the 24th July 1954 as he has been found medically unfit, 
nit the petitioner had been trained in the Nuddea Jute Mill and worked 
ten- for long on different occasions and has worked continuously from 
1th June 1954 to 23rd July 1954, that the petitioner sent an application 
i the Mill Manager and he was informed that the Manager was not 
r<“ pa red to reconsider his case, that at the time of appointment the peti- 
imiei stood second and he was offered job, that the petitioner was net 
niwtlered surplus to the requirement of the company and he was appointed 
u a permanent post, that the petitioner got himself examined by Captain 
l. Sen and he found him fit. for work and later the petitioner was ulso 
lammed by the Civil Surgeon of Hooghly, who too found the petitioner 
pile tit for work, that the company has contravened section 33 of the 
industrial Disputes Act by discharging the petitioner without the per- 
jussion of the Tribunal, that the petitioner prays for reinstatement and 
ky for the period of unemployment. 


552 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 10, 1965 [P A 


The company, on the other hand, states that the petition m 
section 33A is misconceived and not maintainable in law, that the peti 
contains various vague and misleading allegations, that Shri Bhaja 
Ghosh was selected to work as a temporary pin boy after proper trade 
on 23rd June 1954, and in accordance with the prevailing practice of 
company he was sent to the Mill Medical Officer on the same date for 
examination regarding his physical fitness for employment, that 
Medical Officer found him medically unfit but he wanted to re-exan 
him after 15 days, that pending his re-exaraination the petitioner 
allowed to work in the mill on the understanding that he would be oj. 
the temporary employment of a pin boy only after he had been der) a 
medically fit, that on 12th July 1954 the petitioner was declared meilica 
unfit for work and he was informed that he could not be appointed at 
temporary pin boy, that the company submits that the complainant ; 
only selected for the post of a temporary pin boy and waB not appoi U i 
in a permanent post as alleged, that the Medical certificates obtained f r 
outside medical practitioners are irrelevant, that the company reiterii 
that it has not contravened section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, t 
in the circumstances Shri Bhajahari Ghosh iB not entitled to reiiistt 
ment and/or wages for the period of his unemployment. 

DECISION. 

The Registration Form belies the story of the petitioner that he worl 
as a permanent pin boy from 24th June 1954 to 23rd July 1954 and 
on a sudden management discharged him on 24th July 1954. It is x 
fortunate that he was medically unfit. His appointment, if nu ^ 
years ago, was only temporary and from time to time. This time’ on 
he got the Registration Form for employment as a temporary pin bo 
As condition precedent to his appointment he has got to pass" tlu* Tra 
test and then medical test. The decision of the company’s Medical ()Hj f 
in such case is normally the final say. The doctor examined him a ^a 
and again and gave him ample chance but failed to pass him. As a p 
boy he has got to stand on the carding machine and to fit the pins 
man with defective heart cannot be passed by any doctor for the job. T' 
company’s doctor reports that he suffered from apex of heart in tj 
epigestic region. The medical certificates forwarded by the workman all 
show that his defective heart could not go unnoticed by them. In tluj 
circumstances, the company’s doctor’s action and the action of the cmnpuj 
based on this report was justified. He was allowed to work for the nbJ 
period on his instance and as a matter of grace. He cannot take udvd 
tage of that favour. lie was only selected but never appointed ns] 
temporary pin boy. So he cannot get any relief and his application 
not lie and is rejected as not tenable.

THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 10; mo 


558 


Employees’ Association, 249B, Bowbasar Street, Calcutta-12 { regai 
the matters specified below, was referred to this Tribunal for its aaju 
tion, under Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, . 
No. lODis. / D / 13L-6/63, dated the 4th January 1954. 

Both parties filed their written statements in due course. 

In the written statement filed by the Union, it is alleged that Me 
B.P.M’s Press, a part of Messrs. A. T. Dev, Ltd., Btands on a veiy B( 
financial footing. It however treated its workers very harshly. On 
November 1953, the management asked the workers to Bign a declare 
form purported to be a production chart. The workers protested and reft 
to sign. They were willing to sign the Attendance Register. Therem 
the 14 workers named below, were cliarge-sheeted on that account, on* 
very day and the hearing of the charges was fixed on 9th November a, 
On the date fixed, the Secretary of the Union was not allowed to enter 
office for the purpose of conducting the enquiry on behalf of the work 
On the next day, the workers were not allowed to resume their duties 
were turned out of the office. On a reference to the Labour Director 
Mr. S. N. Chatter jee, Deputy Labour Commissioner, amicably settled 
dispute. The management agreed to allow the workers to rejoin their di 
on and from 3()th December 1953. Mr. Chatter jee suggested that 
workers should be paid compensation at 50 per cent, of their basic wi 
and dearness allowance in respect of the entire period during which t 
were rendered idle. In the present dispute, the Union claims that ftO 
cent, of the basic wages and dearness allowance should be calculated on 
basis of the average of six months’ earnings. 

In reply, Messrs. B.P.M’s Press alleged that there was no outstand 
dispute to be referred to a Tribunal for adjludication. The dispute 
settled and the workers resumed their duties on 1st January 1954 in termi 
the settlement. They accepted the first instalment of ex gratia allowa 
on 9th January 1954. 

The issue is — 

(1) Whether suspension of 14 workers named below is justified? 
what relief are they entitled?

AWARD. 

This is a complaint under section 33A by Shri Surath Ram and two others, 
ley were workers in opposite Oil Mill (<Uma Char an Sadhukhan Oil Mill)* 
leir employment was terminated on 6th May 1954. The complainants 
leged that although they were dismissed, they were allowed to live in the 
larters provided by the Mill till 31st .August 1954. During pendency of 
e proceeding before this Tribunal in respect of an industrial dispute 
•tween the Oil Mill and their workmen, the petitioners alleged that they 
,«re forcibly ejected by the Mill management on 1st September 1954. Hence 
e complaint. The complainants accordingly prayed that the Mill should 
• directed to pay them house rent at the rate of Rs. 12 per head per month 
Din 1st September 1954. 

The opposite party denied that the complainants had lived in the Mill 
loiters beyond 6th May 1954. It was pleaded that the complainants left 
e Mill premises on 6th May 1954 when their employment ceased. It was 
rther alleged that this was long before the date of reference to the 
•ibunal and thus there was no contravention of section 33. The opposite 
.rty further stated that there was no contract of service under which the 
nijdainants were entitled to get quarters to live in. In the circumstances 
e opposite party submitted that the complaint should be dismissed. 

DECISION. 

None of the complainants has come to depose before this Tribunal. In 
e absence of evidence it must be held that there has been no contravention 

section 33. In the result, the complaint under section 33A must fail. 

I award accordingly.

Ihe onus to justify retrenchment is on the Company. From the

Regarding the first contention, I agree with the Company that 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, it is the workmen wl 
aggrieved should apply before the Tribunal before whom the inai: 
is pending for adjudication. The matter of representation comw 
the application has been filed. In that view of the matter, certain 
present application is defective. But during the trial these pern 
the application did turn up before the Tribunal. So this defect wh 
after all, a formal one has been c ured. 

Regarding the second contention, it is said that these 25 w< 
were merely seasonal employees, taken for six months or so, and 
^services would terminate automatically by the efflux of time 
when the season is over. Even during the season period their f 
could be terminated by a notice of 14 days on either side. As s 
is contended that no permission of the Tribunal under section 33 


867 


>A*r X] THE CAMTJTO#©AZBTTB, FEBBtJABY 10, 1966 


id was necessary here. Th|t being so,. the application under section 83A 
,{ the Act it is urged u out of place. The Company refers to 
he latter of_ appointment m per Ext. A, and also the notice enclosed 
herewith. I p of course, agtee that in cases of seasonal employees, when 
he season is over, their services automatically terminate. No order is 
necessary, and no notice is called for to terminate their services. In 
uch cases, of course, permission of the Tribunal is not necessary. But 
ehere the services are terminated by a notice, as in the present case, it 
b certainly necessary to have a written permission of the Tribunal under 
nation 33 of the Act, because the services here do not automatically end, 
mt are being terminated by the act of the employer. Such an act 
hould be approved by the Tribunal as a condition precedent to the 
ermination of services when the main case is pending before the 
Tribunal. So, I find that the Company in this case of 25 workmen has 
■ontravened the section 33 of the Act. But as these people were seasonal 
employees, and as they were very near the end of the term of service, T 
lo not grant them reinstatement. I grant them only compensation. ’ T 
illow them compensation to the extent of one month’s basic salary on the 
«ale of pay last drawn. This is payable within one month of the award 
joining into operation. 

Regarding the third and legal objection, viz., that Shri M. C. Banerji, 
Tribunal, before whom the application was' originally filed, was alone 
competent to decide this matter under section 33 A of the Act, ] am 
unable to agree. Of course, normally, under section 33A the application 
should be filed before the Tribunal before whom the original case is 
pending, and that such Tribunal should adjudicate upon the matter. 
But when the original case is withdrawn and transferred to another 
Tribunal by the Government, acting under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, it cannot be contended that the section 33A, proceeding 
must, still be decided by that former Tribunal. The clear intention of 
the section 33A is that the Tribunal which tries the main case is the 
Tribunal competent to try the case under section 33A which arises out 
;<>! it. The reason is also clear. That Tribunal being in seisin of 
the main case, can go right into all questions directly connected with it. 
That is why a miscellaneous case arising out of it is to he decided by the 
said Tribunal. In the present case Government by its order of reference 
mentioned above has transferred the main case to me. So this Tribunal 
is the appropriate Tribunal which should hear the section 33A proceed- 
ing as well. Once the application iR filed before the Tribunal, before 
iom tlie main case is pending, the requirement of the section 33A is 
in plied with. After that it is up to the Government to withdraw" the 
sc and send it to another Tribunal along with the pending appliea- 
>n under section 33A. So the Government order of reference in the 
esent case to this Tribunal is in order, and this Tribunal has been 
■sled with the jurisdiction to try the section 33A proceeding, irrcsjHictive 
the fact that the cause of action had occurred wheu the main case was 
aiding before Shri M. (-. Banerji. So this legal objection is turned 
>wn In the result, the application under section 33A succeeds partially, 
already noted. I make no order for costs, 

Dictated and corrected by me. 

G. DALIT, G. PALIT, District Judge. 

Judge . Chairman. Fifth Industrial Tribunal,

»* main case is pending for adjudication. Now, in the present case 
, the main dispute is pending for adjudication before this Tribunal, this 
rihunnl is certainly competent to go into the question raised by the 
ctioji 33A proceeding. So this objection of the Company is turned 
iwn.

n service condition, it is variable by its nature, having a direct, ratio

make out during the trial, that, the work of these Muster Gang men 
as specific. That work is now being diverted to Labour Contractors,

nipany has filed, show that the work these Muster Gang men did was

ployed according to the volume of work in the Company’s hand. That

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Dispute 
Act, 1947, as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal 
Act, 1950, filed by 8hri M. Banerji, Secretary of Bird A Oo. Laboi 
Union of Calcutta, against the aforesaid Company.

Union. 

1. The original reference out of which this case has arisen was mu 
under Government order No. 3274Dis./D/llL-234/52, dated 26th Nnveml 
1952 and 2331Dis./D/llL-13/53, dated 29th June 1953. 

AWARD. 

2. It is the contention of the Union that during the pendency of 
main case before the Tirbunal, the workers are not being given full wa 
on Saturdays, or wages for half day’s work on other days. The niattoj 
discharge which was in the petition has not been pressed. 

3. The Company in its written statement resists the claim of 
Union. It contends that some of the workers work under Sirdar Suni< 
and Sirdar Hakra. So, for them the Company has no liability. Then 
workers named at pages 4, 5 and 6 are said to be casual employees, 
twelve names at page 7, appear in another application pending before 
Tribunal. The Company contends that the Union’s contention a 
Saturdays’ wages or with regard to payment on other half days is not 
They are paid for the number of musters for which they are engaged 

The learned Advocate of the Company raised a legal objection that 
matter should have been heard by Shri M. C. Banerji, Tribunal, h 
whom the main was pending when the cause of action arose. His st 
objection is that the aggrieved workmen themselves have not made 
complaint as required under the section 33A, but only the Seortary o 
Union has made it. 

Regarding the first objection, I am unable to agree that 
M. C. Banerji, Tribunal, alone is competent to decide this matter he 
the main case was originally pending before him. The Government 1 
order of reference transferred the main case to me along with the appli* 
under the section 33 A. It can never be seriously contended by the Cor 


abt II THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, TEBStUAltY 17, 1955 48ft 


iat though 1 the main case was transferred to this Tribunal, yet Shri 
[ C Banerji should have decided the case under the section 33 A. The 
itention behind the section 38A is that the Tribunal who decides the main 
ase is the appropriate Tribunal to decide the case under the section 33A 
rising out of it. To hold otherwise would go contrary to the spirit of 
he section 33A. That the application under the section 33A was filed 
..fore Shri M. C. Banerji, Tribunal, before whom the main case was 
ending, it was sufficient compliance with the requirement of the section 
flA When the Government could under section 10 transfer the main 
' ' ^ W as cer tainly competent also to transfer the case under the section 
ja A* arising out of that. So the objection raised by the Company on this 
ground is turned down. 

Regarding the second objection, I do not accept the Company’s 
(intention that it is a fatal defect that the Secretary of the Union has filed 

petition, and not the workmen themselves as required under the section 
Sa of the Industrial Disputes Act. I agree that the aggrieved workmen 
bnuld have presented the application before the Tribunal. But in the 
resent case these workmen have given their thumb-impressions on the 
•iiiers filed before the Tribunal. So, in a way, they became the signa- 
tories to the application under the section 33A. 

Regarding the merit of the case, I accept the Company’s contention, 
m fl n i on could not make out that the workmen were paid less wages as 
ll.-tred That was practically given up during the trial. So, I find that 
indication under section 33A is liable to be rejected. 1 reject it 

Lordingly.

ANNEJpJRE. . 

In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Umaoharsi 
Sadhukhan Oil Mills, 95, Harragan] Road, Salkia, Howrah and theii 
workers represented by Telkai Mazdoor Congress, 1, Joy Bhattaoharjec 
Lane, Calcutta^. 

BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 

Present : 

Shri J. N. MAITRA, Judge , Third Industrial Tribunal . 

For the workers : Shri Panchanan Bhattacharya, President, Telkai Mazdoor 
Congress. 

For the Oil Mill: Shri Parbati Nath Mukherjee, M.A., D.S.W., Officer 
Umacharan Sadhukhan Oil Mill. 1 

AWARD. 

1. By order No. 3298Dis./D/15L-21/54, dated the 7th July 1954, the 
Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Umacharun Sadhukhan Oil Mills, 95, Harraganj Road, Salkia, 
Howrah and their workers represented by Telkai Mazdoor Congress, ], J 0 ’ 1 
Bhattaeharjee Lane, Calcutta-3, regarding the matters specified in th 
schedule, to the Third Industrial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of th 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 592 IMb./D/ 12L-5/52 
dated the 23rd February 1953, for adjudication. 

2. After usual notices the Parties entered appearance and filed theii 
written statements after taking adjournments. The pleadings wer< 
completed on 28th August 1954. The parties were thereafter directed t< 
file list of documents. The dispute was then heard on 10th January 1955 

3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order o: 
reference are as follows:— 

(1) If the closure of the Mills was justified and to what relief including 

compensation, the workers are entitled as a result. 

(2) Leave and holidays. 

(3) Retiring benefits. 

(4) Weekly rest and tiffin recess. 

(5) Overtime wages. 

DECISION. 

Issue No. 1. 

Messrs. Umacharan Sadhukhan Oil Mill (hereafter caller the Oil Mill) 
was a proprietory concern. It had in its employment 31 workmen compris- 
ing 4 Mistries, 6 Pressmen, 19 Coolies and 2 female workers. By a notice, 
dated 6th May 1954 (Ext. B), the said Oil Mill was closed with effect from ( 
7th May 1954 terminating thereby the employment of the aforesaid work-; 
men. Hence the dispute. 

The workmen alleged that as they were smarting under variom, 
grievances, they had joined Telkai Mazdoor Congress (hereafter called the 
Mazdoor Congress) in April 1934. They then submitted a charter of demands 
to the Labour Commissioner through the Mazdoor Congress. This enraged 
the employer. The latter to punish the workmen closed the Mill and started 
another mill with new recruits. 



695 


aw I] Tfi& CALtftTllA GAZETTE, FEBRTTABY 17, 1955 


The employe;, ozr th^o^her haw, contended that the Oil Mill was 
curring loss year after yjfkr for some years past and as a result of this 
also due to acqte trade depression and consequent dearth of work the Oil 
ill was closed* as aforesaid. The allegation of having started a new mill 
false. The proprietor has got another smaller oil mill in the same premises 
[rich had been in existence from long before the closure. This mil] of 
tiioh operation was temporarily suspended, resumed work with a comple- 
3 nt of 7 workmen. This is not a new mill starting work for the first time 
ter the closure as alleged. The employer acted bona fide in the matter 
roughout. 

In support of their case, Telkal Mazdoor Congress, representing the 
>rkmen, has examined the Mistry, P.W. 1, Shri Basudeb Dutta and one 
olie, P.W. 2, Shri Ram Chandra Ahir, besides proving documents 
:ts. 1 to 1(c), 2, 2(a), 3, 3(a), 4 to 4(b), 5 and 5(a). The employer 
the other hand, has examined the Chief Officer, D.W. 1, Shri Madhusudan 
.nerjee, besides proving documents, Exts. A to A3, B, C, D and 1)1. 

On giving oareful consideration to the evidence and circumstances, it 
pears to me that the closure of the Oil Mill was justified and had nothing 
do with the presentation of charter of demands or any such thing. 
,e successive balance-sheets from 1350 B.S. to 1349 B.S. (Exts. A to A3) 
to reveal that in each of those years the Oil Mill in question had sustained 
ses of Rs. 40,594-7 and odd, Its. 38,140, Rs. 20,810 and Rs. 35,292 
pectively. The evidence further reveals that in the year 1300 B.S. the 
11 had also incurred loss, the amount of which would be approximately 
. 40 thousand. I have had nothing sufficient to discard these balance- 
rs. The notice whereby closure was directed also makes mention of 
■se facts. P.W. 1 could not deny that the closure was due to the Josses 
urred during successive years. D.W. 1 deposed that the Mill was closed 
its capital was lost in successive years. The other mill which resumed 
rk from Ashar 1361 B.S., it is admitted by P.W. 1, has been existing for 
ong time in the same premises. His evidence also discloses that the said 
11 has separate exit and entrance and was closed temporarily from 
adra 1300 B.S. and was reopened in Jaistha 1361 B.S. It is a very small 
11 having only 7 workmen to run it. It is, therefore, no wonder that 
started crushing oil again. This cannot be construed as showing 
r la fide on the part of the employer. An employer may not be in a posi- 
n to keep a bigger mill going on which has been sustaining losses year 
er year and of which capital has been exhausted, but he may nonethe- 
k choose to operate a smaller one with a small complement involving 
eligible expenditure. It is for the employer to choose which of his mills 
would work and which not. The closure was directed on fith May 1954 
(1 it appears that the Mazdoor Congress did not present its demands 
ibodied in the other issues, 2 to 4, before 7th May 1954 [ vide Ext. 1(b)]. 
is, therefore, obvious that presentation of demands did not lead to Ihe 
)sure in question as alleged by the Mazdoor Congress. In the earlier 
o letters [Exts. 1 and 1(a)] the Mazdoor Congress made grievances 
out other workers and that to the Assistant Labour Commissioner. The 
mauds upon which conciliation started, it appears, were on the basis of 
bsequent letter, dated 7th May 1954. It also appears that the story 
victimisation originated after the closure and not before. The 
roplaiuts to the Factory Inspector and also to the Thana Officer, it 
pears, wore made not before but after the date of closure. I am, there- 
,p : of opinion that the closure was justified and it was not by way of 
itimisation. 


696 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBBUAAY 17, &66 [Paw 

----- r — - -- i 

As to relief, an employer has undoubtedly "thj right* jfap close down hi 
business and therefore no question of remkrifcnwkt ran arise. The onh 
relief which the workmen can get is compensation. * TUft, contention of thi 
employer that in case of closure a workman is noi even entitled t( 
compensation, cannot be upheld. The word “retrenchment” as defined i z 
section 2(oo) after recent amendment, means termination by the employe] 
of the service of a workman for any reason* whatsoever. The retrenchment 
so defined is, in my opinion, wide enough to cover the ease of termination 
of employment on account of closure of the business as well. It j 8 
therefore, obvious that a workman would be entitled to compensation j{ 
he fulfils the conditions of section 25(f) of the Act as introduced by recent 
amendment. In the present case, the list of the workmen annexed with 
the notice directing closure (Ext. B) shows that none of the workm eiL 
except 5 had continuous service of one year before termination 0 f 
employment following closure on 7th May 1954. The employer pleaded 
that in the Mill some were permanent workmen and the rest wire casual 
workmen. From the evidence and circumstances, I accept the employer’], 
version of the case in this respect. So, the workmen, who might have 
been employed from time to time according to requirement, were nothing 
more than casual workers. P.W. 2’s evidence to the contrary i« 
unreliable. In any case, none of them except 5 had continuous employ’ 
ment for a year. Those five workmen who had however continuous 
employment for not less than one year at the date of closure would get 
compensation as below: — b v 

One month's wages in lieu of notice and 15 days* average pay for every 
completed year of service or any part thereof in excess of six 
months. The word “wages" would mean as defined in section 
2(rr) as introduced by recent amendment. 

The Mill is directed to make the payment within one month from the date 
the award becomes enforceable. The remaining workmen are entitled to 
no relief. If the Mill in question re-starts work, it shall give opportunity 
to the discharged workmen to offer themselves for re-employment and the 
discharged workmen who offer tihemselves for re-employment shall have 
preference over other persons. 


Issues Nos. 2 to 5. 

In view of the above findings, these issues need no adjudication. 

I award accordingly as above. 

Dictated and corrected by me.

“1U. Transfer of ownership of a registered vessel . — The owner of an

in another State in India or in any country outside India. The

panied by a treasury challan showing that the prescribed fee 
has been deposited. After obtaining the sanction ot the Gov-

of vessel, the transferer and the transferee shall jointly make a 
report of the transter to the Registering Authority within the 
local limits of whose jurisdiction the transferee lesides or curries

tees have been deposited and, thereupon, such Registering 
Authority, if satisfied that the documents are in order and that 
the vessel is not median ieall\ detective and is ri\erworthy, shall 
enter the particulars ot t lie transfer of ownerdiip of the vessel 
in the certificate ot registration ’ \

No. 365Lab. /G/1R-21/54. — 4th February 1955. — In exercise of the 
power conferred by section 64 of the Factories Act, 1948 (LXIII of 1948), 
the Governor is pleased to make the following rules, the same having been 
previously published as required under section 115 of the said Act: — 

THE WEST BENGAL FACTORIES (EXEMPTION) RULE8, 1954. 

1. Title.—! 'liese rules may be called “The West Bengal Factories 
(Exemption) Rules, 1954. 

2. In these rules — 

(a) “the Act” means the Factories Act, 1948; 

(b) “section” means a section of the .Act; 

(c) “form” means a form appended to these rules; and 

(d) “holiday” includes a compensatory rest period referred to in rule 9 

of these rules. 

3. (1) The following persons employed in a factory shall, under sub- 
section (\) of section 64, be deemed to be persons holding positions of 
supervision or management or persons employed in a confidential position, 
uamel\ : — 

(a) Manager, 

(b) any other person who, in the opinion of the Inspector, holds a 

position of supervision or management or is employed in a confi- 
dential position. 

(2» A record of the names and designations of all persons defined under 
sub-rule (1) shall be maintained correctly, legibly, in ink, and shall be 
available in every factory for examination by the Inspector. 

4. No adult worker exempted from the provisions of section 51 other than 
an adult male worker employed under rule 6 on urgent repairs shall be 
allowed to work for more than 56 hours in any week. 

5. Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules no adult worker 
in respect to whom exemption from the provisions of section 52 has been 
granted shall be deprived of any holiday due to him in accordance with the 
provisions of section 53. 

6. Urgent repairs.— The provisions of sections 51, 52, 54, 55, 56 and 
61 shall not apply to adult male workers employed on urgent repairs, on 
condition that — 

(a) throughout the full period of such work, a notice, stating the 

names of the workers employed thereon* shall be displayed and 
maintained in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2) 
of section 108; 

(b) a notice stating fully the nature of the repairs, the time of com- 

mencement of work on the same and its probable duration, shall be 
sent to the Inspector forthwith; 

(u) no worker shall be employed on such work for more than — 

(i) ten consecutive days without a holiday for a whole day, 

(ii) fifteen hours on any one day, 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 24, 1955 


r I] 


(iii) thirty-nine hours during any three consecutive days, or 

(iv) sixty-six hours during each period of seven consecutive days- 

and 

(d) a statement showing the total number of hours worked each dav m 
the week by each worker shall be sent to the Inspector within 
thirty-six hours after the completion of the work. J 


Explanation ,— “Urgent repairs” means — 

(a) breakdown repairs to the motive power or plant and machinery of 

a factory which if not carried out expeditiously would involve 
danger to human life or safety, or delay resumption of the main 
manufacturing process ; 

(b) breakdown repairs to ships and aircrafts which are essential to 

enable them to leave port ut proper time or continue their normal 
operations in a sound condition; 

(c) breakdown repairs carried out in general engineering works or 

foundries to the motive power or plant of other factories, colli- 
eries, railways, dockyards, harbours, tramways, motor transport, 
gas works, electrical generating and pumping stations which 
are necessary to enable such concerns to maintain their services 
or resume their main manufacturing process with as little delay 
as possible; and 

(d) repairs in connection with a change of motive power, for example, 

from Bteam to electricity or vice versa, when such repairs cannot 
be done without stoppage of the main manufacturing process. 


7. Boiler house and engine room attendants.— The provisions of 
sections 51, 52, 54, 55, 56 and 61 shall not apply to adult male workers 
engaged solely on the work of attending to boilers or prime movers, on 
condition that — 


(a) the manager of the factory shall classify all such workers into 

groups according to the nature of their work; 

(b) a notice showing the group or groups of workers working under Ihe 

provisions of this rule shall be displayed and maintained in 
accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 108; 

(c) an attendance register for such workers is maintained in the form 

appended these rules and in respect of emh such worker the time 
of commencement of each period of work shall be entered thereiu 
beforehand and the time of finishing each period of work shall be 
entered therein immediately after completion of the period oi 
work; 

(d) no such worker shall be employed for more than fourteen consecutive 

days without a holiday for a whole day; and 

(e) no such worker shall be employed so as to w r ork in excess of any of 

the limits specified in sub-section (4) of section 64.

male workers and the provisions of sections 5r>, 5b and > s

55 shall not apply to adult male workers employed in gramophone factories, 
on the work of electrical deposition of copper on and reconditioning of wax 
matrices, on condition that-— 

(a) the manager of the factory shall classify all such workers into groups 

according to the nature of their work; 

(b) a notice showing the group or groups of workers working under the 

provisions of this rule shall he displayed ami maintained in 
accordance with provisions of sub-section (2) ol section 108; 

(c) an attendance register for such workers is maintained in the ionn 

uppended to these rules and in respect ol each Midi 
worker the time of commencement of each pedad ol work shall 
he entered therein beforehand and the time of finishing each penial 
of work shall be entered therein immediately a Her completion 
of the period of work; and 

(d) no such worker shall be employed so as to work in excess of the 

limits specified in clause (i) of sub-section (4) of section 04. 

16. Rubber Factories.—- Curing by autoil^vrs .— The provisions of 
sections 55 and 56 shall not apply to adult male workers employed in rubber 
factories on the work of curing by autoclaves, on condition that— 

(a) the manager or occupier of the factory, beior he avails himself 
of this exemption, has served on the Inspector and displayed in 
the factory a notice of his intention so to avail Jiimseli, aw 
whilst he avails himself of the exemption, shall keep the no ue 

so displayed; and 


m 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 24, 1955 


[Pai 


(b) an attendance register for such workers is maintained in the form 
appended to these rules and in respect of each such worker the 
time of commencement of each period of work shall be entered 
therein beforehand and the time of finishing each period of work 
shall be entered therein immediately after completion of the 
period of work. 


17. Milk Pasteurising Factories. — The provisions of section 52 shall not 
apply to adult workers engaged in milk pasteurising factories using a 
mechanical or electrical process on condition that no worker in such factories 
shall be employed for more than fourteen consecutive days without a holiday 
for a whole day.

Alter usual summons the parties entered a])pearancc and filed their 
u slalements. Tile pleadings were completed on 1 1 tli An ■ ■ f r : i . 
unties were thereafter directed to file list of documents and then the

ll>c matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order ot

l) Dearness allowance.

- - ^ i - i - 

? DECISION. * * ^ * 

Messrs. Chandbali Steamer Service Co., Ltd. used to carry on coastul 
shipping trade. ItB head office is located at 29, Strand Road, Calcutta. 

The workmen alleged that they were smarting under various grievances. 
Accordingly Chandbali Steamer Service Workers’ Union % was 
formed. It presented a charter of demands wl|ereuiJbn con. 
cilintion proceedings started. In course of the # said con- 
ciliation there was a joint conference before the Assistant Labour 
Commissioner. There an agreement was arrived at between the ^Company 
and the Union regarding hours of work, holiday allowance, overtime allow- 
auce, leave rules, casual leave, sick leave and date of payment of monthly 
salary. The questions of dearness allowance and cheap canteen however 
remained to be settled subsequently. As no settlement was eventually 
arrived at, the matter of dearness allowance has been referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. The workmen prayed for payment of dearness 
allowance at the rate of 110 per cent, of the basic pay from 1st November 
1952. 

Tbe Company, on the other hand, pleaded that it was passing through 
serious financial crisis and was heavily involved in debts and had no 
capacity to pay deuruess allowance over and above wbat it has low been 
paying as consolidated wageB. 

The dispute was fixed for hearing on 31st January 1955. Neither tht 
Company nor the Union representing the workmen appeared and tool 
steps. In the circumstances, it is taken that there is no dispute to be 
adjudicated by this Tribunal. 

I award accordingly.

sought to be made out in the written statement put forward at the time of 
hearing and argument, of retrenchment for economic reasons, has also no 
leg to stand upon. Any termination of service except by way of disciplinary 
action is retrenchment and the Act provides a remedy for it. Here again,

there can hardly be any justification for retrenching the nine workmen and

that there was no dearth of work for which all these nine hands had to bp 
discharged. The washermen, the boys, who are not members of lie 
Laundry Workers’ Union, were not touched. Could it be Baul with any 
show of reason that the alleged reduction in work did not affect any of 
them at all? But in actual fact, none of them was retrenched. That 
being the case, retrenchment on the ground of economy also fails. X n 
formal notice was given to these workmen before this discharge. On fj le 
other hand, this came as a sudden blow for which they were probably not 
fully prepared. In any view of the matter, the termination of services 
of the workmen appears to be unjustified. 

Now the question is what relief they are entitled to. I have anxiously 
considered the question of reinstatement which is the normal relief in these 
circumstances. From time to time, duriug the conciliation proceedings, 
the proprietor expressed his willingness to take back some of these work- 
men into his service. The workmen refused to join unless all of them 
were taken in. Mr. Wong, the proprietor, thereafter agreed to take all 
of them into service on contract basis. That happened during the eon. 
filiation proceedings. So it is nobody’s case that the parties have lost 
their confidence in each other. The case of the present staff does not 
present any real difficulty for they had their eyes opened when they joiner! i 
the service temporarily. Of the nine workmen, lllius (No. 7) was* ahead’ 
re-employed. The remaining S should be reinstated in their former pos 
within a week from the date of the operation of this award. 

Now as to compensation for loss of employment during this period 
claimed by the workmen, the workmen are no doubt entitled to some cam 
pensation in the circumstances of the case. The proprietor had to engag. 
the staff to carry on his business soon after the termination of the service 
of these workmen. And these workmen, who are still unemployed, u 
times, refused to join unless all of them were taken in. On a careful con 
sideration „of all the relevant, facts and circumstances of the cunh. as alsi 
the hardships of both sides in this matter, 1 think that one mouth's wage 
at the rate last drawn, w'uuld be sufficient compensation (now that 1 hey an 
being reinstated) for Iorr of their employment. The payment under thi 
award should be made within one month from the date of publication m 
this award to all the workers except lllius who is already in service «l 
the company. I answer the issue accordingly. This is my award.

DECISION. 


Issues 1, 2 and 3 are taken up together for consideration. 

In support of his case the workman, Shri Dudnath Kurmi, has himself 
deposed (1WV. 1) besides proving his Employment Book (Ext. 1) ami
