Shri Dudnath Kurmi admittedly joined as Lifter (Tulumlnr) in the 
Jute Handling Department of the mill of this Company. The employment 
book produced by liim (Ext. 1) shows that he had first worked under the 
contractor in this mill from 1st January 1943 and then directly under the 
Cnnipnuy since 1st January 1948. Formerly the work in the Jute Hand ling 
Department used to be managed on the basis of contract labour. Vnder the 
award ot the First Jute Textile Tribunal published in 194S, there was 
recommendation for abolition of the contract labour system and for direct 
engagement of labour in place thereof. It appears from Ext. n, that the 
Company under the instructions of the Managing Agents, Bird & Co. Ltd., 

, gsiu* effect to the said recommendations and took the workmen including 
1 ^liri Dudnath Kurmi in its direct employment from 1st April 19-1S and gave 
■redit for length of their past service under the contractor. Tt appears from 
die said document that workman. Shri Dudnath Kurmi started work under 
llie contractor in 1943 and the Company gave credit for the said past 
service from 1st January 1943. Thus the total service of the workman 
heiore termination oi his employment was for a period of 9 year* 10 months 
and not 30 years as alleged by him. The workman in his evidence had to 
admit that he had joined the mill onlv sometime before homh'i.g in Calcutta

AWARD. 

Issue No. 1. — On behalf of the employer it has been pointed out that 
although there are apparent irregularities between the scale of pay as 
framed by the First Tribunal, on an analysis it is found that there are 
defferent scales for a particular type of workers as noted in the Memorandum 
filed by the Company. The apparent irregularity, therefore, is no irregu- 
larity and I hold that the scales as framed by the Tribunal were those as 
are noted in the Memorandum. Within these grades a separate scale of 
pay was allotted to each worker at the date of trial by the last Tribunal. 
The pay that he was then drawing in the scale was shown as a minimum 
pay of his personal scale. His pay on that date was calculated according 
to the number of years of service that he has put in. So, in the case of 
Clerks I find that there were two other grades— 

60 — 2J — 90. 

74-4—106. 

and the other grades are as noted in Company’s Memorandum. j 

i 

The last Award was made in 1949 when Tribunal as well an the Uni< 
leaders were influenced by the balance-sheet of 1947 which showed the ] ( i 
of Rs. 17,269. The Union had accordingly agreed to low grades of salai 
with regard to these employees, particularly the Clerks but since then 
years have passed. Although the previous agreement embodies all Ion 
term matters, still in the circumstances of the case, the grades urgent 
require a revision in order to keep pace with time and the present day co. 
of living. It was pointed out by the learned Lawyer for the Company thi 
in 1951 the Club suffered a loss to the extent of Rs. 11,675 but in the y« 
1952 it earned a profit of Rs. 575-14-6 and again in 1963 it suffered a In 
of Rs. 4,354 and odd. The sum total of the profit and loss of the thre 
years show that the loss was even smaller than what it was in 1947 alow 
However, on that date the Company stood pressure of the last Award quii 
well and its financial condition has not deteriorated than what it was tH 
In the circumstances a revision of the wage scale, which it is necessary, 
be granted to keep pace with time and the cost of living should in 
fitness of the circumstances be granted.

present, emoluments. 1 do not think that any further increase on tlu* \m 
dearness allowance will be justified. So, the claim for increase of ih 
dearness allowance is turned down. 

Issue Mo. 2. — No particular case of hardship has been brought to lit

MEDICAL AND PUBLIC HEALTH DEPARTMENT 
Medical 

NOTIFICATION. 

No. Medl . / 1013 / 1-8 / 55 . — 8th February 1955. — In exercise of the ] 
conferred by clauses (a) to (h) of sub-section (1) of section 96 o 
Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 (XXXIY of 1948), the Gover 
pleased to make the following 1 rules, the same having been prey 
published as required by sub-section (1) of section 96 of the said 
namely: — 

THE WEST BENGAL EMPLOYEES’ STATE INSURANCE (MED! 
BENEFIT) RULES, 19SS. 

PART I— Genehal. 

1. Short title, extent and oommeneement.— (1) These rules shall 
called the West Bengal Employees’ State Insurance (Medical Benefit) It 
1955. 

(2) They extend to the whole of West Bengal. 

(3) They shall come into operation in such areas of WeBt Bengal am 
such dates as the State Government may, by notification in the 0jj { 
Gazette , appoint. 

2. Definitions.— In these rules unless there is anything repugnant 
the subject or context, — 

(1) “Act” means the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 (XXX 

of 1948); 

(2) “Corporation" means the Employees’ State Insurance Cornorati 

set up under the Act; 

(3) “Drugs” includes all medicines for internal or external use i 

human beings and all substances intended to be used ftu oriutj 
treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease in human being 

(4) “ Medical Practitioner ” means a person holding a quali 

granted by an authority specified or notified under section ;■ 
Indian Medical Degrees Act, 1916 (VII of 1916), or spec 
the Schedules to the Indian Medical Council Act. 1TO {’ 
of 1933), or a person registered in the medical register o 
Bengal meant for the registration of persons practising alb 
system of medicine; 

(5> "Medical Referee " means a medical officer appointed as such 
Corporation ; 

(6) “ quarter ” means any one of the periods from the 1st day of Ja 

to the Hist day of March, the 1st day of April to the M 
of June, the 1st day of July to the 30th day of Septemke 
the 1st day of October to the f31st day of December; 

(7) “ regulations ” means the Employees* State Insurance (Gel 

Regulations, 1950, framed under section 97 of the Act; 

(8) "State Government" means the Government of the Sta^l 

Bengal ; 



r II THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 24, 1955 


841 


(9; “State Insurance medical formulary ” means a list of prescriptions 
and injections lud down by the Corporation from time to time; 

10) All other words and expressions used herein but not defined sh ill 
have the same meaning as is assigned to them in the Act' ihe 
Rules, made under section 95 of the Act or the Regulations und«r 
section 97 of the Act, as the case may be. 


PART II — Provisions relating to medical benefit. 

b Scale Of medical benefit. — The medical benefit provided under these 
s shall be according to the following scale: — 

(1) General medical services which shall include treatment at the clinic 

of an Insurance Medical Practitioner or other institution and 
shall consist of — 

(i) all treatment other than treatment involving the application of 
special skill or experience; 

(ii) such preventive treatment as vaccination and inoculation;

1. The original reference out of which this case has arisen was raa 
under Government order No. 38Dis. /D/11L-219/52, dated the 3rd J anua 
1953. 


AWARD. 

The contention of the worker is two-fold, viz., (1) that he was a pennanfl 
employee in t lie Tablet Department of the Company having completed 
period oi probation; and (2) that his discharge should have been preface , 
a nolice, and by having secured the prior permission of the Tribunal beifl 
whom tlie main case was then pending. 


r ^ THE CALCUm GAZETTE, MARCH 3, 1965 W5 


The Company denies all these things. It alleges that the applicant in 
,tion was a temporary employee and, as such, no permission of the 
iunal under the section 33 of the Act was necessary here. Besides, the 
pany did not require any longer the services of this employee. 

;t can never be argued that obtaining of permission from the Tribunal 
ir section 33 of the Act is out of place when the worker discharged 
jens to be a temporary hand. The section 33 might be out of place 
ii a temporary hand is employed either for a specific period, or for a 
ified employment. In such a case the appointment of the temporary hand 
dnates when that period is over, or when that work is finished. No 
ce from the employer is necessary to terminate such services. Such 
lination is automatic, more or less. No overt act on the part of the 
loyer is called for. In such a case, of course, no permission of the 
)unal is necessary. But where the nature of the employment is such 
. it does not bring the employment under any of the above two specified 
is, prior permission of the Tribunal is necessary even though the man 
rht to be discharged happens to be a temporary hand. If any authority 
ceded, I should refer to the case of the Eastern Chemical Co. (India) 
Gangaram and nine others (Rastriya Chemical Kamgar Sangh) reported 
he L.L.J., December 1953, page 882. 

doming to the facts of the present case, the worker has not examined 
self. His representative has filed a copy of the award given by this 
iunal, published in the Calcutta Gazette of the 19th November 1953. 
m this it is clear that the applicant’s service was terminated during the 
lency of the main case before the Tribunal, the date of termination being 
February 1953 ( vide Ext. A). The next question is whether any 
nission of the Tribunal was necessary under the section 33 of the Act 
the termination of his services. That no such application under the 
Ion 33 was made, is admitted. Exhibit Al, of course, shows that this 
icant was appointed on a temporary basis in the leave vacancy of one 
Satish Saha on 10th July 1952. That, of course, displaces the 
icant’s contention that he was a permanent employee. But it is not the 
of the Company that Shri Satish Saha returned to liis duties, and as a 
It, the applicant was thrown out of employment, he being a mere hadli 
ser. That has not been stated to be the cause of his discharge. ITe was 
laced by one Madhab Pattabardhan, a permanent worker {vide Ext. A). 
P. W. 1, the Company’s witness, gives the following reasons for the 
harge of this man: — 

“In OctoW 1952 about 34 men were retrenched. Among them there 
were some permanent workers also. In expectation of coming 
of some machines this man was retained. Those machines 
actually came towards the end of January or early in February 
1953. As his work was no longer necessary, he was discharged. ’ 

Refers to certain correspondence ending on the 22nd January 1953, which 
p that these machines were received sometime in the end of January 
. If this witness wants to say that the coming of these machines 
fcred the services of this temporary man unnecessary, then lie stands 
'adicted by his own document, Ext. A. Therein I find that one Madhab 
ibardlian, a permanent worker, was appointed to do his work consequent 
te discharge of this man. So it can never be contended tha * the coming 
tose machines rendered the services of the petitioner redundant. Of 
e, what the witness wants to say is not very clear. He says that this 
was retained in the expectation of coming of some machines. If the 


946 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 3, 1965 - [Pah 


man was allowed to continue in the service so that he might be utilised 
the work of the new machines, then there can be no point in dischargj 
him when the machines did actually arrive. So the Company cannot sati, 
the Tribunal as to the real reason why this applicant was discharged, 
least, the reasons which the Company has shown do not carry convict^ 
In his argument the learned Advocate of the Company wanted to say tj 
as some permanent men were retrenched, and that retrenchment was f 01I 
justified in the main case, this temporary hand could be discharged 
without any reason. Such an argument can never hold water. If thi 8 lns 
being a temporary worker, was liable to be chucked out before the pern^ 
hands were discharged, then why was he retained P He might have b e 
retained graciously by the Company, but that does not give the Comp a , 
any justification to retrench him at any time it pleases. At all events t] 
Company should have taken prior permission of the Tribunal under t] 
section 33 of the Act. So the Company's act in discharging this wurt, 
cannot be justified. The section 33 has been infringed, and the p e titi 0 
under the section 33A does lie. 

Now, coming to the relief which I should grant to the applicant, in j 
present case, I find that he has been displaced by a permanent hand, ft; 
also in the published award that some permanent hands were retrench 
The claim of a permanent hand to the service is certainly stronger than ft. 
claim of a temporary hand, so far as retention in the service is concpmej 
So I cannot set aside the order of discharge in the present case. But 
should grant some compensation to this applicant for his irregular discharge 
Ho might be a temporary hand, yet lie should not have been disdain 
without the sanction of the Tribunal and without good reasons. So I ffraj | 
him compensation to the extent of four months' wages on the scab of m 
last drawn, I mean, basic salary and dearness allowance. This is mai 
payable within one month of the award coming into operation. 


I award no cost in this case.

In respect of the above grades, the Union suggests that the grade D slioi

Rs. 80 — 5 — 120 — 74 — 180.

Against this the Company contends that no revision of the grades should 
be made until and unless the Mercantile Tribunal’s award is revised. There 
has been no change of circumstances since the said award which could 
warrant such a drastic revision. 

The Union, on the other hand, contends that the Mercantile Trilmr 1 ^ 
award did nothing more than giving an extra amount of Rs. 10 on a flat * 
on what was allowed by the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. So it wai 
ad hoc basis. It had no solid foundation on scientific basis. As such 
Tribunal will be perfectly justified in granting revision of the grades, e 

Let me consider the matter in this perspective. 

The Mercantile Tribunal had before it 237 companies. Being a ms 
Tribunal, it had to consider not only big commercial concerns, hut i 
concerns of comparatively insignificant status. In such a case, the high 
common factor was generally fouud out and prescribed so that it might i 
work out hardship on any. Now, if the present workmen want that the ss 
award had outlived its utility, and it should be revised, they should do 
by a froutal attack and not bv a lateral one as here. The Goverumej 
should have been approached. If the Government thought it expedient, J 
could have set up another major Tribunal to go into the question, and Jj 
make appropriate revision to answer the requirements of time. But W 



r*ffl THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 3, 1955 


)t done. What is done iftj approaching the matter in a round about way. 
ome firms are selected, and their grades are revised, this Tribunal would 
esponsible for provoking fresh disputes where there is none. In the 
It, Government’s hands will be forced much against its will. That is 
>r conducive to industrial peace. 

Phere is another aspect from which the matter should be considered. 

, major Tribunal dealt with in a comprehensive manner all conceivable 
utes, actual and probable, in respect of the industry. Very good results 
> also been achieved by other major Tribunals to promote industrial 
e. For instance, the major Engineering Tribunal has secured peace 
i good number of years. So aho the major Cotton Textile Tribunal, and 
najor Jute Tribunal. What I mean to say is that awards of such major 
unals should not be disturbed in this piece-meal manner. If they call 
my revision, that should be done in a collective manner as by another 
>r Tribunal. 

'he learned Advocate of the Union argued eloquently before me that the 
pantile Tribunal did not have any opportunity of having the Pay 
mission’s Report. That does not appear to me as a fact. Even if it 
so, I do not think that the decision would have been otherwise than 
; it has been. Even the grades prescribed by the Pay Commission were 
mbstantially different from what were given by the Mercantile Tribunal’s 
d, if the liberal dearness allowance is taken together. The award of 
Mercantile Tribunal was never tentative. It was quite broad-based, 
use there was the Bengal Chamber of Commerce’s decision about grades 
mg its basis. The very liberal decision about dearness allowance was 
before it. There was also an agreement among all the parties figuring 
•p it regarding the acceptance of the suggested grades and scales. In 
context, what the Mercantile Tribunal decided was a well considered 
ion. I am not here to sit in judgment over the said decision. Even 
thought fit to modify the recommendations in certain respects, I would 
in from doing so for reasons referred to above. 

ext, it was very seriously contended by the learned Advocate of the 
ti that the Mercantile Tribunal did not base its decision on scientific 
What tlie learned Advocate really meant by “scientific data” is not 
clear. If he meant that the Mercantile Tribunal did not arrive at 
grades by going into the questions of subsistence wages, then I would 
hat the argument does not go very far. The Tlon’ble Labour Appellate 
mal in its award in respect of the Caltex (India), Ltd., in November 
■ decided that Rs. 67-8 was the minimum wage for a clerical employee 
19o2, L.A.C., page 402). So, if Rs. 70 is fixed as the minimum of 
owest grade, no complaint can really he made. Their Lordships, of 
c. in the Caltex (India), Ltd., case fixed Rs. 80 as the minimum of the 
i grade. But that was because it was an Oil Company. Oil CumpnniHS 
iy a unique position amonp the* companies trading in India. They 
huge foreign capital at their back. They make collosal profits. They 
J monopoly business. So what grade ean be viven in case of oil 
inies in general, and Caltex (India), Ltd., in particular, can never 
Pen literally in case of other firms. If we take a dispassionate view 
all at once see that such a step would be attended with serious 
uence. Oil is a commodity which is used commonly either by the 
eople or by commercial concerns, but engineering commodities or

der the Managing Agency of Messrs. Martin Burn, Ltd. Of course, the

plementing the award under section 20 of the Industrial Dispute 
.ppellate Tribunal) Act. But in the present case, the Union has specified 
ose companies in its written statement, and the Company has also

the contention of the Company that the Managing Agents cannot be,

ought into the picture. They must present their say before the Tribunal,

itten statements. So this formal objection is not tenable. The specific 
ntention of Messrs. Martin Burn, Ltd., is three-fold, viz., — 

(1) Regarding Railway Companies Nos. 2, C, 7, 10, 11 and 17. The 
appropriate Government is not the Slate Government, hut the 
Central Government. So the present Tribunal is not competent 
to go into the case of those companies. This contention lias 
been conceded by the learned Advocate of the Union. I also 
accept it. So, I award that the companies Nos. 2, 6, 7, 10, 11 
and 17 as per written statement of the Union altogether six 
companies, will not be bound by my present award. 

(l 2 ) The Company’s contention regarding the Electricity companies is 
that profits are limited to 5 per cent, under the Electricity Act, 
1948. So if the expenditure is increased by the Tribunal, in 
granting relief to the workmen, that will contravene the said 
Electricity Act. These Electricity Companies are Nos. 1, 3, 4, 
14, 16, 19, 20 and 21, i.e., altogether eight companies. 1 do not 
accept the Company’s aforesaid contention. The Statute may 
have fixed the dividend or profit which the Companies are 
entitled to earn being public utility concerns. But that is no 
reason why the wages of the lal>ourers or workmen working in 
the said concerns cannot be increased. The expenditure never 
is, or can be fixed. The heads may be specified. So the Com- 
panies are certainly bound by my award. 

(3) Regarding the other companies, the general objection of Messrs. 
Martin Burn, Ltd., is that under the order of reference two 
conditions must co-exist, and be satisfied before they can be 
made liable under the award. These conditions are viz., —

NOTIFICATION. 

Burdwan.— No. 1580/ M13R-52/ 54.— 25th February 1955.— -Whereas i| u , 
Commissioners of the Dainhat Municipality in the district of JUinLvun 
have made the following rules under section 75 of the Bengal Municnnl 
Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), and have applied to the State Uo\ em- 
inent for confirmation of the said rules under section 50G of the said Ad- 

And whereas — 

(a) notice of the intentiou to apply for such confirmation of the said 

rules has been duly given one month before the making of 
application for confirmation as required under clause (i) of Mil,, 
section (2) of section GOG of the said Act, and 

(b) for one month before the making of the application a copy of I lie 

said rules has been kept at the office of the Commissioners of the 
said municipality and 1ms been open during office hours thereat 
to the inspection of the inhabitants of the said muninpalitv, 
without fee, as required by clause (ii) of sub-section (2) ot 
section 50G of the said Act; 

Noiv, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 50( of 
i lie Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), the Governor is 
pleased to confirm the following rules, namely: — 


Rules regarding Iaav6| fining, suspension and removal of municipal officers 
and servants and the nature and amount of security deposits to be 
furnished by them. 

1. Casual leave for n period not exceeding 7 days at any one time, or 
15 days in 12 months, and leave on medical certificate for any peiiwl nol 
exceeding a month, may be granted by the Chairman with or without pay 
rind with or without, the" appointment of a substitute, to any officer or servant 
L)f the Commissioners. 


2. The Chairman may also grant to n female servant of the Commis- 
sioners maternity leave on full pay for a period which may extend up to tli* 1 
end of 3 months from the date of its commencement or to the end of G weeks 
from the date of confinement, whichever be earlier. Leave of any other 
kind may be granted in continuation of maternity leave, if the request, for 
grant bo supported by a medical certificate. 

3. All other leave must be granted by the Commissioners at a meeting 
provided that the leave and leave allowances granted to any employee ni 
tho Commissioners shall in no case exceed that, or those to which he would 
be entitled if he were a Government servant. 


4. The Chairman may inflict for neglect of duty a fine not, exceeding 
one-fourtli of a month’s pay upon an officer or servant, of the Commissioners: 
provided that the orders of the Chairman inflicting a fine on an oncer 
drawing Rs. 20 per mensem or upward shall be submitted for the continua- 
tion of the Commissioners at their next ordinary meeting. 

5. Tlie Chairman may suspend any officer or secant of the Oommis- 
sioners for misconduct, or incompetence: provided that, in every < a, 
which the officer’s salary exceeds Rs. 20 per mensem, the matter shall bo lam 
before the Commissioners at their next ordinary meeting. 

6. Before any officer is removed or dismissed the charges ojjniiisj him 
shall he reduced to writing and communicated to him and his rtj) >, 

shall be recorded.

11. In exceptional cases, the municipal Commissioners may, with the 
sanction of the State Government, vary or alter the above rules in favour of 
particular officers for reasons to be recorded in writing. 

12. Store-keepers, sub-store-keepers and subordinates entrusted with the 
custody of stores shall be required to furnish security of an amount calculat- 
ed to cover the following proportion of the value of the Btores under their 
charge: — 

(a) Heavy tools and plant (rollers, machines, etc.) — Nil. 

(b) Heavy stores not readily saleable in the locality (joists, largest 

sections, etc.) — Half value. 

(c) Light stores for which there is u ready sale in the local market — 

jFull value. 

If any departure is desired from this scale owing to the circumstances of 
any case or local conditions the sanction of Government will he required. 
The municipal Commissioners shall determine whether the amount of the 
security will be paid in a lump sum or by deductions from pay. The 
security shall be invested in the manner prescribed in rules A and 9.

No. 1004M.P.— 28tli February 1955. — Whereas 
Messrs. Tamraiipta Go-operative Electric Supply 
Society, Limited, the licensees of the Tamluk 
Electric Licence, 1950, have made an application 
for making certain amendments in the terms and 
conditions of the said licence, so as to suitably 
reduce the requirements contained in clause 11 
thereof, providing for the maintenance of con- 
tinuous supply of energy for twenty-four hours 
throughout the year; 

Ami whereas, in the opinion of the State 
Government, the public interest permits the 
making of such amendment in the said terms and 
conditions ; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by clause (h) of suit-section (3) of section 4 
of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), 
the Governor is pleased, after consultation with 
the local authority concerned, namely, the Com- 
missioners of the Tamluk Municipality, to direct 
that during the continuance in force of this 
notification, clause 11 of the said licence shall 
have effect as if in the said clause for the words 
and figure “for 24 hours throughout the year” 
the words “from half past five o'clock pout 
meridian every day to naif past four o’clock 
ante meridian next following” hud been substi- 
tuted. 

This notification shall remain in fore? up to the 

31st March 1966. 

By order of the Gtotenw, 

V. DAS. S*y.

7. On taking such possession the said Govern- 
ment may sell or otherwise deal with the said land 
as it may think proper. 

(i) Should the said Government sell the land the 
said Government after deducting the expenses in- 
curred in connection with the said taking of 
possession and with such sale shall pay the proceeds 
to the Company. 

(ii) Should the said Government decide not to 
sell the land, the said Government shall retain the 
said land* in which case the Governor shall repay 
to the Company the market value as on the day of 
re-entry of the land and all sums received 
from the Company in respect of all and every 
compensation as provided in the foregoing first 
clause dess the statutory allowance of 15 per cent, 
and less any amount received on account of trees 
which are not in existence at the time of resump- 
tion), but will not repay any sums paid and received

i 

(iii) Should the said Government decide to sell 
the land only upon such sale, the Governor shall 
after deducting the expenses of taking possession

from the Company in respect of the compensation 
for the land (less the statutory allowance of 15 per 
cent, and less any amount received from the Com- 
pany on account of trees which are nut in existence 
at the time of resumption), but will not repay any 
sum paid and received on account of costs, charges 
and expenses. 

8. The public shall be benefited by this acquisi- 
tion iu the following manner: — 

(i> fl) The Company shall admit annually for 
regular and systematic training 8 Trade Appren- 
tices in the various processes carried out in the 
Company’s factory. 

( 2) The apprentices shall be selected by a Joint 
Committee consisting of one representative of the 
Company and the I h rector of Industries, West. 
Bengal, or his representative. The Company shall 
not charge any fee or premium for such training. 

(3) The duration of training of each apprentice 
shall be one year. The first batch of 8 apprentices 
should be taken immediately after the notification 
of the agreement. 

(4) In making selection preference shall be given 
to the candidate who is a permanent resident of 
West Bengal. 

(5) During the training period the Company shall 
pay Rs. 35 per month to each trainee as subsistence 
allowance in addition to free residential accommoda- 
tion, 

(6) The Company shall submit periodical reports 
on tne progress of work of the apprentices and shall 
grant certificates of proficiency to those apprentices 
who successfully complete their training. 

During the period of training, the apprentices 
shall abide by the existing rules and regulations of 
the pompany as .regards attendance, conduct, etc. 

(8) In appointing officers and employees under 
the Company, it shall give preference to the 
apprentices trained under this Scheme. 


(9) Should there be any adverse report 
any apprentice it should forthwith be bn 
his notice and a copy of the report togetl 
the explanation of the apprentice concerned

work of the car drivers, it is necessary that their hours of work should be 
fixed. Under section 65(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, a driver should not 
be allowed to work (a) for more than five hours before he has had o.i interval 
of rest of at least half an hour ; or (b) for more than nine hours < u one da 
or (c) for more than 54 hours in the week. The hours of work and perio 
of rest have been explained in rules 88 and 89 of the Bengal Motor Vchirlt 
Buies, 1940. It is not clear from the Union’s chart whether hours of wni 
for drivers shown in Ext. 7 include interval of rest. The best thing, i: 
the circumstances, to do is to fix the Bame hours of work as have been dou 
under section 65 of the Motor Vehicles Act and I do so in this instant case 
The drivers are now required to work on Sundays when necessary. Thi; 
cannot be totally avoided for the factories are mostly situated in om of tfei 
way places, accessible only by cars, and accordingly urgent and emergenn 
cases require the attendance of the drivers at all hours and on all days. I 
gather tnat some of the drivers are provided with quarters in the faclory- 
premises and with good reason. The drivers, therefore, should wot !"’ 1 
Sundays when required. Of course, they are to be paid overtime whir 
now being paid under the Standing Orders (Order No. 20) in accord: 
with the provisions of the Factories Act. The Works Manager and 61 
dhury Babu could not give the rate of allowance payable to drivers worl 
on Sundays and holidays. They said that the drivers are paid seme i 
allowance for these days at the rate between Be. 1 to B». 2 per day. J 
Tribunal does not encourage any difference in treatment in this res] 
between factory workers and drivers particularly when the Standing 6ri 
aTe made applicable to them. They are, therefore, entitled to get 1 
accordance with the provisions of the Factories Act. 


Pabt I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 10, 1965 


1053 


Regarding the Sweepers employed within the factory premises, they get 
; he same leave facilities and enjoy the same hours of work as other workers 
Employed in the factory under the Factories Act. They are not required 
to attend on Sundays. But Sweepers who are employed for work outside the 
Factory have the same hours of work but they are required to attend on 
Sundays. They do not get festival holidays and extra leave under the Award. 
No case has been made out justifying any change either in the hours of work 
)r in leave and holiday facilities. 

The Gardeners are not required to work on Sundays. Their hours of 
vork as shown in Ext. K are 8 per day. But during argument, Shri Bose 
laid that they had no regular hours of work and that only one of them was 
employed in the factory and seven outside it. They get 14 days privilege 
leave, 15 days sick leave and 10 days festival leave. No case lias been made 
)ut justifying any change in the existing arrangement. 

The Bearers enjoy with the Durwans and the Car Drivers privilege leave 
r>f 21 4 a y®> casual leave of 7 days and sick leave of 15 days on hulf pay. 
They also enjoy the festival holidays and are not required to attend on 
Sundays. They get uniforms. Their usual hours of work are 8 per day. 
These do not call for any change at present. 

I do not think that any compensatory holiday should, at present, be 
jiven to any of the said workers who is liable to be called for duly on 
Sundays. But they should be paid overtime at the rate mentioned above, 
[t is desirable that overtime should be avoided as far as possible and only in 
argent and emergency cases, the decision of which will rest with the 
management, the worker will be required to do it. Overtime work has 
caused considerable irritation among the drivers and there are good reasons 
to believe that the privileges now enjoyed by some of the staff for free use 
of cars is now being abused without the knowledge of the management. 
This should be stopped. The calling of the drivers to duty on Sundays and 
holidays should be made in urgent and emergency cases only, and formal 
notices should be given in advance wherever possible, and formal warrants 
nr log book containing orders be handed over to the drivers where the hours 
of departure and arrival with dates and nature of duty be noted. It appears 
that warnings are not noted as required under the Standing Orders in the 
registers and service sheets and the service record of at least one driver pro- 
duced before the Tribunal, disclosed a very unsatisfactory >;tate of affairs. 
This was not maintained correctly and up-to-date. In the interest of security 
of service, service records should be kept properly and in due course of 
business and not perfunctorily as has been done in the case of Pra Iliad Ring. 

I answer the issue accordingly. This is my award. 

Dictated and corrected by me.

(XIV of 1947), tlie Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, b

SCHEDULE. 

(1) Additional bonus for 1952 payable to the clerical employees of tb 
Company in Calcutta District Office and installations in the 
Calcutta industrial area. 

AWARD. 

Admittedly the Company has paid bonus for the year 1952, equivalent 
to one month's wages to the clerks concerned in this present prorefldir ff 1 
The said employees however claim six months * wages as additional bon 
for the said year. The Company having refused to produce the llalanf 
Sheet, it is contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal is 
presume that if the Balance-Sheets were produced the hugeness of profit f 
the year 1952 and the previous years would have been disclosed. 

The Company does not take the plea of incapacity or want of means i 
pay the additional bonus as claimed by the Union but the Companj 


1055 


■as® I] THE CALCUTTA #A*ETTE, INARCH 10, 1965 

ontention is ^feat it should not pay anything which will not be reasonable 
n the circumstances of the case and the circumstances as contended are as 

ollows: — 

That the Company indents petrol and other products from foreign 
countries and stores them here and sell the same at profit and that 
the Caltex Company is only one of the many such companies 
dealing in the same commodities and amongst the three companies, 
viz., Burmah Shell & Co., Standard Vacuum Company and Caltex 
(India), Ltd.; the present Company, i.e., Caltex (India), Ltd., 
occupies the third place. 

It is argued on behalf of the Company that the average basic wage paid 
to a workman of this Company amounts to Us. 165 per month and if the 
average dearness allowance and the money value of other benefits which 
the workmen at present enjoy are added together, the total emolument 
would exceed the living wage figure even upon calculation on the basis of 
390 as the cost of living index. 

It appears from Ext. 3, produced by the Union that Burmah Shell 
imported about 11,74.64,089 gallons of oil and Standard Vacuum imported 
about 7,90,01,447 gallons of oil whereas Caltex (India), Ltd., imported 
3,93,34.318 gallons of oil during the year 1952. From this statement it 
appears that the position of Caltex (India), Ltd., is in the ratio of about 
half of Messrs. Standard Vacuum Oil Company and about one-fourth of 
Messrs. Burmah Shell. So we should consider the amount of bonus which 
Burmah Shell and Standard Vacuum gave to their workmen for 1952. 
The Secretary of Burmah Shell Employees’ Union, Shri Banamali 
deposed : — 

that the scale of wages is from Rs. 80 to 470 per month and only three 
or four clerks draw lts. 470. Dearness allowance is in accord- 
ance with the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale. There is 
provision for pension and to the employees who do not qualify 
for pension, gratuity is paid subject to a maximum of fifteen 
months’ wages and that employees putting in less than JO years 
of service are not paid any gratuity. ITe further says that in 
final analysis of the pension and gratuity rules, the actual 
pension would work out at 23 per cent, or 25 per cent, only of 
the retiring salary and not 40 per cent, as alleged by the 
employer Messrs. Burinah Shell. 

W\ 3 Shri Indu Bhusan Chakravarti, the General Secretary of the 
mdard Vacuum Employees’ Union, deposed that— 

the wage scale of Messrs. Standard Vacuum is from Rs. 80 to Rs. 400 
and that there are only five clerks who draw above Rs. 400 per 
month which is a special category. In this Company also dearness 
allowance is paid in accordance with the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce Scale. There is no gratuity scheme except for the 
particular period prior to til© introduction of the Provident. Fund in 
1948. As regards Provident Fund contribution Standard Vacuum 
Company contributes only 7 per cent, of the basic wage whereas 
Caltex Company contributes 10 per cent, of the basic wage 

Caltex Company has got Provident Fund and gratuity both . 1 do not 
link that the total emoluments given by Caltex (Tndin), Ltd., are in any 
ay below per with the Standard Vacuum and Burinah Shell which are far 
ore solvent than Caltex. 

It has been shown by evidence that Burmah Shell and Standard 
actium Companies have been involved in reference cases over the question 
E bonus for 1952 and that the awards now pending appeal at the instance 


lose THE Gl^LCUm GAZEH# MAJtpH 10, 1955 [Past 

1 4 i- — 


of the. workmen have aj/te n three ninths' wages as bonfb. For I960 
Caltaft also, wa^ direete<Fby the 'tribunal to pay burns equivalent to thr& 
months' wages.; At that time, it should be noted, the minimum wage wm 
Rs. 70 or 7/> but not Bs. 80. The wages were increased to Bs. '80 witl 
effect from 1951. It appears from the award of Messrs. Burmah Shell 
published on June 17, 1954, in the Calcutta Gazette , that Burmah Sheij 
voluntarily gave one month's wages as bonus for 1952 and later on U 
award wages for two months more was directed to be paid as additional 
bonus for the said year. Considering all these circumstances I think that 
the claim of the Union for six months’ wages as additional bonus is highly 
exorbitant and it should not be granted, I am of opinion that two months' 
wages should be paid as additional bonus for the year 1952, to the work- 
men concerned in this proceeding, and the payment be made within a month 
from the date of publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette . 

The Company’s contention, on the basis of average income at 16G 
month is highly faulty. It would be doing immense injustice to the 
workmen earning low wages by fastening average incomb upon them 
calculated along with the high wages paid to others. 

I need not enter into the question of “ living wage " figure, particularly 
when, no such figure as yet been laid down by any authority and when 
the approximate living wage figure is obviously a far cry from the 
now being paid by the Company. 0 

It has been prayed on behalf of the Union that additional bonus for 
1952 may be made payable not only to the workmen now in service .but also 
to those who have retired and to the heirs of the workmen who have died 
during 1952 or afterwards. 

The demand for bonus was made for the first time in February 1953 
Therefore the workmen who retired after that date or the heirs of the 
workmen who died after that date provided the workmen hid worked durini? 
1952, may be entitled to get benefit of this award, whereas the workmen 
retiring before date or the heirs of the workmen dying before that date 
should not be held to be entitled to the said benefit of the award.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 


RESOLUTION No. 1035Dis./D/9L-79/54. 


Calcutta, the 11th March 1955. 

The Governor is pleased to constitute a Com- 
mittee to be designated the Tandu Tea Estate 
Flood Damage Enquiry Committee on the terms of 
reference set out. below : — 

(1) To enquire and report into the causes of 

high death roll among workers in the 
Tandu Tea Estate in the district of 
Jalpaiguri due to flood in North Bengal 
during the months of July-August 1954. 

(2) To establish the responsibility for the 

heavy casualties, if possible. 

(3) In particular to recommend remedial 

measures, which can be parried out, for 
avoidance of such calamities in future. 

The personnel of the Committee shall be as 
follows : — 

Chairman. 

1. Commissioner, Presidency Division. 

Members. 

2. Shri R. N. Bose, I.A.S., Labour Commis- 

sioner. 

3. Shri S. B. Ray, I.A.S., Deputy Commis- 

sioner, Jalpaiguri. 

4. Shri I. B. De, I.S.E., Chief Engineer, 

Irrigation and M a ter ways. 

5. Shri Upendra Nath Barman, M.P. 

6. Dr. Mrs. Maitrayee Bose, M.B., M.D. 

7. Shri Sashadhar Ear, M.L.A. 

Secretary. 

Personal Assistant to the Commissioner, Presi- 
dency Division at Jalpaiguri. 


Order. 

Ordered that the resolution be pub- 
died in the Calcutta Colette and that copies be 
irwarded to the members of the Committee and 
ie Departments concerned. 

By order of the Governor, 
D. S. I*. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

ANNEXURE. 


he matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Casting Corporation 
(India), Ltd., 45, Madhusudan Pal Chowdhury Lane, Howrah and their

the Company : Shri U. N. Roy, assisted by Shri M. Guha.

AWARD. 

Tins industrial dispute between Messrs. Casting Corporation (India), 
., 45, Madhusudan Pal Chowdhury Lane, Howrah and their workmen 
resented by Casting Corporation (India), Ltd. Mazdoor Union, 1, Haja- 
\ Das Lane, How’ran, regarding the matters mentioned below in the issues 
referred to this Tribunal for its adjudication under Government of West 
pi, Labour Department, order No. 3292Dis./D/llL-169/54, dated the 
July 1954 and subsequent corrigendum No. 4207Dis./D/11L-lG9/54, 
d the 2nd September 1954. 

Mh parties filed their written statements in due course. 

i the written statement filed by the Union, it is stated that it submitted 
barter of Demands” to the management of the Casting Corporation 
a), Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the “company”), to which the 
igcnient did not even give a reply. On 19th January 1954, Shri 
unsh Kantra, a permanent worker of the company, was discharged wilJi- 
tny charge-sheet and without any scope of defence. He fell ill in his 
on 3rd January 1954 and left with the permission of the Alisln of 
lepartment, Slin Bhupati Majhi. The reason of his absence was 
■u to the management which verbally granted him leave, lie came to 
on 19th January 1954 with a medical certificate but he was refused 
and was dismissed for his said absence. This was against all principles 
dural justice and as such, the worker is entitled to reinstatement witli 
wages for the entire period of his unemployment.

It further states that the company has no fixed rote of pay, far I, 
scale of pay. The existing rate is poor and a flat rate of increment 
m inimum pay should be given with retrospective effect. It does iw 
any dearness allowance. The Union claims dearness allowance at th7 
Rs. 31 up to Rs. 60 per month and Rs. 42 up to Rs. 1()( j 
month. The company does not grant any leave and the Union claim, 
and holidays for the staff. At present, there is no retiral benefit f 
employees of this company and the Union claims one month’s pay 
year of service as gratuity on death or termination of service 
voluntary, for everybody. 

The company, in reply, said that it was suffering recurring losses f, 
last four years in business. The total amount of net loss was Rs. 33,199 
Due to this critical financial position, the company had to stop work 
few months last year. It is a small Beale engineering concern dene 
purely on job works and employs at present permanent employees an 
ing 40. It allows full statutory leave under the Factories Act and 10 
festival leave. It has been contributing to the Employees’ State I n9 „ 
Fund and sick leave would be covered oy that Fund. It is unable t 
anv retiral benefits. Shri Ambarish Santra was absent from duty 
4th January 1954 to 19th January 1954 without any intimation to the. 
On 7 th January 1964, he took his wages from the Accountant but dii 
join to his duty. On 19th January 1954, he came to join his duty wl, 
refused on the ground of his intentional absence for more than 15 days 
out any intimation. The workers of the company are all daily rated 
monthly paid. Dearness is also paid to the workers. 

The issues as per schedule to the order of reference are : — 

(1) Is the discharge of Shri Ambarish Santra justified To what 1 

by way of reinstatement and/or compensation he is entitle 

(2) Wages. 

(3) Leave and holidays. 

(4) Retirement benefits. 


FINDINGS. 


Issue No. 1. 

p W 1 Shri Ambarish Santra said that he was absent from duty beti 
4th January 1954 and 19th January 1954. He had an attack of dysentery 
suffered from it from the 3rd of February till he attended on the 1 
He was under the treatment of Dr. U. Khan who granted him a md 
certificate (Ext. 1). The company refused to give him work when hen 
to duty He said that, one of his nephews Panchanan Maahi, unempk

ary 1954 when he informed the office about his illness. He ; cm* to t 
on the 7th in a rickshaw and obtained his wages. He said that he to 
Cashier and the Chota Babu (Ashish Babu) about his dlnewfie' 
without any employment between the date of bis dismissal and ^ ^ 
S. C. Das & Co., two months ago. He asked for reinstatement 
wages. In cross-examination, he admitted that he did no f t 
company’s doctor, I)r. D. K. Das, during his illness. No witness b 
examined on behalf of the company. The learned Advocutefr^^ 
accordingly asked this Tribunal to believe the evidence of bhn »

DECISION. ^ 

Messrs. Poddar Automobiles (hereafter called the Company), 113 p 
Street, Calcutta, is a workshop for repairing and services of autoinohV 
Their workmen represented by Engineering Masdoor Union (hereafter cn 
the Union) laid claim for bonus for the year 1952-63 under two head&Jli^ 
on the basis of profit-sharing and the other as Plija bonus. They c j • ^ 
3 months’ basic salary /wages under each of these heads. The 
resisted the claim. ^ 


The financial year of the Company is from July to June. The foi 
sheet of the Company for the year ending June 1953 shows a small 
Ks. 2,835-14-3 pies. According to the Ftill Bench formula bonus can l 
be paid should there be a residue after deducting prior charges and] 
after making provisions for the return on working capital. On such d h 
tions, it is obvious, there would be no available surplus. Thus the claim * 
bonus on the basis of profit cannot be sustained. During hearing Iv 
Union’s representative also filed a petition stating that he did not ^ 


claim on this head. 


pre« 


As regards Puja bonus, the Union’s representative also stated bv ft 
above petition that the workmen had no dispute regarding the quantum f 
Puja bonus for the year 1952-53 in question. He also stated that the w ! 
men had received one month’s wages as Puja bonus for the year in quest' 
and did not press further claim. In the circumstances, claim for additi 0 °! 
Puja bonus must also fail. The contention of the Union that such p ■ 
bonus is a condition of service, cannot be gone into when the dispute reuard 
ing the said Puja bonus for the year in question ceased to exist. Tli 
Tribunal can go into the question during the subsistence of the dispute an! 
not otherwise. As in the present case the Union’s representative states tha 
the workmen had since received payment of the Puia bonus for the vea 
in question in full and final settlement, it is obvious that the dispute ceaset 
It being so, the question, whether the said bonus is a condition of smii 
or not, cannot be gone into and is left open. The Union’s claim, therefor 
fails. 


I award accordingly.

remark “Left”. Thereupon the Government in the Labour Depart^,

present address of Tarapada Biswas cannot be obtained despite the K,

of the employer wherein he is alleged to have been residing. The sunuj 
was accordingly sent to the employer at the said residential addregg i 
registered post with acknowledgment due, but this too was returned « 
served with the remark “Left”. The Union prayed for service of « 
summons by publication in the newspapers, 1 find no such provision/ 
service of summons. The provisions m the Civil Procedure Code regardi 
service of summons on the parties have no application. Rule 12 0 f t? 
Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1947, provides for service of sumnjo,! 
notice, process or order in the following manner: — 

(a) it may be sent by registered post; or 

(b) if such notice, summons, process or order is to be served within th 

local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court of Small CauJ 
Calcutta, it may be sent to the Registrar of that Court for 8er ’ 
vice, accompanied by a conveyance charge of annas 4 in respect 
of each notice, summons, process or order to be served; and tfo 
Registrar shall, on receipt thereof, proceed as if it had been 
issued by the Court of Small Causes, Calcutta, and shall then 
return the same to the Court or Board or Tribunal together will 
the record (if any) of the proceedings with regard thereto. 

In the present case clause (b) has no application as the addrees of tie 
employer given is outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court 
of Small Causes, Calcutta. So the only mode for service in the present, 
case was by registered post. The said channel was resorted to and on all: 
the occasions summons was returned unserved. 

DECISION. 

In the circumstances, when the proper address of the employer is 
available and, ns a result, summons could not be served upon the emplo; 
it must be held that the reference has become infractuous. 

I award accordingly.

“The decision of the management with regard to a charge of misennd

of principles of natural justice; or 

(iii) there is a basic error of facts; or 

(iv) there has been a perverse finding on the materials. 

(Also see Bathgate & Co. Ltd.’s case, 1953, L.A.C., page 149)

Issue No. 2 (Bonus for 1953). 

This relates to Bonus for the year 1953. The Union demanded a bonus 
n condition of service equivalent to 65 days’ basic wages tor workmen 
l 2 J , months’ basic wages for clerks and other monthi.s rated workmen, 
doing so, it stated among others, that the management agreed hi writing

It also said that since its offer for payment of bonus for 35 chi,\s 
; not 42 days, as alleged, was refused, it should lie treated as withdrawn. 

Neither party adduced any oral evidence on this issue. There is no 
rial on record to support the Union’s contention that bonus is paid a> 
idition of service. In fact, there is no evideiwe of its payment, in the 
years. Naturally, the claim is to be decided on the general principles 
h gnu»rn all cases of payment of bonus to workers. 

i a dispute arising out of a claim for payment of bonus to woikers, the 
mals now follow the well-established principles laid down 1>\ the 
nr Appellate Tribunal in its Full Bench Decision in Mill Owners’ 
nation, Bombay vs. Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangli, Bombay, 
ted in 195*2 L.A.C., page 433. The Full Bench Decision has now 
red the approval of the Hon’ bio Supreme Court of lndiu in a case 
sen Moir Mills, Ltd. and Suti Mill Mazdur Union, reported ii. 19 m, 
'•L.L, page 1. It held that, “the quantum of bonus must depend

upon the relative prosperity of the ooncera during the year under re 
and that prosperity is best reflected in the amount of the residuary 8U , 
of profits.’ ’ The Hon’ble Supreme Court held in the above meati 
case that, “there are however two conditions which have to be sat* 
before a demand for bonus can be justified and they are (i) when 
fall short of the living standard; and (n) the industry makes huge

increasing production. The demand for bonuB becomes an industrial ■

wages. If in any particular year, the working of the industrial com.*

ily when a man is appointed to fill a permanent vacancy in a post and

AWARD. 

iis is a oomplaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
Dn 11th September 1954 by Shri Bibhuti Singh and 15 others. They 
sd that they were employees of the opposite party Company and 
red Puja bonus at the rate of 15 days’ wages in 1953 and that they 
•stood that the opposite party Company was not going to pay swh 
i this year. They accordingly prayed that the Company should be 
ted to pay them the usual bonus. 

In* Company opposite party contended that the application as framed 
tot maintainable in law, nor did the same disclose any cause of action 
pt the Company. As regards merits of the case, the Company denied 
baymcnt. of Puja bonus ever formed any part of the terms and condi- 
[ot service and pleaded that on or about 22nd September 1954, it paid 
ktitioners 15 days’ basic wages as bonus for the current year except 
ji Bibhuti Singh, who was found guilty of misconduct on or about, 
anuary 1954 and for whose dismissal an application for permission 
ibmitted on 13th February 1954 to the Labour Commissioner, West 

s point which therefore arises for determination is whether the 
lint as framed is maintainable. 


DECISION. 

tav straightaway note that I agree with the Company opposite party 
ie complaint as framed is got maintainable. Only when an employer 
penes section 33, the employees aggrieved by such contravention may 
\ complaint in writing under section 33 A and not otherwise. In the 


1282 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 24, 1956 ^ 

present case, the complaint did not disolose that there had been alter, 
m the conditions of service applicable to the workman. It merely 
that the workmen understood that there would be no payment V 
current year. Then it was not also stated in the complaint that, pav? 
of Puja bonus was a condition of servioe. In these cmmmgj 1 
prima facie there has been no contravention of section 33 of the Act 
as such the complaint under section 33 A is not maintainable, ft eg :V 
appears that there has since been payment at the rate of 15 days’ |! 
wages as Puja bonus for the current year to the petitioners e , 
Bibhuti Singh. Regarding the latter (Shri Bibhuti Singh) the 
of non-payment to him cannot be gone into when no such coumji* J 
before me. 

So, to be precise and to conclude, I find that the complaint uni 
tion 33A must fail. It is awarded accordingly. Uef|

pany has not been wound up but it has closed down the Hosiery Inin 
on the allegation that the business was entailing loss and that then* 
no chance of profit on account of the keen competition in the market 
Company’s contention is that there were 39 workmen and that bemn? 


> aB t n CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 24, 1955 1297 


, j u g down alike Hosiery business, the Union was taken counsel with and 
was resolved;!** the 2nd July 19511, in the General Meeting of the Com- 
an y that the ftosiery Mills should be closed down and the workmen are to 
M iVtrenched Wltft effect from* 15th July 1953, and that accordingly a notice 
h given of the. said Resolution and that the Draft Notice was corrected 
ul approved of by the President of the Union. The Draft Notice is marked 
x ( § To support this contention of the Company that the closure was 

1( .’to financial difficulties and heavy losses incurred hy the Mill, the Com- 
|11V produced the Balance Sheet also. 

It appears from the evidence that in 1950, the Mills were once closed 
,\vn involving discharge of 79 workers. There was a Refeienre case arising 
{ \ of the some discharge. The Award was published in the Calcutta 
'i:rtte, dated January 11, 1951. In the uward, there was an ohseivation 
“the Management contemplates to re-open the departments gradually 
J lo re-appoint the discharged workers according to necessity”. The 
•ihunal held that the closure of the Mill was on bona fide trading'grounds. 
►ter the passing of that award, the Mills were restarted by the Company 
d it appears from the evidence that only 39 workers formed the total 
•engih this time. On the side of the Union, there is no evidence at all. 
further appears that on the 1st May 1954, the Company sold away the 
jsieiy Mills business to one Sumernmll Pa inlay a for Rs. 10,000. The copy 
the conveyance is marked “J)’\ In the evidence, however, the Coin- 
,iv ’s witness admitted that the sale* was for consideration of Rs. 80,000 
d that nothing was received in cash and that the entire purchase* money 
s set up against outstaneling debt due to the purchaser. ^ 

K appears that workmen were not paid any gratuity or any retiral benefit 
the time of the first closure in 1950. On the one hand, the workmen were 
reached for no fault of theirs although they were serving this Company 
m before 1950. On the other hand, the Company had to close down the 
uness on account of bona fide trading reasons. The question is whether 
the circumstances, the Company should pay compensation to the workmen 
ol* the attenuated capital. The Balance Sheet does not show any 
prve money in the hands of the Company. Even if wo suppose that the 
npany received Rs. 80,000 in cash from the Purchaser us purchase money, 
fact remains that the paid up capital far exceeded that amount. It has 
ii held in Associated Rubber and Plastic Works vs. Workmen, 1954, 
i.L.J., page 183, by the Appellate Tribunal that an employer has the 
lit to close his business and compensation is payable only if it is proved 
i the closure is not for bona fide trading reasons. 

The decision in that case was not influenced at all by the fact that the 
Knien also by their irresponsible conduct contributed to the trade depres- 
l. This case has been properly reported in 1954, 6 F.J.R., page 195. 

In New India Commercial Company vs. Jyotirmoy Ghose, 1954, 1 L.L.J., 
, it was held — 

“that compensation in the case of the termination of services of a work- 
man on account of closure of business should be awarded on the 
same basis on which compensation is awarded, in case of re- 
trenchment 1 \ But in that ease the closure was not duo to 
bona fide trade reasons or to economic difficulties of the einployci. 

hat ease, the business was closed and the firm was dissolved due to the 
;renee between the partners. Therefore, the decision in that case is not 
icable to the facts of the present case. I, therefore, hold that tin*

workmen are not entitled to get any re-instatement order nor any cojm^ 
tion but I recommend that the purchaser of the business may lie p] ea J g 
employ workmen out ofi these retrenched hands, if and when any occal 
would arise and that there should not be any discrimination in the j n 
of recruitment, so far as these retrenched workmen are concerned. ]

AWARD.

No. 1623W.T.— 23rd March' 1966.— In exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 

1919 (Bengal Act I of 1919), the Governor is pleased to niake the follow- 
ing by-laws for the Vishnupur Municipality in the distriot of Bankura, 
namely : — 

1. Appointment and duties of the Registering jMItoer.—Everv rickshaw 
in the Vishnupur Municipality shall be annually registered by the 
Registering Officer appointed for registering hackney-carriages. 

2. Qualifications of bearere.— Every person applying for a bearer’s 
license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer — 

(a) that he is not less than 18 and not more than 45 years of age; 

(b) that he knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and is in all 

respects a fit person for such employment; 

(c) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 

places in and around the town of vishnupur; 

(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and 

distances prepared by the Commissioners; 

(e) that he knows the rules of the road and signals used by tin* 

bearers and drivers of vehicles and by the traffic police. 

3. Contents Of license. — There shall be nffixed to each license, issued 
to a rickshaw bearer — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 

(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him; and 

(c) a printed table of fares and distances prepared by the Commis- 

sioners, for which no charge shall be paid by the bearer. 

4. Production Of licenses. — Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carry 
with him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so by an\ 
Commissioner, traffic police or other person authorised by the Commis- 
sioners. He shall exhibit the tables of fares and distances on a prominent 
part of the vehicle. 

5. Condition Of riokshaurs. — (a) The body of the rickshaw- shall be 
sound and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. 

(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by 
pro])erly fitted splash boards. 

(c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and 
properly ri vetted and free from rust. 

(d) The iron supports at the back shall be properly curved and securely 
fixed at each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

(e) The shaft shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and 
furnished at the fore ends with a ring-shaped metal support and connected 
by collision guard. 

(f) The hood, apron and cushions shall be made of and covered with 
good cloth, canvas or other materials approved by the Commissioners at a 
meeting. 

(g) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
tight. 

(li) Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps — one facing the front 
and one in the rear. 

(i) Each lamp shall have a red glass window in the back and shall Ije 
so placed that the light from the window is visible from a jwrint ten yards 
in the rear of the centre of the vehicle. 

(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle bars or cross 
bars on the cycle and it shall be so constructed that it can be operated by 
fingers and can give continuous ringing as and when necessary. 

6. Dimension! end pattern of riokshaws.-All rickshaws shall conform 
to the following dimensions and he of such patteqi as may be fixed by tliu 

^Commissioners at a meeting: — 

Width of the seats 2 feet 3 inches. 

Height of the seats ... i foot 4 inohee. 

Height of the cushions ■ ... 4 inches.

!). Speed and halting Charge.— When a rickshaw is hired the bearer 
shall ordinarily drive the same at a speed of not less than eight miles per 
hour. If a rickshaw after being hired is made to halt, halting charge 
shall be paid according to the scale laid down in the above fare table. 


(Half an hour shall be allowable as grace in all cases but the hirer 
shall in no circumstance detain any bonked rickshaw if intimation as to 
booking thereof is given to the hirer before or at the time ol hiring the 
rickshaw). 


10. Passengers to pay Other oharges.— Passengers shall pay the ferry 
and other charges while going to and coming from the railway station over 
and above the rates payable to the bearer of rickshaw. 

11. Maximum load to be carried in rickshaw.— Passengers ami luggage 
shall not ordinarily exceed four maunds in weight. It shall not he 
permissible to any rickshaw bearer to refuse to ply except on reasonable 1 
grounds. 


12. Advertisement on rickshaws.— No advertisement shall he fixed on 
the body of the rickshaw without, the previous permission ol the Commis- 
sioners and it shall be fixed at such place as not to cover the number plate 
and fare table affixed to the rickshaw. 


13. Riokshaws to wait at Stand.— The rickshaws while at rest shall 
wait at a stand fixed by the Commissioners for such purposes. 


14. Power Of entry.— It shall be lawful for a Commissioner or any 
other person authorised in that behalf by the Chairman of the Cmmuissionyrs 
at. any time between sun-rise and sun-set. to enter any premises in which 
any licensed rickshaw or other things used therewith are kept Jn to 
carry out any provision of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1*1U, , <>i 
these by-laws and the owner or occupier of the premises or Ins agent s u 
afford every facility for inspection by such Commissioner or person.

Jails 

RESOLUTION No. 2893H.J. 

Calcutta , the 12tli November 1954. 

Subject: — -Rend the report on the administration 
of the Jails in West Bengal for the year 1952. 
During the year under report, 28,619 convicts 
constituting 04 per cent, of the total figure were 
sentenced to imprisonment not exceeding a month. 
Government note with regret that the admission 
of such short term prisoners remained as high as 
before. Short term imprisonment is undesirable 
ns it exposes the prisoner to the contamination of 
prison life and nt. the same time gives no chance 
for their reformation. The Government have 
passed the West Bengal Offenders (Release on 
Admonition and Probation) Bill, 1954, and it is 
hoped that there will be noticeable improvement 
in this direction. 


6. Government note with pleasure tt 
total quantity of " Jail garden produce was 
13,197 mds. during the year as against 
mds. in 1951 and that, many of -the j u j| 
almost self-sufficient with regard to vegetal)] 
some of them were even able to sell to the 
vegetables worth Rs. 7,774 after mectinn 
own requirements. As the co-operation ^ 
Agriculture Department in the matter 0 f 1 
tion of the jail garden is always desirubU 
department have been requested to <]j r J f 
Agricultural Officers to exercise greater 
vision over jail garden and to render 
advice for further improvement of ( 
produce. e f 


• , i - . uppuruimtv of r 

in* their appreciation of the services render 
Dr. P. K. Biswas as Inspector-General of ]l 

during the year. Jr 


2. The average period of the detention of 
under-trial prisoners during the year as compared 
with that of the previous year was slightly 
shorter in respect of Magistrates* eases but was 
longer in Sessions cases. The State Government, 
however, note with pleasure that the Government 
of India have introduced a Bill in Parliament 
which aims at more speedy trial. This may 
result in considerable reduction in the daily aver- 
age number of under-trial prisoners in jails as 
also the period of detention. 

3. Government are also alive to the problem 
of over-crowding in Sub- jails. In recent years, 
proposals for extension of the following Sub-jails 
were administratively approved and funds provid- 
ed there! or — 


1952- 53. 

Diamond Harbour Sub- Jail. 

1953- 54. 

Kalimpong Sub-Jail. 

Raigunj Sub-Jail. 

1954- 55. 

Mathabhanga Sub-Jail. 

Lalbagh Sub-Jail. 

Asansol Sub-Jail (conversion into a Special 
Jail).

4. Government have noticed with regret the 
large number of admissions of juvenile and 
adolescent offenders in the jails, though there has 
been some decrease compared to those in 1951, so 
far as adolescent offenders are concerned. The 
existing facilities for the training and reforma- 
tion of such offenders in the Industrial and 
Borstal School *1 at Berbampore are adequate and 
the Borstal Institution provides accommodation 
for as many as 500 inmates. In spite of these 
arrangements for their treatment on Borstal lines, 
it appears that the Courts have not taken as much 
advantage of these facilities as could have been 
expected. In order to avoid such state of affairs, 
the District Officers have already been directed to 
instruct the Prosecuting Officers to draw the atten- 
tion of Courts to. the various provisions of the 
laws dealing with juvenile and adolescent 
offenders. 


6. Subdivigional Officers are ear officio Superi 
feudwts to Sub-jails. Under the existing rul 
the Superintendent has to visit the Sub-jail 
least twice a week. Government note with regi 
that the number of visits in some cases, partic 
4 ®“?°!’ Vishnupur, Basirhat, Jangipoi 
Mekl m frh|iri, Kurseong and Ralimpoi 
were as low a* 11, 11, 5, 10, 5, 3, 4 and 9 time 
respectively, during the year. Government hav 
therefore, issued a circular directing the Subdiv 
sional Officers to pay more frequent visits to Sul 
jails as laid down in the rules.

No. 152(iW.T.— S4tli March 1955. — In exercise of the power content'd 
by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta TTnckney-enrringe Act, It) 1 H 

( pen. Act 1 of 1919), the Governor is pleased to make the following by-laws 
or the Ihilurglmt Municipality in the district nf West Oinnjpur, 
namely : — 

BY-LAWS. 

1. Appointment and duties of the Registering Officer.— liven rickshas 

in the Balurghut Municipality shall he annually registered hy a registering 
officer appointed for registering* hackney-carriages. 


2. Qualifications of the bearers. — Every person applying for a hearer’s 
license shall he required to satisfy the Registering Officer: — 

(a) that he is not less than 18 and not more than 45 years of age; 

* (h) that lie knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and is in all 

respects a fit person for such employment; 

(e) that lie is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 
places in and around the town of Balurghat; 

(d) that he lias a thorough knowledge of the tables ot fares and 
distances prepared hy the Commissioners; 

(«) that he knows the rules of the road and signals used hy the hearers 
and drivers ol vehicles and by the traffic police. 


It. Contents Of license. — There shall he affixed to each license, issued In 
a rickshaw hearer — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the hearer; 

(h) a photograph of the hearer to be supplied hy him; and 

(e) a printed table of fares prepared by the Commissioners, for which 
no charge shall be paid hy the bearer. 

4. Production Of license. — Every hearer of a rickshaw shall carry with 
him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so b.\ any 
Commissioner, traffic police or other person authorised hy the Commissioners. 
He shall exhibit the tables ot fares and distances on a prominent part ol the 
vehicles. 


5. Condition Of rickshaws.-— (a) The body of the rickshaw shall ho 
sound and clean and all the hoards strong and properly secured. 

(b) The wheels shall he rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall he protected by properly 
fitted splash Ixiards. 

(c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and 
properly riveted and free from rust. 

(d) The iron supports at the hack shall he properly curved and securely 
fixed on each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

(e) The shaft shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and furnish- 
ed at tlie fore ends with a ring-shaped metal support and connected h\ 
collision guard. 

(f) The hood, apron nnd cushions shall l>c made ot and covered with 
good cloth, canvas or other material approved hy the Commissioners at a 
meeting. 

(g) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
right. 


00 Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps — one facing the front and 
one in the rear. 


(i) Each lamp shall’ have a red glass window in the hack and shall lu* 
?° placed that the light from the window is visible from a point fen j'ards 
ln riie rear of the centre of the vehicle. 


(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle liars or cross 
bar on the cycle and it shall be so constructed that it can he operated by 
fingers and can give continuous ringing as and when necessary. 


6. Dimensions end pattern of riekshawe.— All rickshaws shall conform 
to the following dimensions and be of such pattern ns may he fixed hy the

NOTIFICATIONS. 

Midnapore.—No. 5842L.A.— 25th March 1955. 
— Whereas the functions of the Central Govern- 
ment under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (I of 
1894) t in relation to the acquisition of land for the 
purposes of the Union, have been entrusted to the 
State Government by notification No. 123/50- 
Judl., dated the 30th September 1950, issued by 
the Government of India, iu the Ministry of Home

Original Side 

NOTIFICATION. 

Calcutta, the 31st March 1955. 

It is ordered by the High Court at Calcutta that 
with effect from the date of its publication in the 
Calcutta Gazette, the following Rule do come into 
force as a rule of the Court and that it be inserted 
in the Original Side Rules after Rule 17, 
Chapter XXV as Rule 17A and under the head- 
ing “Additional Deposits”: — 

Rule 17A. ( i ) In addition to the sums initially 
deposited, the Sheriff may from time to 
hum ask for a deposit in advance of such 
further sums on account of fees uml 
charges as may reasonably be required 
for the service of any writ or process or 
the execution of any decree or order or 
for the continuance of an attachment or 
of a seixure of moveable property, includ- 
ing in both cases charges for the custody 
of the property and, in the latter case, 
those for the maintenance, repairs or dis- 
posal of the property, where necessary.

AWARD. 


It is admitted by the Company that in West Bengal, the rule of th* 
Company regarding retirement is that only on completion of 60 years of 
an employee is to retire and that there is no such rule in West* Bengal that 
on completion of certain period of service an employee is to retire ami that 
such rule exists in Pakistan. The question therefore is whether the peti- 
tinner is an employee of River Steam Navigation Company iu India or 
whether he is an employee of River Steam Navigation Company m Pakistan 
and whether the petitioner is a workman or not within the definition of the 
term in Industrial Disputes Act, and whether the petitioner has completed 
35 years of service. 

Petitioner Shri Debendra Chandra Dey admits that he was an Audit 
Inspector of the Company at the time of the forced retirement in question. 9 
From the exhibits marked on the side of the petitioner it appears that the j 
petitioner Shri Debendra Chandra Dey was an Audit Inspector but Ext. F, 
filed by the Company, where there was an agreement- between the j "* ' 
Steamer Companies and the Bengal Mariners' Union in Pakistan and 
which the Company relies, shows that the Audit Department emplo 
are treated as “clerical and subordinate staff" for the purjiosc of retirem 
There in clause (4), the provision is that: — 

“Retirement should normally be effected at 60 years of age or on r 
pletion of 35 years' service", and this provision in under 
heading “Retirement ot clerical and subordinate staff". 

Therefore the position appears to he admitted that the Audit inspector 
the Company is nothing but a clerk. The Company has not produced i 
paper to show nor any oral evidence to make out that an employee like 
petitioner Shri Debendra Chandra Dey, nomenclatured as Audit Jasper 
is anything other than “clerical and subordinate staff", and that rcgardi 
such officer (as distinguished from workman) there is any retirement a 
prescribed by the Company or any award or agreement. 

From the evidence it appears that the petitioner was recruited ty U 
.■Joint Agents Office at Barisal and it was confirmed by the Head lfr J 
Calcutta. At the time of the creation of Pakistan the petitioner was 
somewhere in Fast Bengal (now Pakistan). In 1950 he was transferred

[Tnder the reference the dispute was between Messrs. Rivers Steam

in y conclusion is that the application under section 33A is inaintain- 


.dniittedly there is no rule in the Company so far as India or West 
jal iH concerned that an employee is to retire on completion of 35 
T service. The rule is that an employee is to retire on completion of 
pars of age. Admittedly the petitioner Shri Debendra Chandra Dev

any has not been at all able to make out that the petitioner Shri

estion. 


ith regard to the petitioner’s contention, that the Provident Fund
