AWARD. 

This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Ad 
filed on 31st July 1954 by Mr. A. Magermans. He waH a receptionist a 
the opposite party hotel. Two notices — one dated 1st April 1954 (fotj 
and the other dated 11th June 1954 [Ext. l(n)l — were admitted!) issued « 
him, the last one terminating his employment on the expiry of 31st M 
1954. After suc h service of notice and before actual termination rf 
employment from 1st August 1954, an industrial dispute between tkj 
opposite party and their workmen was referred to by Government 
order No. 3404Dis. / T>/ 1 1I/-91(A) / 54, dated the l^th July 1954, t 
Tribunal for adjudication. 

The complainant alleged that as his employment was terminated i 
the pendency of the said proceeding without permission, the opposite 
had contravened section 33 of the Act. The opposite party, on the 
hand, contended that as the notice of termination of service was served i 
complainant at a time when there was no proceeding pending befoi 
Tribunal, no permission was necessary and they had not violated secti 
of the Act. It was accordingly pleaded that the application under « 
33A was not maintainable apart from other considerations. 

As the objection goes at the root of the case, it has been heard h 
preliminary objection. 

DECISION. 

Mr. A. Magermans admittedly joined service of the opposite party 
receptionist for one year from 1st August 1962 on the basis of app® 1 ®" 
letter, Ext. A. His term of service was thereafter extended bv b‘wr • 


gT I] XJMS UAXiUUlTA liAZJSTTE, APRIL 7, 191$ 


41017 


„d July 1963 (Ext. B) for another year from 1st August 1963 to 31st July 
54. By ext< 9. f at ** ^fh Wr !B63, Mr. Magermans acknowledged 
*ipt of the e|id letter dated 22nd July 1963. Then the opposite party 
tt ed the notich dated 1st April 1964 (Ext. 15 informing Mr. Magermans 
,t bis services would not be required after 80th June 1$64. On 2nd April 
j 4 the latter (Mr. Magermans) replied that he could not accept the said 
ire as valid as his terms of employment with the opposite party were for 
l full and complete year from 1st August 1953 to 31st July 1954 ( vide 
I)). Then the opposite party issued another notice on 11th June 1964, 

! 1(a), to Mr. Magermans to say that his period of employment would 
lire on 31st July 1954 and would not be extended and that this should be 
sited as a notice of termination of employment. 


Admittedly at the time no proceeding before the Tribunal was pending. 
p proceeding commenced on 13th July 1954. It was contended on behalf 
the complainant that as his employment was terminated on 31st July 
4 without permission from the Tribunal, section 33 of the Act was con- 
vened. The opposite party, on the other hand, contended that as the 
.ice of termination of employment was served when there was no proceed- 
pending, section 33 had no application. 


On giving careful consideration to the arguments advanced on either 
>, it appears that the contention of the opposite party should prevail, 
tion 20(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act lays down that proceedings 
ire a Tribunal Rhall be deemed to have commenced on the date of the 
srence of dispute for adjudication. In the present case it was so referred 
m 13th July 1964 when the dispute must be deemed to have commenced 
tion 33 prohibits the employer from discharging or dismissing a work- 
i during pendency of the adjudication proceedings before the Tribunal 
lout express permission of the Tribunal. The notice terminating the 
iloyment, ext. 1(a), was however served on 11th June 1954 before the 
mcnccment of the proceedings on 13th July 1954. When the termina- 
followed the notice as a matter of course without any further action on 
pari of the employer, it is obvious that the employer did not do anything 
ng the pendency of the proceedings since 13th July 1954. So, section 
iad no application m the present case. The fact that termination of 
joymont took place during the pendency of the adjudication proceedings. 
Id be of no Lein as the act, namely, service of notice, from which 
i mat ion followed had been taken before the commencement of the 

^'ofdlscW^ 011 A U ^ UtS i a x an j° ® n actio “ the employer in the 
ceding TwL dismissal, etc., during pendency of the adjudication 
eedmgs In the present case when such action, naraelv, service of 

ousYhai’Tb take “ pn0r comme ncement of the proceedings, it is 

rr* here waB . no elation of section 33. I am, therefore of 
“dingly faif compam * ; un ^er section 33A is not maintainable and must 


awiird accordingly.

FINDINGS. 

Issue No. 1. 

Of the 28 dismissed workers, Shri Haradas Marick was placed Un( ]., 
order of suspension on 16th January 1964, pending an enquiry into a, 
charges of misconduct and was dismissed with effect from that date u 
is number 1 of the list of .dismissed workers, attached to a! 

order of reference. The workers, No. 2 to No . 19 of the said list, w ." 

suspended on 19th January 1954, pending enquiry and were dimnW,i 
for misconduct with effect from that date. The remaining four worW 
(No 20 to No. 23) were placed under orders of suspension on m 
February 1964 and were dismissed on 15th February 1954, on th 
ground of misconduct. The Union s case is that these workers wen> 
victimised for their Union activities and were dismissed, in a violation 

of tte principles of natural justice on false allegations of misconduct 

The management of the company, a proprietory concern, justifies this 
act of dismissal on the ground of serious misconduct, viz., ,,| 

adopting go-slow tactics in work and inciting others not to do any work 
The workers (No. 20 to No. 23) were dismissed on additional 
of stay-in-strike on 13th February 1054 and for wr° n & f ully confining the 
proprietor and the manager after the working hours. Ur. S. K. Bost- 
on behalf of the Union, challenged the legality of the order alleging 
that the workers were all dismissed without the permission of this 

Tribunal, and also of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, within 30 duvn 
of the publication of an award of this Tribunal and during the 

pendency of an appeal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Shri I*. 1( 
Mukherjee on behalf of the company, supported the said ordei 
of the management, both on grounds of law and on fVts 

He said that the order of dismissal was passed at a time when perniwum 
of the Tribunals was not necessary. It appears from Ext. F, that a 
compromise award between the parties, of this ^ Tribunal, dated 15th 
December 1953, waH published in the Calcutta Gazette on 7th January 
1954. It is true that 19 out of 23 workers of this dispute were suspended 
on 16th January 1954 /19th January 1954, but they were dismissed by 
an order, dated 13th February 1954. The order of dismissal took effect 
from the date of the order of suspension, viz., 16th January 1954/19th 
January 1954. It is, therefore, clear that the order of dismissal was 
passed after 30 days of the date of the publication of the compromise 
award Under the certified Standing Orders (Ext. N), the ordw of 
dismissal takes effect from the date of the order of suspension. In these 
facts and circumstances, it cannot be said that the order ul 
dismissal was passed in contravention of the provisions of section 33 ol 
the Industrial Disputes Act, without the permission of the Iribui 
Shri P. R. Mukherjee frankly concedes that an appeal against i 
compromise award was pending before the Labour Appellate Tribu 
when the orders of dismissal of these workers were passed. Hut be w 
the appeal was incompetent in law and, therefore, would not attrar 
provisions of section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tnbui 
Act. In fact, neither party to the compromise award preferred 
appeal. It was some of the workers of the Masdur Union, who ww 
parties to the award preferred the appeal, which was summarily dunw 
fn these circumstances, the permission of the Tribunal would not 
necessary for dismissing the . workers found guilty of miw 
this contention of Dr. Bose fails.

Quention now is whether the action of the management in dismissing 
, e w orkera ia justified. Of the 23 workers mentioned in the schedule, 
q were charged for intentionally not doing any work and inciting 
d instigating others under threat of assault to stop work. As a 
“it there was no work in the factory for 15 days. These workere 
e placed und*r suspension pending enquiry, and were asked to submit 
vnl a nation within 7 days. The remaining four workers were given 
karge-sheets on I2th February 1954 and on 13th February 1954 for 
\ not doing any work for some time past, inciting and instigating 
tier workers not to do work under threat of assault ; and for 
j) leaving the place of work at about 9-30 a.m. with the machine open 
nd unattended and inciting some workers actually engaged in work to 
ome to the office and create a row and intimidate the management with 
lireat of creating dangerous situation unless the 19 suspended workers 
ere given employment; and (iii) for joining a sit-down strike on 13th 
ebruary 1954, after the working hours and misbehaving within the 
ictory premises in spite of the requests of the manager not to do it as 
ho not permitting the proprietor and others who were inside the factory 
i leave it. Ext. N is the certified Standing Orders of the factory, 
hese were certified on 9th March 1954. The certified Standing Orders 
ere sent to the company by the Certifying Officer on 15th March 1954. 
r. S. K. Bose filed an uncertified copy of the same which is marked 
xt. i. Hr. Bose asked the Tribunal to accept his copy of the Standing 
rders and reject that of the company on the ground that the company’s 
:anding Orders were not finally adopted for it was in the process of 
rtificatton. I could not follow his point here. Ext. N is the certified 
,py of the Standing Orders. There is nothing in it to show that it was 
»t’ finally adopted by the Certifying Officer. On the other hand, 
r. Bose’s copy (Ext. 1) shows many corrections and interlineations 
<1 does not appear to be certified by the proper authority. Be that as 
may, the Standing Orders were not in force at the time of the alleged 
•ident in January and February last year. Accordingly, the Standing 
•tiers are not of any material help in this case. 

The charges of adoption of go-slow tactics and inciting workers not 
work in the factory are admittedly serious cases of misconduct, 
niflhahle with dismissal from service. The stay-in-strike and 
ongfully confining the management after working hours’ are also 
m of misconduct. It has been held by the Labour Appellate Tribunal 
a case reported in 1953, L.A.O., page 414, that a deliberate go-slow 
liry is not a legitimate weapon in the armoury of labour. It is an 
iidioun method of undermining the stability of the concern. It has 
mi made a misconduct under the “Model Standing Orders” prescribed 
the Industrial Employment Standing Orders Act, 194C. There cannot 
two opinions about the fact that a deliberate go-slow policy is a serious 
conduct. 

Question for decision in this case is whether the allegation made by 
management in the charges are true. In this case, the management 
J in its statement before this Tribunal that the workers did not 
mut written explanation to these charges and refused to accept the 
irge-sheets when tendered to them. The Union jammed six out of 
workers in this case, who said that they duly submitted written 
uanation to the charges. There was no enquiry after that and they 
e most arbitrarily dismissed from service on false allegations. 
?y relied on a receipt (Ext. C), admitted on the side of the management, 
!• 8 " ow « that written explanations from 19 workers were 
uved by the then Manager on 25th January 1954. Shri R. N. Mallick,

would be justified in going into the merits of the rase where— 

(1) There is want of bona fidrit; 

(2) There is violation of the principles of natural justice; 

(3) There is basic error of facts; and 

(4) There is perverse finding qp the materials. 


On the facts established in this case, the Tribunal should enter mto

Minimum wages cannot depend upon the employer’s capacity to 
Richardson in his book on Minimum Wages says that : 

“The criterion of capacity to pay is not a relative factor to: 
purpose of deciding the living wage.” 

I use the expression “minimum wage” as distinguished from the 
“living wage”. The Fair Wage Committee, 1949, classified wage* 
three heads — 

(1) Minimum Wages. 

(2) Fair Wages. 

(3) Living Wages. 

Here Rs. 47-8-6 per month including dearness allowance represent 
minimum wages, but fair wages. It has been held by the Appell. 
Tribunal in many cases that : 

“capacity to pay is not to be taken into consideration in fiungt 
minimum wages”. 

I cannot recommend increment to all categories of w orkmen nor to tl 
unskilled labourers who are at present getting Rs. 51-3 per month or won 
but the unskilled workers who are at present getting only Its. 4NH 
including dearness allowance per month are to be paid Rs. r»l-3 jn-i montl

I may straightway note that having regard to the issue referred

Section 10(4) of the Industrial Disputes Act lays down: 

“Where in an order referring an industrial dispute to a Tribunal 
this section or in a subsequent order, the appropriate < lover

An employee, whether he is employed in an industry or not, can abando

Regarding the manner of termination of employment, the case of tli 
uployer seems to me more probable and natural. I, therefore, accept th 
iiiu*. The workman’s version that he was dismissed on 13th May J95 
itliout notice and without any cause is not convincing. The fact that h 
as admittedly shown as absent in the attendance register from 13th Ma 
would rather support the employers version of the case. Had lie bee 
ismissed on 13th May 1963, he would have marked himself present. Th 
ri deuce shows that the workman was irregular in attendance. Tt is, then 
)re, very likely that he started to absent from 13th May 1953 without noth 
nil intimation as alleged by the employer. Nonetheless, I find no justifies

[wonted from 13th May 1953 without notice, he was not liable to be dit

iding automatic termination of employment on account of such abseuci 
a iin\ case, none should be punished without issue of formal charge-shoe 
ad affording opportunity to explain his conduct. So, in all fairness, wlie 
hri Sitaram lloy Ohoudhury was u monthly salaried workman, lie wa 
iititled one month’s notice or one month’s salary in lieu of notice fo 
jrmmatiug Ins employment. In this view of the matter I think, he shoul 
et niie month’s salary in lieu of notice as compensation. 

Resides the evidence shows that Shri Sitaram Roy Ohoudhury joine 
arvice in this concern in February 1952 and was subsequently confirmed o 
nt August 1952 on the basis of the agreement, Ext. C, on a salary of its. 5 
er month. According to the employer his employment was terminated o 
ltli June 1953. The workman had thus served for more than one yea 
efore his employment was terminated. 

Taking all these facts into consideration as qIho the previous offer am 
reef dunce, I allow, in all, 1£ month’s salary as compensation (1 month’

MTicc) which 1 think to be fair and equitable. The employer is directed t

The complainant has put in about 29 years’ service in the Department 
0 { the Ludlow Jute Mills. A small particle of burnt coal dust 
4 ° ti into the sole of the complainant’s feet within the Mill precints and 
f w davs after, the coal globule was extracted, but the portion from where 
4 16 as extracted became septic. He was all along under the treatment of 
Ik Mill Doctor. The above incident occurred in the month of Bhadra

a was X-raved by the Mill Doctor m the month of Falgoon 1360 B.S.,

01 iured. The complainant protested against this action of the Company

for 23 years' service.

Exts. A ami B were marked for the Company. Ext. 1 is his service record 
and Ext. 2 is the payment receipt of his provident fund, and Ext. 3 is his 
(iratuitv receipt. It appears from Exts. A and B that the complainant 
retired from service on 25th February 1954. The proceedings before this 
Tribunal commenced on 7th April 1954, i.e. y about one and a hall* month 
after he was discharged. In the circumstances, we hold that the applica- 
tion under section 33 A is not maintainable and is accordingly rejected.

ti “Security of service” in the Award, dated 1st March 1951, there is 
,e (13) (ft) which provides for suspension on the ground of proved 
omluct and sub-clause ( h ) of clause 13 speaks of suspension pending

Piaoa systam. 

Under this issue the workmen contend that this system should J 
abolished and that the basic monthly salary of a piece-rate worker should! 
fixed at par with his average monthly earnings plus Rs. 28 as deans 
allowance ; on the other hand the employers contend that there is no justia 
cation for the abolition of the piece-rate system and that this s J 8 * en V[ 
prevailing in Printing Industry from time immemorial. It is by 


1643 


^ i] l«E CALCUTTA GAZETTE* APRIL 14, 1965 


nlovers that if this piece-rate workers are to be converted to monthly- 
L P workers, their present average earnings per month should be exclusive 
the dearnealf Allowance of Rs. 22 and also of the overtime earnings for 
k done in «cess of 46 hours per week. I think, the contention of the 
clovers is reMOhable. None of the piece-rate workers has been examined 
a witness *lld the Tribunal is not in a position to know whether the 
ra te workers would be benefited or not by the abolition of piece-mte 
Item ns desired by the workmen. In the Omnibus Award of 1948, to 
*ich those employers were not parties it was accepted on both sides that 
Jtain departments in the printing industry should continue the piece- 
[ e system. I way quote the agreement between the Companies and the 
aions in the said Award. 

“It is accepted that ordinarily all workers in the printing presses will 
be employed on the basis of monthly wages. There exist, however, 
certain works, e.g., envelop making, other classes of stationery 
manufacture and book binding, which are usually done under the 
piece-rate system. Therefore, the piece-rate in this limited sphere 
may continue in the industry. It is agreed that piece-mte system 
does not include work on contract basis.” 

'hen such a large number of undertakings which were parties to the Award 
1948 accepted the above principles by collective agreement, I find no 
awn to treat the present case differently. Piece-rate system is branch of 
e system know as “payment by results”. In a text-book on the subject, 
is matter has been put thus 

“Straight piece-work — this means payment of an uniform price per unit 
of production. This system is most appropriate where production is 
repetitive in character and can be easily divided into similur units, 
piece-rate is easily divided into two classes, vis., (/) money piece- 
work, (m) time piece-work. In the former the employees is paid 
a flat money price for each piece or operation completed. In the 
latter there is time allowed. For the particular operation or job 
involved, the worker is paid at his basic or piece-work operative 
rate per hour for the time allowed. If he finished the job in less 
than the time allowed he gains the advantage of the time saved 
as he is still paid for the original time allowed.” 

am of opinion that in the present case the existing piece-rate system should 
mtimie for some time and the question of conversion of this system to 
lonlldy rote should be taken up for decision in a proper case in future. 

> has not been shown that the existing piece-rate system is not doing good 
I the workmen concerned.

p * i] ¥BE CALCUTTA GAZETTE; APRIL 14, 1955 


p fj states in his evidence that no bonus was paid in 1950, 1951 and 
>2 and bonus for one month was paid in 1954 and 1949. The claim of 
itomary bonus is, therefore, not sustainable and must be rejected. The 
[ v question for consideration is whether any bonus is payable in view of 
/relative prosperity of the concern during the year under review, in view 
the principles laid down in the case of Millowners’ Association, Bombay, 
)52 L.A.C., 433). It is in evidence that bonus was paid to the employees 
1954, but no bonus was paid in 1953. The question is if any bonus was 
vable in 1953 on the working of the previous year. The learned advocate 
; Company pointed out that the bonus is payable in the month of 
tober and it is paid every year on a consideration of the profits accruing 
the two preceding half-years. It is, therefore, stated that no bonus was 
id in October 1953, on a consideration of the profits of the Company in 
a h a lf-year ended 30th June 1953 and 31st December 1952. It appears 
mi balance-sheets, Exts. E and E(l), that in the half-year ended 31st 
‘cember 1952, the Company incurred loss to the extent of Rs. 1,77,445 
d odd, and in the half-year ended 30th June 1953, the Company incurred 
loss of about Rs. 52,000. Considering the fact that bonus was to be paid 
the month of October 1953, and bonus was actually paid in October 1954, 
e (contention of the learned advocate for the Company that the bonus 
yablc in October 1953 was not paid in view of the losses incurred during 
e two preceding half-years appears to be acceptable. In view of these 
reumstances, it is awarded that- no bonus is payable by the Company in 
53. 


The description of the issue being bonus for 1953 is a little misleading 
bonus for 1953 is really payable in 1964 on a consideration of the trading 
suits for the year 1953. In view of the fact that bonus was actually 
lid in October 1954, I consider this issue to mean as to whether bonus 
is payable in October 1953, on a consideration of the trading of the two 
muling half-years, as suggested by the learned advocate for the Company, 
i has been mentioned above, on such consideration, no bonus is payable 
• the employees. This issue is accordingly answered.

do not show the name of Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose. This wit 
states that Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose did not do any other work e D 
that of Overseas Corporation, but he was paid at the rate of 9(5) r 
mensem from the Calcutta Jute Manufacturing Co., and that as h ! 
not a permanent employee, his name did not find mention ritber bit 
cash book or in the attendance register. He states that it is not a fa 
that Sailesh Chandra Bose was discharged because of his being a nimh 
of the Union. He further states that as there was paucity of wd 
Sailesh Babu was discharged. 

In the written statement of the Union, it is stated that on 1st Apri 
1953, Shri S. N. Chatterjee, Secretary of the Union, wan retired fron 
service, by way of victimisation, and that under force of circumstance*, 
Shri Chatterjee had to agree to the offer of the management. It i* 
further stated that Sriman Bose next took a leading part of the Unioi 
and he also, as a result of his trade union activities, vs 
retired from service. It is, therefore, clear that although Sim Sailed 
Chandra Bose states in his examination-in-chief that tin 1 Nccretan ol 
the Union lost his job for bis Union activities, he was really retired 
from service on 1st April 1952. Considering Ext. A, the letter d 

Shri S. N. Nath, the President of the Union, dated 29tli January 19 

to the Company, incorporating the demands of the Piuon in "luuli 
claim has been made for retirement on completion ol 55 years id age, a 
also mentioning in an Annexure, the age of Shri S. N ('haitHj 

as 68 years, it is but natural that in implementing the claim 
enforcement of the age of ertirement on completion <>i year 

Shri S. N. Chatterjee would be the first to retire and his Hipim 
could legitimately come on the 1st of April, 1952. This 
of the fact of the retirement of Shri S. N. Chatterjee bv lb«* ^ 
Advocate for the Company, therefore, appears to be acceptor) e 
allegation of Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose that the Company a ‘ s 
removing the officials of the Union one after another does no 
to be justified. It appears from the evidence on 



i Sailesb Chandra Bose was given a temporary appointment in the 
! tfa Jute Manufacturing Co., on l*th January 1953, on the verbal 
ar 0 f the Manapiny Director, Shri DayAram Poddar and lhat 
loujrh he was paid his salary from the Company, he was engaged 
the most of his time in another Company, beinp the International 
rseas Corporation, in which the Directors of finis Company were 
jested. The clajm of this 'Company that Shri Sailesh Chandra 
e had no sufficient work to do in this Company is, Iherefore, 
ified*. Exts. B and C, being the attendance registers and salary 
i {dors' of this Company, do not show the name of Shri Sailesb 
ndru Bose. The demands of the Union over the items of claim 
ch have been subject matter of this proceedings were made before 
date of Ext. A, dated 29th January 1953, and Shri Sailesb Chandri 
e states that he was a member of the Union not earlier than Mai oh 
4 He was discharged on 30th April 1954. It is a fact that on 
j t April 1954, the Company received a letter from the Union showing 
t Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose was appointed as Treasurer of 
Faion. It is also in the evidence of P.W. 1 Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose 
( only 0 out of 24 employees of the Company, were members 
the Cnion. Considering all these circumstances, it does not ippear 
t Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose has any Union activities to his credit 
[ might actuate the Company to get rid of him, as alleged. What 
really appears is that Shn Sailesh Chandra Bose was appointed 
lo sundry works of International Overseas Corporation, but was paid by 
Calcutta Jute Manufacturing Co., Ltd. It also appears from the 
ance-sheets, Exts. E and E(l), that in the half-years ended 31st 
;ember 1952 and 30th June 1953, the Calcutta Jute Manufacturing 
, Ltd., incurred losses. Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose was discharged 
proper notice with effect from 1 st May 1954, because he had not much 
do for this Company. This conduct of the Company cannot 
assailed as an unfair labour practice, or as a conduct by way of 
^imisation for trade union activities of the employee. It has been 
l down by the Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in the 
? of Buckingham and Carnatic Mill's case, 1952, L.A.C., 490, that 
the case of a discharge of an employee on notice or in lieu thereof, 
niffit of wages for a certain period* without assigning any reason, 
las to be seen whether the employer acted with an honest' purpose! 
:uis also been stated by the same Tribunal in the case of D. B. R. Mills 
leralmd, Deccan, reported in 1952, L.A.C., 540, that discharge on 
ice could be challenged only if the discharge proceeded from 
r mala fide, s on the part of the Company, for victimisation or unfair 
pur practice. The same views have been expressed in the case of 
inr lire Bricks Workmen, reported in W53, L.A.C., 81. From wliat 
"T n discussed above, it is clear that the Union has failed to 
lisli that the discharge of Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose proceeded 
imy mala fides on the part of the Company or any victimisation or 
ir labour practice. It is, therefore, awarded that the claim for 
■uteiuent of Shri Sailesh Chandra Bose cannot be supported ami 
tie rejected.

retrenchment, he is entitled to compensation.

tuiB issue is accordingly answered.

Original Sidte 

NOTIFICATION. 

Calcutta, the 7th April 1955. 

It is ordered by the High Court at Calcutta that with effect from the 
date of publication in the Calcutta Gazette , the following new Rules be 
adopted and that the said Buies be included as Appendix 7 A of Part II of 
the High Court Original Side Rules, 1914 (4th Edition) and be substituted 
in place of the Buies now included in the said Appendix. 

In exercise of powers conferred by section 45TT and section 45M of the 
Banking Companies Act, 1949 (Act X of 1949), the clause 37 of the 
Letters Patent of 1865 and section 129 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 
1908 (Act V of 1908), the High Court is pleased to make the following rules, 
to come into effect on and from the date of their publication in the Calcutta 
Gazette : — 

1. In these rules unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 
context: — 

(i) “The Act” means the Banking Companies Act, 1949, as from 

time to time modified or amended. 

(ii) “Appendix” and “Chapter” mean appendix and chapter of the 

Buies of the Original Side of the High Court. 

(iii) “Judge” means the Judge taking Company Matters or such other 

Judge as the Chief Justice may from time to time appoint. 

(iv) “Liquidator” means the Official Liquidator of a banking Company 

including the Court Liquidator. 

(v) “Company” means a company to which the provisions of the Act 

apply. 

(vi) “Code” means the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. 

(vii) “Company Buies” mean the rules made by the High Court at 

Calcutta under the Indian Companies Act. 

(viii) “Registrar” means the Registrar of the Court in its Original 

Jurisdiction and includes the Company Registrar or any other 

officer authorised to perform the duties of the Registrar. 

2. The rules of the Original Side of the Court for the time being in 
force and the Company Rules as also the general practice of the Court 
including the course of procedure and practice in Chambers shall apply to 
all proceedings under the Act and to proceedings transferred under this Act 
and the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act of 1950, so far as applicable, 
except and so far as is otherwise provided by the Act and these rules. 

3. All proceedings under the Act other than suits shall be intituled 
m the matter of the Act and in the matter of the company and in the case 
of a company being wound up under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, also 
m the matter of that Act. 

4. A Register called the “Register of Transferred Banking Company 
Matters” and a Ledger called the “Ledger of Transferred Banking Company 
Matters * shall be kept and maintained in the Registrar’s office, in which 
'I 8U1 *? an ^ ma ^ rs transferred under section 11 of the Banking Companies

10. The petitioner shall, before the date fixed for the further hearing 
of the petition, cause to be made and filed an affidavit, stating that all 
directions given in the matter have been complied with. 

11. When an order is made under section 37 of the Act, a minute 
thereof shall be sent forthwith to the Registrar by the officer in attendance 
and the Registrar shall cause the same to be drawn up and filed immediately. 
Thereafter a copy of the said order rhall forthwith be sent by the Registrar 
to the Reserve Bank. 

On the Bame day that such an order is made, an application for drawing 
it up shall be made by the petitioner by a requisition in writing to the 
Registrar on payment of the usual fees. If the petitioner failB to make such 
an application, the Registrar shall forthwith place the matter before the 
Judge for appropriate directions. 

12. Where the Judge grants relief under the proviso to section 87(2) 
of the Act, the officer in attendance shall forthwith send to the Registrar 
a copy of the minutes of the order. The Registrar shall thereupon call 
from the Roserve Bank a report on the affairs of the company. On receipt 
of such report, the Registrar Hhall place the same before the Judge and the 
Judge may either rescind the order passed or pass such other order and 
give such directions as he may think fit. 


Special Officer. 

18. The Special Officer shall be allowed such remuneration and 
necessary expenses as the Judge may direct. 


14. The duties of the Special Officer shall he discharged by him us an 
officer of the Court and subject to the control of the Judge. For the purpose 
of discharge of his duties and for the purpose of acquiring and retaining 
custody and control of the assets, books, documents, effects and actionable 
claims of the company, the Special Officer shall have all the powers of a 
Receiver appointed under Order XL, Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure ('ode 
read with rules made by the High Court in respect thereof and such other 
power as may be conferred by the Judge. 


15. The Special Officer shall as soon as possible take out a summons 
for directions and the Judge may give directions on all matters that imn 
be necessary or expedient from time to time upon the hearing of the summons 
and where necessary, upon restoration of the summons supported by an 
affidavit. The Judge may direct service or reservice of the summons or of 
a further summons on any person.

19. The Judge shall, if satisfied that there is reason lor doubting such 
entries or any one or more of them, by an endorsement on the report, 
direct the Liquidator to call for proof of them. The report, with the

Banking Company 8uits. 

21. The order of appointment of a Liquidator Bhall be proof of bis com- 
petence to sign or verify pleadings, unless otherwise ordered by the Court. 
Pleading shall include plaints, written statements, statements of tacts, 
counter-statements of facts and petitions. 

22. In all suits filed by the Company the plaint shall be marked with 
the words “Banking Company Suit” in addition to the usual endorsement. 

23. In all suits, by the Company, the writ shall be in Form No. 2 and 
shall ordinarily be served by the Liquidator himself by registered post. 
The writ shall have annexed to it a copy of the plaint. 

24. Until the defendant shows to the contrary, the service of the 
writ shall be deemed to be effected on the defendant by addressing to his 
last known place of business or residence and posting by registered post a 
letter containing the writ and to have been effected at the time at which 
the letter would be deliveied in the ordinary course of post. When the 
defendant or the defendants has or have been sued in his or their firm name, 
the Liquidator may, at his option, serve the writ on any one or more of 
the partners of the person in control or management of the partnership 
business in India. 

25. Where the sole defendant has, or all the defendants have failed 
to enter appearance or where the sole defendant has, or all the defendants 
have failed to file a written statement or written statements within the time 
specified in the writ, the Liquidator shall affirm or cause an affidavit to be 
affirmed, stating that the writ or writs of Summons has or have keen duly 
posted and verifying the facts stated in the plaint as true to the deponent s 
own knowledge or true to his belief, stating in the latter case the grounds 
of such belief or true to his information, stating the source from which the 
information is derived and affirming that he verily believes the same to be 
true. 

2G. The affidavit or affidavits mentioned in rule 25 along with a letter 
of the Liquidator or his attorney claiming a judgment shall be filed with 
the Registrar. Thereupon the Registrar, on being satisfied, shall certify 
that no appearance has been entered or written statement filed by or on 
behalf of the sole defendant or any of the defendants within the time 
specified in the writ and Bhall draw up a minute of the decree to be passed 
in the suit and shall place the Bame along with the records before the J udge. 
The Judge may thereupon, if he thinks fit, pass the decree by signing it 
with or without modifications. 


27. If the sole defendant or any of the defendants, if there are more 
than one defendant, enters appearance and files written statement, the suit 
shall, on the expiry of one month from the date on which the time for filing 
the sole or the last written statement, as the case may be, expires, be set 
down in the daily list of the Judge for directions. Seven days* notice of 
the appearance oi the matter for directions shall be given by the Registrar 
to the parties appearing. 


28. When the suit comes up for directions under the last preceding 
™ie, the Judge may give orders, as he may think proper, as to discovery, 
inspection, particulars, delivery of interrogatories, amendments ami further 
proceedings in the suit and generally for a speedy hearing thereof. No 
party shall be entitled to apply for discovery and inspection until the suit 
nas been Bet down in the list tor directions as aforesaid.

46. The party served with notice shall file with the Registrar an

shall forthwith be given to the Liquidator at the address mentioned in the 
notice. The affidavit shall be filed not later than seven days before the dale

47. If any party fails to file the affidavit within the lime allowed 
therefor, the claim of the Banking Company as appearing in the list shall 
be deemed to be admitted and the Judge may settle the claim ar partr 
against him and grant such relief as he may think fit, or may direct fresh 
notice to be issued and served in such manner as he may think fit. Where 
a party has filed the affidavit within the time allowed therefor, ihe Judge, 
if not satisfied with the affidavit that the party has any defence to the claim, 
may settle the claim against him forthwith or may, subject to such terms 
as to giving security or otherwise as the Judge may think fit, direct ihe 
matter to be tried on evidence. 

48. The Judge may adjourn or fix a fresh date for consideration of Ihe 
claim from time to time and may give directions for affidavits, discovcrv , 
inspection, particulars, interrogatories, amendments or otherwise as may be 
necessary for the speedy settlement of the claim. The Judge may settle (he 
claim on affidavits or may set down the matter for hearing or otherwise. 

49. The provisions of Order XX XII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 
1908, shall apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings under section 451) of the 
Act where the party is a minor or is a person adjudged to be of unsound

or mental infirmity to be incapable of protecting liis interest. The certi- 
ficate under section 45D(6) of the Act shall be issued and signed by the 
Registrar. 

50. The Judge will have power to assess and settle the costs of such 
proceedings in such manner as he thinks fit. 


Publio Examination under 8ection 45G of the Act. 

5J. The report of the Liquidator pursuant to section 450 of the A cl 
shall state the names of the persons intended to be examined and the opinion 
required by the section and shall state in a narrative form the facts and 
matters which the Liquidator desires to bring to the notice of the Court upon 
which such opinion is based. 

52. The Liquidator shall submit the report to the Judge and shall 
obtain an appointment from the Judge for the consideration thereof and 
shall give not less than 14 days’ notice to everv person mentioned in the 
report who is intended to be examined. The notice shall bo in Form No. 7 
and shall be accompanied by a copy of the report and shall be sent by 
registered post. 

53. Every person served with the notice under rule 52 may show cause 
by an affidavit which shall be filed not less than three days before the date 
fixed for the consideration of the report and notice of the filing thereof shall 
he given to the Liquidator forthwith. 

64. Where the Judge makes an order under section 45U directing any 
person to be publicly examined and attend thereat he shall fix a date for 
such examination. The notice of the day so fixed shall be given by the 
Liquidator to the person who is to be examined by sending such notice by 
registered post. Tne notice shall be posted at least seven days lief ore the 
date fixed for such examination. 

55. The substance of the order made under the preceding rule shall be 
advertised seven clear days before the date appointed for examination in 
such newspaper or newspapers as the Judge may direct and by posting on 
cue notice board of the Court House. The advertisement shall be in Form 
No. 8.

62. The provisions of Chapter XXXI of the Buies of the Original Side

Rule under Section 45Q of the Aot. 

63. When an order under section 45Q of the Act is made the principal 
officer in attendance shall send to the Registrar a copy of the minutes of 
the order and the Registrar shall forthwith send a copy of the order to the 
Reserve Bank The report of the Reserve Bank Bliall be placed by the

Request under Section 458 of the Aot. 

64. Whenever the Liquidator of any Banking Company wants to make 
a request to the Chief Presidency Magistrate or any District Magistrate 
under the provisions of section 45S of the Act and in doing so he finds it 
necessary to send such letter through the Registrar, he shall submit Ihe 
same together with a duplicate thereof to the Registrar. The Registrar 
may thereupon countersign the original and forward the same to the Dis- 
trict Magistrate at the cost of the bank and shall keep the duplicate with 
the records of the proceedings of the bank. 

Petitions for winding up. 

65. Rules relating to winding up petitions in Appendix 7 shall apply 
mutatis mutandis to a petition for winding up of a Banking Company 
under the Act. Notice of such petition shall be served on the Reserve Bank. 

Other application. 

66. Save as otherwise provided by these ruleR all applications under 
the Act shall be made to the Judge by petitions verified by an affidavit. 

67. On the hearing of an application under the Act the Judge may 
make such order or orders and give such directions as he may think fil an 
to the proceedings and more particularly with regard to the following 
matters, namely, the giving of notice to parties who are likely to be affected 
by the application and the inode or manner in which such notice is to In* 
given. 

Costs. 

68. In all applications arising out of the winding up of the Banking 
Company the Liquidator shall not be entitled to engage an advocate unless 
at the first hearing of such application he obtains the sanction of the Court 
in that behalf. 

69. The Liquidator shall not be entitled to engage a lawyer for the 
purpose of carrying out the provisions of the following rules: — 

Rules 17 to 20, 23, 31, 43, 52, 54, 55, 64 and 72. 

70. Unless otherwise ordered, the costs of the proceedings transferred 
to this Court under section 11 of the Banking Companies (Amendment) An 
of 1950 and under section 45C of the Act shall be governed by the rules oj 
costs applicable in the Court from which such proceedings were transferred 
to this Court' 

71. In non-con tentious matters and in matters which do not relaii 1 to 
proceedings in this Court, the bill of costs shall, on being presented to t 
Company Matters Department, be checked in the presence of the solici 
concerned by the Assistant Taxing Officer who shall certify the nmoun 
has allowed in the bill for payment.

RULES UNDER SECTIONS 45J, 45N AND 45U OF THE BANKING 

COMPANIES ACT. 

]. The offences triable Humniurily under sub-section (1) of section J.'i.l 
of the Act shall he such among the offences contemplated by the sub-section 
as are punishable with imprisonment not exceeding two years or with tine of 
with both imprisonment not exceeding the aforesaid limit and fine and shall 
he so tried unless the Judge to whom the complaint in respect of any such 
offence is presented otherwise directs. 

2. A proceeding under sub-section (1) of section 45J shall lie commenced 
by a complaint in writing which shall he presented before the Judge dealing, 
for the time being, with the proceedings for the winding up of the Rank nig 
Company concerned or such other Judge as the Chief Justice may, by a 
general or a special order, direct. 

On the presentation of such complaint, the Judge shall dim! Ihc 
complainant and where the liquidator is not the complainant, the liqunlnto?. 
to attend in his Court on a date specified by him and shall, on such date or 
such other date as he mnv fix, examine cm oath the complainant oi the 
complainant and the liquidator, as the case may be. 

4. Upon such examination, the Judge* may dismiss I be complaint it hr 
he of opinion that there are no sufficient grounds for proceeding or on tin* 
ground that it is not expedient to try the case in a summary manner and in 
either case he shall briefly record the reasons for his order. 

f>. If the Judge does not so dismiss the complaint, he shall issue a 
summons or a bailable or non-bailable warrant against the accused as be 
may deem fit and on the accused appearing or being brought before him, 
.shall proceed to try him in a summary way; 

Provided that the Judge may release the accused cm bail and may also, 
after lie* lias granted bail, cancel the same subsequently if be finds suificicnt 
ground to do so at any stage of the trial. 

G. The* provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, except so far as 
they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act or these* rules, shall 
apply to such trials. 

7. The dismissal of a complaint under Rule 4 hereof on the giound Ihul 
it is not expedient to try the case in a summary manner shall be no bar to a 
fresh complaint under sub-section (4) of section 45 J. 

8. A proceeding under sub-section (4) of section 45J shall be* commenced 
by a complaint in writing which shall be presented before the Chief Justice 
or such other Judge, not dealing, for the time being with the* proceedings 
for the winding up of the blinking company concerned, as the Chief Justice 
may, by a general or a special order, direct. 

9. On the presentation of suc*h complaint, the Chief Justice o: otliei 
Judge shall proceed in the manner laid clown in Pule ‘1 and mnv, after he has 
done so, dismiss the complaint, if he be of opinion that there are no sufficient 
grounds for proceeding, recording briefly in eury case bis reasons for so 
cloiug. 


19. If the Chief Justice or other Judge does not dismiss the complaint, 
he shall proceed in the manner laid down in Rule 5, except that the trial 
shat] not be in a summary form. 

11. When the complaint is presented to the Chief Justice, be may. 
utter he has issued process for the appearance or production ol the accused, 
transfer the ease for trial, instead of trying it himself, to an\ Judge ol the 
Umrt, other than the Judge dealing, for the time being, witli the* proceeding?* 

nr tbe winding up of the Banking Company concerned. 

12. The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall, so far as 
they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act or these* Rules, app y 
to trials under section 45J(4). 

All processes in connection with trials under sections 4oJ(l) and 
(4) shall issue from the office of the Clerk of the State.

In course of hearing the workmen filed a petition praying that 
special increment should be allowed at 2 annas per hour Up to -a total 0 
vears. The question is whether this special increment should he 
rate of 2 annas as contended for by the workmen or at the rate of j 
as proposed by the Management. I accept the proposal that this S|)( 
increment should be at interval of three years and the total period of , 
increment should be nine years, but regarding the rate of increment 
cannot but consider the following circumstances. In the proposed g^ 
scheme (ride Annexure A to the written statement hied by the 
there is a remark that promotion of a workman to a higher grade 4al 
given in cases of special merit and that ordinarily a workman shall re n 
for two years at. the top of the grade before he is considered for promo 
to the next grade. So it appears from the grading scheme itself , 
promotion from lower grade to the higher would not take more than 
or three years after reaching the maximum. In these circumstances, 
special increment up to a total period of 9 years before promotion to 
higher grade is too lavish for the mesne period, buch long range nchi 
with regard to special increment which is nothing but a mesne between 
grades, should not be entertained by the Tribunal. When there i, 
expectation that a workman may get promotion to the higher grade 
course of two or three years after reaching the maximum oi the | 01 
grade in which he might be placed, we should not bother at all 
whether this mesne increment after the maximum of the ftrailp sho 
continue for 9 years or 14 years. Similary we should not consider 
seriously whether the workmen should get special increment during 
mesne period at the rate of 1 anna per hour or 2 annas per hour. It i», 
a stop gup arrangement for the interval. V\ hen the ordinary inn™ 
within the grade is at the rate of 2 annas per hour, 1 do not think Hint 
special increment for the mesne period in between the two grades sk 
be more than 1 anna per hour. I am of opinion, the proposal made by 
Management in this respect is lo be accepted.

No. 2344W.T.— -27 th April 1955. — In exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 
1919 (Bengal Act I of 1919), the Governor is pleased to make the follow- 
ing by-laws for the Basirhet Municipality in the district of 24-Parganas, 
namely : — 

BY-LAWS. 

1. Appointment and duties of the Registering Offloer.— Every rick- 
shaw in the Basirhat Municipality shall be annually registered by the 
Registering Officer appointed for registering hackney-carriages. 

2. Qualifications of the bearers.— Every person applying for a bearer's 
license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer — 

(i) that he knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and is in all 

respects a fit person for such employment; 

(ii) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 

places in and around the town of Basirhat; 

(iii) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and 

distances prepared by the Commissioners; 

(iv) that he knows the rules of the road and signals used by the* 

bearers and drivers of vehicles and by the traffic police; 

(v) that he is not less than 18 and not more than 45 years of age. 

3. Contents of license. — There shall be attached to each license, issued 
to a rickshaw bearer — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 

(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him; and 

(c) a printed table of fares and distances prepared by the Commie 

sioners, for which no charge shall be paid by the bearer. 

4. Production Of licenses. — Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carr; 
with him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so by tli 
traffic police, any Commissioner or other person authorised by the Com mis 
sioners. He shall exhibit the table of fares and distances on a prominen 
part of the vehicle. 

5. Prohibition Of smokingi eto* — No bearer shall smoke while driving 
nor shall he muffle up his face and head in such a manner as to endangei 
the proper driving of his vehicle. 

6. Condition Of rickshaws. — (a) The body of the rickshaw shall be 
sound and clean and all the lvoardw strong and properly secured. 

(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by 
properly fitted splash boards. 

(c) The springs and axles shall be of good metal, strong and properly 
riveted and free from rust. 

(d) The iron supports at the back shall be properly curved and 
securely fixed at each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

(e) The hood, apron and cushion shall be made of and covered with 
good cloth, canvaB or other materials approved by the Commissioners at a 
meeting. 

(f) The shaft shall be of sound • wood, strong, securely fixed and 
furnished at the fore-ends with a ring-shaped metal support and conno, 
by a collision guard. 

(g) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehich 
water-tight. 

(h) Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps, one facing the front 
and one in the rear. 

(i) Each lamp shall have a red glass window in the back andjjha^ ^ 
so placed that the light from the window is visible from a point t y 

in the rear of the centre of the vehicle. 

(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle haw 
bars on the cycle and iU shall be so constructed that it can t»e i 
by fingers and can give continuous ringing as and when nece 

7. Dimension and pattern of rioktlwm.— All riokshaw« i eWJ 
to the following dimensions and be of suoh pattern as may be n 
Commissioners at a meeting: — 

, Width of the seats— 2 feet 8 inches. 

Height of the seats — 1 foot 4 inches. 

Height of the cushions— 4 indies. . * : '

(2) Speed and halting charge. — When a rickshaw is hired the bearer 
shall ordinarily drive the same at a speed of not less than eight miles per 
hour. If a rickshaw after being hired is made to halt, halting charge 
shall be paid according to the scale laid down in the above fare table. 

10. Passengers to pay Other charges. — Passengers shall pay the ferry 
and other charges while going to and coining from the railway station over 
and above the rates payable to the bearer of rickshaw. 

11. Maximum load to be carried in rickshaws.— Passengers and 
j u £ffage shall not ordinarily exceed four maunds in weight. It shall not 
be permissible to any bearer to refuse to ply except on reasonable grounds. 

12. Advertisement on rickshaws . — No advertisement shall be fixed at 
such places as to cover the number plate and fare table affixed to the 
rickshaw.

No. Medl . / 3013 / 2D-1 12 / 54 . — 1 2th 4pril 1956.— The following draft 
of an amendment which, in exercise of the power conferred by section 33 
of the Drugs Act, 1940 (XX11I of 1940), the Governor, after consultation 
with the Board, proposes to make in the Bengal Drugs Buies, 1946, 
published with notification No. HOMedl., dated the 7th January 1946, as 
subsequently amended, is published, as required by the said section, for 
the information of persons likely to be affected thereby. 

2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 7th July 
1955 and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto which may be 
received by the undersigned before that date shall be considered. 


Draft amendment. 

In Schedule E appended to the said rules, for section (B) in Part I, 
substitute the following section, namely: — 

“(B) Provisions applicable to the production of Vaccine Lymph (Vaccinia 

Vaccine). 

1. Definition and proper name.— Vaccine lymph is a preparation of 

the vaccinal material obtained from the vesicles produced on 
the skin of healthy unimals by inoculation of vaccinia virus. 
Its proper name is “Vaccine Lymph”. 

2. Staff of establishment. — (1) The establishment in which vaccine 

lymph is prepared must be under the complete direction and 
control of a competent expert, who must be assisted by a staff 
adequate for carrying out the operations and tests required 
during the preparation of the vaccine lymph and in connection 
with the finished product. 

(2) The entire responsibility for the production, storage, testing and 
issue of safe, potent and reasonably pure vaccine lymph rests 
upon the competent expert. 


3. Condition and housing of animals. — (1) The animals used in the 
production of vaccine lymph must be housed in hygienic 
conditions in premises satisfactory for this purpose. 

(2) Only healthy animals may be used in the production of vaccine 
lymph. Each animal intended to be used as a source of 
vaccine lymph must, before being passed for the production of 
vaccine lymph, be subjected to a period of observation in 
quarantine for at least seven days. During the period of 
quarantine the animal must remain free from any sign of 
disease and must be thoroughly cleaned and groomed. 


4. Precautions to be observed in preparation. — (1) A special room, 
with impervious walls and floor, which can be washed and, 
when necessary, chemically disinfected, must be provided for 
the inoculation of the animals and the collection of the vaccinal 
material. 


(2) The inoculation shall be made on such parts of the animal os are 
not liable to be soiled by the passage of faeces. The surface 
used for inoculation shall be shaved and so cleaned as to 
procure the nearest possible approach to asepsis. Prior to the 
collection of vaccinal material the inoculated area of the skin 
shall be cleaned in a similar fashion. 


(3) (a) Immediately before the vaccinal material is collected, tie 
animal should be killed. Subsequently a thorough pos- 
mortem examination of the carcass shall be made by a V ia ,j 
expert. A complete record of each such examination snaJi 
kept and shall be open to inspection by or on behalf 01 , 
licensing authority at any time. If the examination rev 
any conditions which indicate or suggest that the anim0 ■ j a \ 
suffering from any communicable disease (other than va<w 
the lymph obtained from that animal shall not be issued, 


(b) When lymph is collected from a living animal each such 

shall be kept under observation for a period of at leas ^ 
eight hours after collection of lymph. If during thi PJ yr 
the examination reveals any conditions which , her 

suggest that the animal is suffering from any infee no f 
than vaccinia the lymph obtained from that animal 
be issued. 

(4) All instruments and appliances used in the production 0 f 

lymph shall be previously subjected to W effective P rooww . 
sterilisation. • ■ ■ - . • t, ' .

(6) Laboratories in which vaccinal Material, after removal from the 
animal is being manufactured into lymph must be housed in a 
building separated from stables or animal houses by n 
reasonable distance. Such laboratories must have impervious 
walls and floors and must be capable of being readily dis- 
infected when necessary. 

(6) All processes concerned with the manufacture of vaccine lymph 

must be carried out with thorough aseptic precautions. 

(7) All vaccinal material must be subjected after collection to such 

treatment with glycerol or other partial disinfectants as will 
bring the content of bacteria and other extraneous micro- 
organisms of the lymph within the limit prescribed in 
paragraph 7 of this part of this Schedule. 

(8) (a) From the very time the vaccinal material is collected, it shall 

be kept continuously in cold storage at a temperature 1 below 
0°C. excepting when it is being subjected to Borne essential 
manufacturing process like grinding or treatment with 
glycerol or other partial disinfectants necessary to bring down 
the number of micro-organisms to the prescribed limit. 

(b) When the procedures necessary to bring the content of bacteria 
and other extraneous micro-organisms within the prescribed 
limit have been completed, the vaccine lymph shall be kept 
continuously in cold storage at a temperature below (IT.; 
until it is withdrawn to be filled into containers for issue, 
after which process the filled containers shall immediately be 
returned to cold storage and kept continuously at a temperature 
below 0°C., until required for issue: 

Provided that it shall be permissible to remove vaccine lymph from 
one such cold store to another, if adequate precautions are 
taken during such removal to guard against deterioration. 

(e) A four-hourly record of daily temperature of the cold room during 
day time shall be maintained for inspection. 


f>. Containers . — Vaccine lymph for issue shall be introduced with 
aseptic precautions either — 

(u) in the previously sterilized capillary glass tubes in which case 
each tube shall then be hermetically sealed at each end. Each 
tube shall contain a quantity of vaccine lymph suitable for 
the effective vaccination of one human subject; or 

(b) into tubes or containers of large dimensions which have been 
sterilized before the introduction of the lymph and sealed so 
as to preclude the access of bac teria. 


(i. Labelling . — (1) The label on the container or a label or wrapper 
affixed to the package to which the container is issued tor 
Bale, shall bear a statement that the potency of the vaccine 
lymph cannot be assured for more than seven days from the 4 
date of completion of manufacture unless the lymph is kept 
continuously at a temperature below 10°C. when the potency 
can be assured for fourteen days. Provided that it shall he* 
permissible to state that if the lymph is kept continuously 
below 0°C. the potency can be assured for at least six months. 

(2) For the purpose of Buie 68(3)(b), the date on which the 
manufacture of Idle batch is completed shall be the date on 
which the vaccine lymph is removed for issue from cold 
storage after having been kept continuously at a temperature 
oelow 0 # C., since the date of filling into containers for issue.

Issue No. (1). 


ufltained.

>one into. 


Thu definition of the word "retrenchment” as given in clause (an) of 
tf 7 2 of the Act as introduced by amendment is, in my opinion, 
rv wide so as to cover termination of employment on account of total 
losure of the business. The evidence of the five workmen, who deposed 
afore this Tribunal, shows that they had each been in conti- 
uous service for not less than one year before their employment was 
minuted. In the circumstances, section 25F of the Act would apply 
\ the cases of the five workmen, Shri Madhusudan Sen, Shri Hoshon 
[ian, Shri Siba Prosad Maity, Shri Gonesh Chandra Seal and Shri Devon 
hakroborty. 


Ah regards other three workmen. Shri Walwalla. Shri Majid Mian 
kd Shri Sailen Das, they have not deposed before this Tribunal, 
knexure A to the written statement filed by the Union shows that 
of these three had service beyond six months before retrenchment. 
\uh these three workmen cannot get benefit under section 25F of the Act 


Having regard to the length of service of the five workmen, who 
awed before this Tribunal, the Company is directed to pay, in addition 
one month’s wages in lieu of notice, compensation as below: — 

Shri Madhusudan Sen — 1J months* average pay, 

Shri Hoshan Mian — 1 month's average pay, 

Shri Siba Prosad Maity — 1 month's average pay, 

Shri Gonesh Chandra Seal — 1 month’s average pay, 

Shri Deven Chakroborty — 2£ months' average pay. 


The average pay would mean as defined in clause (aa) of section 2 of 
Act. The wages in lieu of notice and compensation as aforesaid 
told lie paid within two months from the date the award becomes 
orwable.

b. But it affects some of the rights and obligations flowing 
at relationship. Their Lordships in the Punjab National Bank 
53, L.A.C., page 1, at page 16, said, “Moreover, having regard 
onditions of the labouring class and of labour relaiton as is 
v prevalent in India now, it would not, in our opinion, be 
re to industrial peace. If an employer is given a right and a 
an unfettered right to dismiss a workman for his absence due to 

p participation in such a strike If, however, the 

nr workmen who joined the strike ls guilty of violent acts or of 
ve activities such as destruction or attempted destruction of 
re property, intimidation or coercion on loyal employees, etc., 
7 would be different but in such cases the workmen should be 
ly dealt with and the particular workman should be appraised 
jrecise charge against him and should be given a chance to have 
in the matter before he can be dismissed.” In this particular 

ese three workmen along with others were summarily dealt with

nity to meet the charges against them. As the Tribunal

ic termination of services of these* three workmen cannot be 
id. It has been contended by Shri Das Gupto that there is 
‘ against Shri Santiram Ghosh at least to show that he prevented 
al workers from resuming work and therefore the ease of 
n stands on a different footing. To my mind, the mere request 
citation from one worker to another not to work during 

without move does not amount to intimidation or coercion of that 
At least no such evidence is forthcoming in this case against 
> of these three workmen. In the opinion of the Tribunal, there 
n a clear violation of the principles of natural justice in this 
far as these three workmen are concerned. They were not given 
arge-sheet or any reasonable opportunity to put their defence

AWARD. 

i is an application under section 33 A of the Industrial Disputes 
pned by five workers of the Company, and filed by the President 
Workers’ Union for full wages for the period of forced unemploy- 
b a result of lock-out declared by the Company since 17th March 


b staled that the lock-out has been declared without notice and in 
ention of section 23 of the Industrial Disputes Act. A case is 
f before this Tribunal regarding a dispute between the parties, 
learned Advocates of both sides, Shri D. I.. Sen Gupta, for the 
»nd Shri S. C. Sen for the Company. A lock-out is not a condition 
ice and as Huch, Ihe declaration of lock-out during the pendency 
adjudication proceedings before the Tribunal cannot attract the 
)ns of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. Section 33A is, 
re, not maiutainable. 

alleged declaration for lock-out gives rise to a fresh dispute 
1 a ^ ma J' be illegal under section 23 of the Industrial 

» Act, but in any event, this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
in and decide on that dispute in the present proceedings. The 
won is, therefore, not maintainable and is rejected.

AWARD. 

While the aforesaid dispute was pending before the Jute JjJ 
Solemau filed the present application under section 3.iA oi J 
Disputes Act on the ground that he was a permanent wor * 
No. 5 of the Angus Jute Works, that the Manager, Angu« « 


] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MAY* 12, 1965 1099 

)loyfT, that during the pendency of tie adjudication proceedings he 
p ;»hi>d by way of suspension fior four days, from 10th August 1954 
August 1964 out lie was not given any charge-sheet or any opportu- 
expW hia conduct, and that the order was made without permission 
tribunal, it is liable to be set aside. 

■ preliminary objection taken by the Company is that the Angus 
*y and its accredited representatives at the Head Office are the 
employers of the above workmen and not the Manager, Angus Jute 
as alleged by the petitioner. 

point for decision is : Whether the case of the petitioner is covered 
present reference. 

* DECISION. 

irincipal contention and the only contention of the employer is 
Vngus Company and its accredited representatives are the employers 
ove workmen and not the Manager of the Angus Jute Works. So, 
given our thought over the matter and we are o£ opinion that the 
y before us is the Angus Company and not Angus Jute Works, 
etition the name of Angus Jute Works appears, but this is a mis- 
in which does not go to the root of the case because the Union 
at the Augus Jute Company is the employer and the Angus Jute 
has entered appearance through the Indian Jute Mills Associa- 
we hold that the Manager, Angus Jute Works, means the Manager, 
!>mpany and so it has been understood by all concerned. Conse- 
the employers of these workmen mean the Manager, Angus Com- 
, this Company is a party before us. The case of the petitioners, 

, is covered by the present reference. 

s last contended that the petitioners are workmen of the Thomas 
Oo. But this really makes no difference for the purpose of our 
loinas Duff and Co. are only managing agents of the Angus Co. 
is under the managing agents are for all purposes the employees 
ngus Co. itself. This is elucidated by the fact that in the employ- 
es issued by the Company and even in the warning notice itself, 
of Angus flute Works or the Angus Company appears in the place 
iployers. This shows that Thomas Duff & Co. used only to look 
lay to day management and whatever they did they did in the name 
Company with their finance. We, therefore, hold that the em- 
igus Company is a party to the Tribunal and the case of the above 
is covered by the present reference. We, therefore, decide the 
ry objection in favour of the applicant.

re es Jermission » writing from the Tribunal under clause (b) of sec- 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, that in the circumstances the suspen 
order should be illegal and should be set aside, that appropriate relief 
ild be given to the employee. , 

Notice of the aforesaid petition having been served, the Company filed 
objection on 16th September 1955 alleging that the petitioner was 
t lly warned after being duly charge-sheeted ami was found guilty of 
conduct for habitual absence and insubordination under the rules 
Jicable to the River Transport Staff, that the application is misconceived 
that the warning is not a punishment and does not amount to a viola- 
i of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 

DECISION. 

On behalf of the Company no witness was examined but they cross- 
unined the P.Ws. The petitioner is a Dandi under P. W. 2 who is a 
,jhi of Boat No. 5. P.W. 2 admitted that he reported to the office that 
R T . 1 and another Tawakul had been absent without leave on 2nd of 
igust. P.W. 1 Soleman admitted that he was called to the Head Office 
9th of August where Tawakul and P. W. 2 also were present. He 
netted that he put his thumb-impression on a charge-sheet. Charge- 
(Ext. 1) shows that it was duly served on Soleman and he gave his 
nation on the same day. Soleman said that he did not know what the 

it Officer wrote on the charge-sheet. By this he evidently refers to 

xplanation written on the charge-Bheet as also to the statement made 
m before the Labour Officer (Ext. A). But we have no reason to 
leve Ext. A or that the explanation on Ext. 1 is not Soleman’s explana- 
So we believe that the charge-sheet was submitted and the explana- 
jras given by him and an enquiry was held and where Soleman said in 

gh tone that “he had nothing to say and the Labour Officer may do 

•ver he thinks. 1 * Whereas before us he simply said that he did not 
ie Majhi on that day and that the Majhi wanted to get rid of him. 
shows that he was present, and we do not believe that the Majhi has 
cted a false case against him in order to get rid of him. So, the 
iple of natural justice was observed and it further appears that 
lly the company did not punish him with suspension in the long run, 
imply gave him warning notice. P.W. 1 admitted that Shri Mukherji, 
ur Officer, did not give an order of suspension. The witness P.W. 2 
admitted that if any suspension order was mudp, it should have gone 
gh him and that there is no order that Soleman was suspended for 4 
He further admitted that on 9th Tawakul was simply warned in his 
nee. As regards Soleman his own version is that Shri Mukherji told 
verbally that he was suspended for 4 days. Tn view of the admissions 
■ by the witnesses that suspension order should be made in writing and 
nunicated to the maj'his, this verbal suspension order if made on the 
is nothing but taking P.W. 1 to task for his fault. Actually he was 
warned in the long run. The charge-sheet which was with the com- 
is also filed along with the charge-sheet which was filed by the 
Both these show that in the case of light punishment the columns 
aspension, etc., are crossed through the typing machine. It does not 
that there was any punishment at all. Chi the other hand, it shows 
whatever the Labour Officer might have naid verbally no order for 
lament was actually made. An order for warning is not a punishment 
lere was no violation of the conditions of service or any punishment 
n the meaning of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. Besides 
)etitioner has not been made to suffer. The Company took a lenient 
of the petitioner who absented himself for 3 days on the plea that 
Mukherji told him verbally that he was suspended for 3 days. He

1. Plans of privies and urinal to be submitted 
to Commissioners. — (1) Every person who intends

No. lWt<V-Mth May 1965.— : ln exercise ot 
1 he power conferred by the proviso to the first 
paragraph of section 18 of the Bengal Ferries 
Act. 18a”) (Bengal Act I of 1885) and in super- 
session of notification No. 15R., dated the 28th 
July 1939, the Governor is pleased to declare 
that the persons, animals, vehicles and other 
things specified below shall be exempt from pay- 
ment of tolls levied for crossing the river Teesta 
by the public ferry known as the Teesta (Abduar) 
Ferry situated between Karala Ghat on the 
Jalpaiguri side and Barnes Ghat on the Duars 
side in the district of Jalpaiguri, namely: — 

(a) All prisoners under Military escort. 

(b) Executive Officers of the district board 

when travelling on duty. 

(c) Persons carrying dead body or property 

sent in by the Police. 

(d) Vaccinators and Inoculaiors on duty. 

Explanation . — The free passages enumerated 
above are exclusive and do not cover 
relations, servants or employees other 
than the driver of the vehicle of the 
person travelling free. 

II. The exemptions hereinbefore declared are 
ill addition to the exemptions in respect of 

(i) Mails, mail carts, Dak-Runners and 

Government Telegraph Messengers on 
duty; 

(ii) Commissariat stores, animals and vehicles 

when accompanies by a dial Jan from the 
Commissariat Officer; 

(iii) Police and other public officers and 

process-servers, peous, punchayats ana 
village-chowkidars when travelling on 
dutv with their bona fide baggage, horse, 
palkies, motor car and other convey- 
ances; and 

(iv) all officers and men of the Works and 

Buildings Department on duty With 
necessary identification, including coolies 
carrying tools and survey instruments 
employed on road works, which are eiempt 
from tolls under section 18 of the said 
Act; and

UIU a strike is defined as occurring whenever a group of employees 
“Sit o°wn^ erfl j n ^ ere sted in obtaining a certain objective in a parti- 


Ur business forcibly take over possession of the property of 
cul f r business, establish themselves within the plant, stop its 
B d action and refuse access to the owners or to the others 
Xirinff to work. Sit-down strike should more accurately be 
\ fined as a strike in the traditional sense to which is added the 
lament of trespass by the strikers upon the property of the 
employer. All the cases have uniformly outlawed the sit-down 

* strike*'. 

Fansteel decision has placed a quietus upon further indulgence 
by labour in the sit-down strike. 9 


v kel case is to be found reported in U.S.A. Supreme Court in 
n 119 s 305-307. The following extract from the said judgment will 
t^l-t in this case. 

••'I he Company was guilty of unfair labour practice, but reprehensible 
1 as was that conduct of the company, there is no ground for say- 
ing that it made the company an outlaw or deprived it of its 
legal rights to the possession or protection of its property. The 
employees had the right to strike but they had no license to 
commit acts of violence or to seize their employer’s plant. The 
seizure and holding of the buildings was itself a wrong apart 
from any act of sabotage. But in its legal aspect the ousting 
of the owner from lawful possession is not essentially different 
from an assault upon the officers of an employing company or 
the seizure and conversion of its goods, or ihe despoiling of 
its property or other unlawful acts in order to force compliance 
with demands. To justify such conduct because of the exis- 
tence of a labour dispute or of an unfair labour practice would 
be io put a premium on resort, to force instead of legal remedies 
and to subvert the principles of law and order which lie at the 
foundations of society. As the company’s unfair labour prac- 
tices afforded no excuse for the seizure and holding of its build- 
ings, company has its normal rights of redress. Those rights 
include the right to discharge the wrongdoers from its employ.” 

‘‘Tln.se w lio were not actual sit-down strikers but aided and abetted 
the sit-down strikers — are not in a better position. So they also 
cannot as of right claim reinstatement.”

OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF

ORDERS. 

No. 8012C . T . / 2E-7 / 64-55 . — 11th May 1956.— 
In supersession of all previous orders, Shri R. M. 
Deb, Additional Income-tax Officer, District VI, 
Calcutta (since reverted to the post of Inspector), 
is allowed under the Revised Leave Rules, 1933, 
earned leave for sixty-four days, with effect from 
9th April 1954 to 11th June 1954 and thereafter 
half pay leave for one hundred and seventy-two 
days, with effect from 12th June 1954 to 30th 
November 1954. 

It is certified that Shri Deb was likely to

No. 9574L.R.— 20th May 1966.— In exercise of 
the powers conferred liy the proviso to Article dU.» 
of the Constitution of India, the Governor is pleas- 
ed to direH that the method of recruitment m 
respect of the following post and the requisite 
qualifications and eligibility for direct appointment 
to such post shall he as noted Iwlow : — 

1. Name Of port.— Circle Inspector. 

2 Appointing Authority.— Secretary, Board of 
Revenue^ West Bengal, will be the appointing 
authority. 

3. Method Of appointment.— By selection from 
the undermentioned personnel — 

(i^ Employees and ex-employees of Kliasmalial 
and Court of Wards; 

(ii) Employees of the Zemindars and inter- 
mediaries; and 

tiii) Surplus staff of the Food, Relief and Sup- 
plies (Food) Department. 

Selection will be made by a Selection Committee 
t<» he constituted by Government for the purpose. 
In making selection the employees of zemindars and 
intermediaries should have the first priority aleng 
with the staff of the Court of Wards and Khas- 
mahal. 

4. Educational qualifications.— 1 The candidates 
must possess a certificate showing that he has pass- 
ed the I. A., I. Sc. or l.Com. examination of a 
recognised University. Matriculates may be 
accepted provided they have a continuous service 
of at least ft years in Revenue and Zemmdan work. 

ft. Age limits and physical ntness.— The age 

limit should be 40-52 relaxable at both ends in the 
case of persons who are in temporary Government 
service for at least 3 years continuously, and in 
cases of employees or ex-employees of Klinsmann , 
Court of Wards and Zemindars and other inter- 
mediaries having a similar continuity m service 
under their past employers normally up to ,)0 years 
and in very exceptional cases up to «)7 years, such 
cases being examined on merit by the Selection 
Committee subject, to the approval of Government. 

The candidates must be physically fit for out- 
door work. 

6. Communal representation — Fifteen per cent, 
of the appointments will be made from candidates 
belonging to the scheduled castes and b per cen . 
from those belonging to the scheduled tribes, sub- 
ject to availability of qualified candidates. 

7. Training. — The candidates will be required, 
after their selection, to undergo a course of train- 
ing as may be prescribed by the appointing autho- 
rity. In special cases the appointing authority 
may by order exempt a candidate or a class of 
candidates from undergoing the training. The 
trainees will be given appointment on successful 
completion of training. 

8. Pajfu— The scale of pay of Circle Inspectors 
will be Rs. 80 — 4 — 160 — 5—180.

rickshaw in the Raiganj Municipality shall be annually registered by the
