2. Qualifications Of the bearers.— Every person applying for a bearer’s 
license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer- 

fa) that he is not less than 18 and more than 45 yeara of age ; 

(b) that he knowB how to drive and control a rickshaw and is m all 

respects a fit person for such employment ; 

(c) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, workshops. 

factories, offices and places in and around the town of Eaiganj: 

(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fareB aud dis- 

tances prepared by the Commissioners ; 

(e) that he knows the rules of the road and the signals used by the 

bearers and drivers of the vehicles and by the traffic police. 

3. Contents Of lioonse.— There shall be attached to each license -.vied 
to a rickshaw bearer: — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer: 

(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him; and

14. Power of entry.— It shall , he lawful for a Commissioner or any 
other person authorised in that behalf by the Chairman of the Comma, 
sioners at any time between sun-rise and sun-set to enter any premises 
in which any licensed rickshaw or other things used therewith are kept in 
order to carry out any of the provisions of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage 
Act, 1919, or these by-laws and the owner or occupier of the premises or 
his agent shall afford every facility for inspection by such Commissioner or 
person. 

15 Tables Of fares and distanoa.— The Commissioners shall cause to 
bo prepared and kept, for sale to the public, printed tables setting forth the 
fares and distances at a price fixed by the Commissioners. 

1C. Particulars of registers.— The following particulars shall be

(6) The date of expiry of the license. 

(7) A s ummar y of the more important statutory provisions and by-laws 

affecting bearers of rickshaws. 

(8) Signature of the Registering Officer. 


(B) Owner's license. 

(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 

(2) The name, father’s name and residence of the owner, the des-rin- 

tion of the rickshaw and the place where the rickshaw is kept. 

(3) The number of passengers the rickshaw is licensed to carry. 

(4) The date on which the license is granted. 

(5) Date of expiry of the license. 

(6) Signature of the Registering Officer.

Amendments. 

1. In rule 16 of the said rules, for the words 
“quarts or pints” substitute the words “quarts, 
pints or nips”. 

2. For the explanation to rule 16 of the Baid 
rules, substitute the following explanation , 
namely : — 

“ Explanation . — (a) “quart” means a bottle 
containing not less than 22 but not more 
than 26 2/3 ounces of liquor; 

(b) “pint” means a bottle containing not less 

than 11 but not more than 13§ ounces of 
liquor; and 

(c) “pip” means a bottle containing not less 

than 5J but not more than 6 2/3 ounces 
of liquor.” 


No. 489Ex. — 26th May 1955. — In exercise of 
the powers conferred by section 86 of the Bengal 
Excise Act, 1909 (Bengal Act V of 1909), the 
Governor is pleased to make the following amend- 
ment in the rules published with notification 
No. 601S.R., dated 30th March 1915, as subse- 
quently amended, namely: — 


In sub-rule (a) of rule 247 of the said rules, for 
thf words “(a) Brandy, whisky, rum or gin, 
when required to be sold in sealed and capsuled 
containers, shall not be sold except in quarts or 
pints” substitute the following, namely:— 

“(a) Brandy, whisky, rum or gin, when 
required to be sold in West Bengal, in 
sealed and capsuled containers, shall net 
be sold except in quarts or pints.

Land Reforms 

NOTIFICATIONS. 

No. 10.382L.Rpf. — 1st June 1955. — In exercise of 
the power conferred by section 59 of the West 
Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 195d (West Bengal 
Act I of 1954), the Governor is pleased to make, 
after previous publication as required by sub-section 
(!) of the said section, the following amendment 
in the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Rules, 
1954, as subsequently amended, namely: — 


Renumber paragraph 6 of schedule B to the said 
rules, as sub-paragrapli (1) of the said paragraph 
and thereafter insert the following new Bub-para- 
graph, namely: — 

“(2) If during the enquiry and survey referred 
to in sub-paragraph (1) it appears to the 
Revenue Officer that- the area contained 
within the external boundaries of the 
village maps of the previous survey is 
unsuitable as the unit of survey and 
record, he shall, after ascertaining as 
far as possible the opinion of the land- 
lords and tenants concerned, submit his 
proposals for the determination of the 
area to be adopted as the unit- of record 
and survey to the Board of Revenue 
through the Controlling Officers to whom 
he is subordinate. Thereafter the proce- 
dure laid down in sub-paragraph (2) of

NOTIFICATION. 

No. 2240M.V.— -6th Tune 1955. — Whereas it has 
been decided that a “Safety Drive 'Week” will be 
held in Howrah Town and vehicular traffic should 
be closed for two days, viz., 11th and 12th June 
1955, for the proponed “Children's Park", and 
whereas I am satisfied that vehicular traffic in 
Mahatma Gandhi Road, between Howrah Maidun 
and Dalmia Park, on the aforesaid dates may 
create inconvenience to the public; 

I, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
mi me bv the State Government under section 74 
of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (Act IV of 1939), 
for the interest of public- safety and convenience, 
prohibit, tor the aforesaid dates, viz., ilth and 
12th Tune 1955, the plying of all vehicles through 
Mahatma Gandhi lload between Howrah Maidun 
and Duliniu Park.

COOPERATIVE DIRECTORATE 

NOTIFICATION. 

No. 592L. — 26th May 1955. — IWhereas 1 am ot 
opinion,, as the result of an enquiry held into the 
constitution, working and financial condition of the 
Fuliu Textile Workers’ (Industrial) Co-operative 
Society, Ltd. (Registered No. 6 of 1951), in the 
llauaghat subdivision of the district of Nadia under 
sub-section (1) of section 84 of the Bengal Co- 
operative Societies Act, 1940, that the Society 
ought to be wound up; 

Now therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (1) of section 89 of the Bengal 
Co-operative Societies Act, 1040 (Bengal Act XXI 
of 1940), il hereby order the winding up of the 
said Society; 

And further, in exercise of the power conferred 
by section 90 of the said Act, I hereby appoint 
Shri S. R. Biswas, Inspector of Co-operative 
Societies on deputation to Community Development 
Projects and posted to Fulia Development Block 
to be Liquidator of the said Society. 


G. D. GOSWAMi, Registrar.

NOTIFICATIONS. 

No. 1749M.P./2R-8/55.— 31st May 1955.— 
Whereas Messrs. Tamralipta Co-operative Electric 
Supply Society, Limited, the licensees of tne 
Tamluk Electric License, 1950, have made an 
application for making certain amendments in the 
terms and conditions of the said licence, so as to 
suitably reduce the requirements contained in 
clause 11 thereof, providing for the maintenance 
of continuous supply of energy for twenty-tour 
hours throughout the year ; 

And whereaN, in the opinion of the State Govern- 
ment, the public interest permits the making of 
such amendment in the said terms and conditions; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred bv clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 4 
of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), 
the Governor is pleased, after consultation with 
the local authority concerned, namely, the Com- 
missioners of the Tamluk Municipality, to diiect 
that during the continuance in force of this 
notification, clause 1 1 of the said licence shall have 
effect as if in the said clause for the words and 
figure “for 24 hours throughout the year” the 
words “from half past five O’clock Post Merit! it n 
every day to half past four O’clock Ante Meridian 
next following” had been substituted. 

This notification shall remain in force up to the 
30th June 1955. 


By order of the Governor, 

N. DAS, Secy.

(11) If any workman fails to join his work within If, days from the date 
of signing this agreement he will forfeit Ins claims assured to 
him by this agreement. The Union undertakes to inform the 
workmen concerned, no other notice will he required from the 
Company for this purpose. All claims under this agreement 
would be settled within one month. 


(12) Janardan and Ram will be made permanent from dale and given 

benefit of provident fund. 

(13) The Provident Fund Account will Ik* made known to the respective 

workmen at least once a year. 

(14) The following grievance procedure is agreed upon : — 

The worker would report his grievances to the Foreman in the first 
instance. The Foreman would try to remove ns many as he 
can and refer the case to the Labour Welfare Officer/ If the 
worker doeB not get any redress from the Foreman or the 
Labour Officer he should approach the Manager. If the 

f rievance still remains he should report tin* matter to the 
Fnion and the Union can then take up the matter with the 
Manager or Labour Officer. If there is no settlement, within 
a reasonable time then the matter should he proceeded in a 
constitutional manner. Meanwhile workmen would not go on 
. illegal or irregular strike, slow down production or do any 

overt act or indulge in any indisciplinarv activities. 

(15) In case the Union fails to implement the terms of this agreement 
in so far as they relate to discipline, slow down and strikes the 
management shall have the right to de-recognise the Union alter 
giving 15 days’ notice. 

(16) All cases hitherto pending in Tribunal and withdrawn by the 
respective parties. 

(17) The agreement would in no way negate the rights of workmen 
assured to them under legislation.

2. ' Qualifications and duties Of bearers.— Every person applying for a 
bearer’s license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer — 

(a) that l>e is not less than 18 and not more than 45 years of age; 

i 

(b) that he knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and iB in all 

respects a fit person for such employment; 

(c) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 

places in and around the town of Dinhata; 

(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and 

distances prepared by the Members; ** 

(e) that he knows the rules of the road and signals used by the bearers 

and drivers of vehicles and by the traffic police. 


3. Contents of liOOnsOi— There shall be affixed to each license, issued to 
a rickshaw bearer: — 

(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 

(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him ; and 

(c) a printed , table of fares prepared by the Members, for which no 

charge shall be paid by the bearer. 


4. Production Of license. — Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carry with 
him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so by any 
Member, traffic police or other person authorised by the Members. He shall 
exhibit the tables of fares and distances on a prominent part of the vehicle. 

5. Condition of rickshaws. — (a) The body of the rickshaw shall be 
sound and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. 

(h) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, Btrong and sound, so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by pro- 
perly fitted splash boards. 

(e) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and 
properly riveted and free from rust. 

(d) The iron supports at the back shall be properly curved and securely 
fixed on each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rusl. 

(e) The shaft shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and 
furnished at Ihe fore ends with a ringshaped metal support and connected 
by a collision guard. 


(f) The hood, apron and cushions shall be made of and covered with 
good cloth, canvas or other materials approved by the Members at a 
meeting. 

(g) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
tight. 

* 

(h) Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps — one facing the front and 
one in the rear. 

(i) Each lamp shall have a red glass window in the back and shall be 
so placed that tne light from the window is visible from a point ten yards 
in the rear of the centre of the vehicle. 

(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle bars or yross 
bars of the cycle and it shall be so constructed that it can be operated by 
fingers and can give continuous ringing as and when necessary.

2 . Qualifications Of the bearers — Every person applying fur a hearer’s

3 . Contents Of license. — There shall be affixed to each license, issued to

missioners in that liehalf. He shall exhibit the table of fares and distances 
on a prominent part of the v ehicle. 

6. Condition Of rickshaws,— (a) The body of the rickshaw shall be 
sound and clean and all the boards strong* and properly secured. 

(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound, so as to run 
smoothly and without rattliug or shaking and shall be protected by properly 
fitted splash boards. 

(c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and 
properly riveted and free from rust. 

* (d) The iron supports at the hack shall be properly curved and securely 
fixed on eheh side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

(e) The hood, apron and cushion shall be made of, and covered with, 
good cloth, canvas, or other materials approved by the Commissioners at a 
meeting. -

(e) Tin* Secretary of the Council or of a Committee shall under the 
direction of the Chairman thereof give not less than 10 days* 
notin' to the memliers of the Council or the Committee, as the 
case may bo, of the date of an ordinary meeting. Not less than 
7 days before the date of the meeting, the Secretary shall Bend 
to each such member an agenda paper: 

Provided that the Chairman shall be entitled to enlarge or abridge the 
time for giving notice for a meeting. 

(d) The Chairman of the Council shall preside at the meetings of the 

Council. The Chairman or such other member of the Board as 
tlie Chairman may nominate in this behalf shall be the ex officio 
Chairman of a Committee and shall preside at the meetings 
thereof. e 

(e) No matter other than what iB included in the agenda paper shall be 

considered or discussed at a meeting of the Council or of a Com- 
mittee except with special permission of its Chairman. 

(f) One-third of the members of the Council or of a Committee shall 

constitute a quorum at meetings of the Council or the Committee, 
as the case may be. If there is no quorum within 15 minutes 
of the time appointed for the meeting, no meeting shall be held 
and the Chairman of the Council or the Committee, as the ease 
may be, may then and there adjourn the meetihg to a specified 
date. • 

(g) No further notice may be given of an adjourned meeting. 

(h) If at any time (luring the progress of the meeting after its com- 

mencement there is no quorum, it shall not be dissolved but shall 
continue to be held. 

(i) No quorum shall he necessary at an adjourned meeting. 

(j) No matter shall he considered at an adjourned meeting other than 

matters left over at the meeting from which the adjournment 
took place, provided that the Chairman of the Board may bring 
or direct to he brought any new matter which in his opinion is 
urgent, before an adjourned meeting of the Council or of a Com- 
mittee with or without notice. 

(k) Any point of order raised at a meeting shall he decided by its Chair- 

man and his decision shall he final. 

(l) No proceeding of the Council or of a Committee shall he invalidated 

by reason merely of a vacancy or vacancies, existing in the 
Council or the Committee, or by reason of non-receipt, of the 
notice or the agenda paper provided it was duly issued or hy 
reason of any irregularity in the conduct of the business of the 
meeting. 

Explanation . — A notice shall be deemed to he duly issued if it is sent 
within the prescribed time to the registered address of a member 
by post or hy peon. 

(ni) Every member shall have one vote. 

(n) All matters placed before a meeting shall be decided hy a simple 

majority of votes of the members present. On putting anv 
matter to vote the Chairman presiding at a meeting shall call 
for an indication of the opinion of the members hy show of hands, 
first in the affirmative and then in the negative and shall declare 
the result accordingly. The Chairman at a meeting shall l>o ■ 
entitled to vote and in case of equality of votes also to have a 
second or casting vote. 

(o) The Chairman at any meeting may direct any member of the Council 

oi of a Committee whose .conduct at the meeting is in his opinion 
disorderly, to withdraw and anv such member so ordered shall 
T»e deemed to have withdrawn from the meeting even though in 
fact he mav not withdraw. 

(p) Tn cases not expressly provided for in these rules for the conducl of 

a meeting, the decision of the Chairman presiding at, the meeting 
on all matters relating to the conduct of business at the meeting 
shall he final.

(3) Subject to the provisions oi these rules, every mortgage granted by 
the Board shall be in such form as may be specified in this behalf by the 
Hoard. 

4‘2. Stock and bonds issued and mortgage created by the Board under 
these rules shall be respectively called West Bengal State Electricity Board 
Stock, West Bengal State Electricity Board Bonds or Debentures and West 
Bengal State Electricity Board Mortgages. 

43 The Board shall keep an index of the names of (a) the holders of 
stock, (b) the holders of the bonds, (e) the mortgagees as appear in their 
respective registers. 

44. Appointment of Registrar . — The Board may for maintaining regis- 
ters of stock, bonds and mortgages appoint officers on such terms as they 
may determine. The officers shall be called Registrar of Stocks, Registrar 
of Bonds and Registrar of Mortgages respectively. 

45. Registers of stocks , etc . — The Registrar of Stock shall keep in one 

or more books a register of stock holders and enter therein the following 
particulars : — * 

The names and addresses und the occupation of the stock holders, the 
uinount of the stock, the period, the date of redemption, security 
if any, the amount if any transferred, the name of the transferee, 
the date of transfer, tfie balance amount and such other particulars 
as the Board may from time to time determine. 

4b. The Registrar of Bonds shall keep in one or more books a register 
of the holders of bonds and enter therein the following particulars: — 

The names and addresses and the occupations, it any, of the holders of 
the bonds, the amount, the period, the date of redemption, security 
if any, the name of transferee if any, the date of transfer and 
such other particulars as the Board may from time to time 
determine. 

47. The Registrar of mortgages shall keep in one or more books a 
register ot the mortgagees and enter therein the following: — 

The names and addresses and the occupations, if any, of the mortgagee, 
the amount of the mortgage, rate of interest date for payment of 
interest, security, transfer if any, the date of transfer, the date ol 
redemption and such other particulars as the Board may from time 
to time determine. 

48. The registered holders of stocks and bonds and the mortgagees 
whose names appear in the register shall, so lar as payment of interest and 
principal to be made by the Board is concerned, be regarded as the owners 
thereof and on payment being made, the Board shall be discharged tor the 
amount paid. 

49 If a certificate for any stock, l>ond or any other security is lost, torn 
or deiaced, the Board may on the application of the person entitled to such 
security and payment of a fee of Rs. 20 by him and production ol such 
evidence as the’ Board think sufficient, issue a duplicate certificate which 
shall be marked “duplicate” and on issue of such duplicate certificate, the 
appropriate Registrar shall make consequential rectification in the proper 
legists 11 . 

50. Temporary investment . — The Board may invest any money not 
required by it for the time being in approved security. 


PART VI. 

51. The Board shall consult a Committee, when constituted, on such 
of its business as the State Government may from time to time direct. 


PART VII. 

General, 

52. No notice of any trust, express, implied or constructive shall he 
entered in the register or be receivable by the Board or the Registrar. 

53. Until the Board arranges to print its own forms it may make use of 
the forms now in ubc in the Electricity Development Directorate of the State 
Government with necessary modifications.

Fine, Rs. 10. 

8. Lights. — No person shall drive any of the undermentioned vehicles 
or animals, or convey any palanquin, on any public street, between half- 
an-liour after sunset and half-an-hour before sunrise, unless lights are 
provided as follows: — 

(a) every carriage must carry two conspicuous lights, one on each 
side; 

(ft) every cart must carry one conspicuous light; 

(r) every elephant, camel or palanquin must be accompanied by one 
conspicuous light ; 

(d) every cycle must carry one conspicuous light in front. 


Fine, Rs. 50. 

9. Signals on motors and cycles.— No person shall drive any motor 
car, or ride any motor cycle or any tricycle or bicycle on any public street 
unless it has attached to it a bell, horn or other suitable signal in good 
order. 


Fine, Rs. 50. 

10. Maximum load for carts.— No cart shall, without the general or 
special permission of the commissioners, curry on any public street a load 
in excess of twenty maunds. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 

11. Vehicles laden with girders, etO.— No. person shall drive upon a 
public street any vehicle laden with iron girders, rails, beams, bullas, 
bamboos, planks or other materials of a similar character which exceed 
twelve feet in length, unless the vehicle be accompanied by another person 
and be loaded in such a way that no portion of the said materials touches 
the ground. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 

y>. Vehicle laden with bricks, stones, etc.— No person shall drive upon 
a public street any vehicle laden with bricks, stones or other materials of a 
similar character, unless such materials be so secured that they cannot 
full on to the street. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 

18. Animal laden with bamboos or timber.— No person shall convoy 
on any public street bamboos or timber placed on the back of any animal 
in such a way that any portion of such bamboos or timber touches the 
ground. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 

14. Taking elephants or oamels along a public atraot.— No person 
shall, without the general or special permission of the commissioners, 
tuke any elephant or camel along any public* street. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 

15. Taking an alaphant ower a bridge.— No person shall allow any. 
elephant in his charge to go over any bridge on any publio street unless 
the bridge be constructed of arched masonry, steel or ferrow-ooncrete or 
similar durable material. 


Fine, Rs. 50. 

16. Loaded peok-enimelta — No person shall drive upon * publio street, 
at the same time, more than two loaded paok«aoMde»

OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT MAGISTRATE 
OF NADIA.. 

ORDER. 

Krishnagar, the lfith Juno 1955. 

Whereas it has been brought to my notice 
that a large-scale smuggling of cotton cloth and 
cotton yarn from Indian Union to East Pakistan 
is being carried on in the border areas of the 
district of Nadia, and whereas other measures to 
prevent the same have proved ineffective, aftd 
whereus in my opinion it is necessary, for main- 
taining supply of cotton cloth and cotton 
yarn which are essential to the life of the 
community, to prevent the movement of the 
said commodities, viz. , cotton cloth and cotton 
yarn within a depth of three miles along 
the entire East Pakistan-Nadia border of 
this district, and whereas the previous order 
No. 1133(52)-.]., dated 14th March 1965, made 
under sub-section (1) of section 20 of the West 
Bengal Security Act, 1950, to this effect 
expires on 21st of. June 1955 and a fresh order is 
considered necessary and expedient, I, Shri S. 
Butt-Mazumdar, District Magistrate, Nadia, in 
exercise of the powers conferred on me by order 
No. 621 8P/ 446/ 50, dated 19th September 1950, 
issued, by the Government of West Bengal, Home 
(Political) Department, do, by this order under 
sub-section (1) of section 20 of the West Bengal 
Security Act, 19 .j 0, prohibit the movement of 
cotton cloth and cotton yarn within a depth of 
three miles excepting the movement of the above 
commodities by bona fide dealers, weavers and 
consumers under a permit from the President 
Union Board, the local Inspector or Sub-Inspector 
of the Food and Supplies Department or , any 
other Superior authority as shown in the * list 
below along the entire East Pakistan-Nadia 


This order will remain in force for a^periot 
three months with effect from the 22nd j 

Given under my hand and seal this lfUh 
of June 1956.

of filing written statement have put in a joint petition of compromig

are as follows: — * “

was justified. ' uu * 

(2) Whet relief he is entitled* to f 

- DECISION.

2. The reference was received in the original Tribunal on 27 th 
November 1952, where the written statements were filed by the Unions. 
^The Company filed written objection on 12th February 19&3. The issues 
were framed on 27th February 1953. The Mazdoor union filed one com- 
promise petition on 17th June 1953. Thereafter the case was transferred 
to this Fifth Industrial Tribunal on 11th July 1953. The different Unions 
could not agree among themselves to present one united front to the 
Company. The result was 'that they fell out among themfeelve^ as to 
which of the Unions was most competent to represent the workmen >in the 
present case. Quite a lot of time was taken over this matter till ultimately 
the Tribunal found, on the admission of the Company, on 2nd March 1955, 
that; Shri Subodh Banerji of the Labour Union could represent the 
Company’s regular employees as well as Sirdars’ men. So the Unions 
weie called upon to give evidence inspite of tho compromise petition filed 
by the Mazdoor Union which was on record. The actual trial took place 
on 2nd March 1955 and continued till 4th March 1955. It was taken up 
again on 27th April 1955 and continued on 28th April 1955 and 29th April 
1955 when the hearing including the argument was concluded.

our Muster Gangmen They also do miscellaneous other jobs 

which we do not like to give to Sirdars' men". This is not disputed. So 
it is dear that the workmen employed at those plaoes are comprised partly 
of the Company’s permanent staff, and partly of Sirdars’ men. Regarding 
the Sirdars’ men, the Company disowns any relationship of master ana 
servant between them and the Company. Now this is the position which 
cannot be disputed. Sirdars’ men to all intents and purposes are con- 
tractors’ men. The Company gives contract to Sirdars for certain jobs, 
and makes payments accordingly. The Sirdars employ their workmen 
and. execute the work. They draw payment from the Company, and in 
their turn make payment to the workmen they employ. In this state of 
things the relationship of master and servant cannot be foisted on the 
Company regarding those contractors’ men. This is also the legal position 
accepted by the Tribunals under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. In 
Bombay the position is different because the local Act did provide for 
contractors’ men. But here in West Bengal we do not have any such 
special provision. The Union tried to show that the Company did make 
provisions for rations of Sirdars’ men when the rationing was in force. 
That by itself cannot give rise to any such relationship. It is in evidence 
that these workmen drew rations on the strength of their ration cards. 
They took rations to the Sirdars’ house and divided the same among them- 
selves. They also paid for such rations. Next, it is contended that the 
Company made provisions for some medical relief regarding those men. 
That was only an act of generosity on the part of the Company. But that 
does not create any obligatory relationship between the parties. The only 
point ie be decided is whether the Company did employ these men. Tne 
Union tried to show .that the Sirdars merely recruited labour for the 
Company. But that has not been proved by any tangible evidence. So 
on the evidence on record I find that the Company is justified in disowning 
the relationship of master and servant at those places visa vis the con- 
tractors’ men. 

(b) There is no evidence that in those places workmen serving under 
the Sirdars worked also as contractors of the Company. The Sirdars 
employ Munshis, etc., to supervise the work, but these men have no 
relationship of master and servant with the Company. If the Company s 
officers looked after the execution of work at times, that is only in the 
fitness of things. That, however, falls short of establishing any such 
relationship as the Union would like to suggest. So I answer it in the 
negative. 

(c) Having regard to the above, I can say unhesitatingly that there 
is no industrial dispute between the Company and the Sirdars men as such.

between the Company and the workmen. In that agreement it is stated

dispute Besides, the very terms of the settlement would show that there 
did P exist a dispute regarding the terms and conditions of service of the 
employees Serving under the Company. The Company next contends that 
even if it be assumed that there was a dispute, that must be taken as 
MMttled by the aforesaid compromise petition. That would have heen s

•a the present scales of pay given by the Company I find that 

it suffers from certain shortcomings. Ordinarily, 10 years should be the 
period which must intervene between the starting pay and the maximum 
of it. The increments should be adjusted accordingly. If 'this interven- 
^ saor ^ er » the difficulty will be that an employee will within 
a short time reach the maximum limit of his pay and stagnato there, 
ouch stagnation certainly does not help efficiency. But at the same time 
it will not do to forget that when the grude is fixed, the maximum of the 
grade must very nearly approximate to the job value. These are the 
accepted principles of wage fixation. Now, if I examine the scales given 
by the Company what do I find P In the scale of coopers I find that it 
starts with Rs. 30 and ends at Its. 45, and the increment, presumably 
annually, is Rs. 2. This shows that the man will reach the maximum of 
the grade within 7£ years. But in the cafso of overseers No. Ill the grade 
starts with Rs. 45 and ends at Rs. 75 with an increment of Rs. 3 annually. 
This shows that the period of service would be 10 years when one reaches 
the mhximum. In the case of clerks the scale starts with Rs. 00 and ends 
at Rs. 100 with an annual increment of Rs. 5. It will have a tenure of 
eight yours* service when one reaches the maximum. In the case of over- 
seers No. II, the scale starts with Rs. 50 and ends at Rs. 75 with an annual 
increment of Rs. 5. This shows that the man will reach the maximum 
of his grade at the end of five years. What is worse, his* maximum pay is 
the same as of Oversser No. III. It cannot be said that both do the same 
kind of work. Overseer No. Ill starts with Rs. 5 less than the overseer 
No. II. His increment is also less, viz., Rs. 3 annually. Then why 
should the maximum salary of both of them be the same? There is no 
reason for it. 


Regarding Overseer No. 1, the starting salary is Rs. 80, and the maxi- 
mum is Rs. 155. The annual increment is Rs. 10. The length of service 
to reach the maximum is 7^ years. 1 need not consider the rest as they 
suffer from the same defect. I think, the scales of pay should be based 
on one uniform principle as far as possible. I have no reason why I should 
grant increase of pay as proposed by the Union. The scales of pay given 
by the Company compare very favourably with the scales of pay given 
by the Major Engineering Tribunal. The dearness allowance is also 
handsome. So, I cannot accept the suggested scales of the Union, but 1 
revise the present scale slightly to the advantage of the present incumbent.

Regarding the Muster Gang labourers I am required to give a special 
finding. They are treated as casual labourers And «iheir minimum pay i B 
Be. 1 per day. They want a grade. Some of them have put in 10 to 15 
years’ service. While dealing with the first isstife I have shown the duties 
done by these Muster gang men, as also admitted by a responsible officer 
of the Company. Now, why should they be denied the benefit of any 
fixed scale of pay ? They say, and the evidence has also established that 
these men sit idle for a good many days in a month. It is entirely at the 
discretion of the Company just to give them enough Vork or not, because 
the work done by them is more or less the* work done by Sirdars’ men. 
So their grievance is reallv genuine. I find no reason why these men 
should not occupy the rank of coopers and enjoy the same scale of pay 
as enjoyed by the coopers. But there is & little practical difficulty. 
These men have so long been treated as casual labourers, and I do not 
know if there is any record of services rendered by these men in the past. 
Now, if these men are put at the bottom of the coopers* grade after 10 or 
15 years of service under the Company, I should say it would be less than 

{ 'ustice. I had to depend upon the Company to a certain extent under this 
lead. Wherever the service records are available, and' the length of 
service can be ascertained, these men should be put in the coopers’ grade, 
as I have already fixed, taking three years’ service warranting one incre- 
ment. But where such service records are not available, they should be 
put by the Company in the Coopers’ grade at a point where they can lit* 
fixed after having hel^ local enquiry by the Company’s officers. Justice 
so long was denied to them, and Jthe Company must # make amends. 
Denied justice is often retributive in its nature, but there is no help. But 
in all cases, in fixing a man in the above grade the maximum should not be 
surpassed. 

Regarding the Muster Gang Sirdars, the Company does not say any 
thing. The Union has wanted an increased pay by Rs. 10 or so with 
increased annual increment. As the Muster Gang Sirdars should as of 
necessity get a little more pay than the Muster Gang labourers, I fix their 
grade at Rs. 32—2 — 52. They should be fixed in the grade according to 
the principles enunciated above in the case of Muster Gang labourers. It 
is pointed out by the Company that I have already found the Muster Gang 
labourers as casual labourers in the Section 33A proceeding. That may 
be so. In such a proceeding, the Tribunal merely takes note of the exist- 
ing state of things to decide the dispute. But in a reference the Tribunal 
considers not only the existing state of things but also things which ought 
to exist. In that view of the matter my present finding may differ a little 
from what I have found in the section 33 A proceeding between the parties. 

Regarding the fitting in of the Muster Gang Sirdars in the above, grade 
my directions noted above in the case of Muster Gang labourers would 
apply mu toft* mutandis subject to the only qualification that the maximum 
of the scale in no case should be exceeded. 


Regarding the other workmen whose cases I have considered ^>ove. 
the question of fitting in does not, strictly speaking, arise because I have 
not disturbed the grade to any appreciable extent. All that I have done 
is to step up the maximum of the grade. So these men should be put nj 
where their existing pay justifies. But whose the pay P 0 . 1 ^ calculate* 
according to service in the scale is a little, above, and the existing pay falls 
between two such points, the pay should he twisted up to occupy the nt* 
higher point in the grade. But this will be with no retrospective wffect.

Regarding the piece-rate system, the Union wants 20 per cent, increase 
all round over the present rate. But the Company in its statement at 
page 8 states “There is no workman employed by this employer who is 
piece-rated”. Therefore, this question does not arise. If I look to the 
compromise petition filed by the Mazdoor Union and the Company, I see 
that this point has been given up. In the Labour Union’s written state- 
ment also, as per the charter of demands, I find that piece-rate system has 
been sought to be introduced with a guaranteed minimum of Rs. 80 in the 
case of ordinary workers. But I am not prepared to introduce any now 
system of piece-rates in the 'present case, as the evidence is hardly sufficient 
in this respect. Thus this issue is disposed of. 

Issue No. 4.— Dearness allowance. 

The Labour Union wants as per the charter of demands, dearness 
allowance at the rate of 100 per cent, for the first Its. 100, at the rate of 
50 per cent, for each subsequent Rs. 100 of pay subject to the minimum 
of Rs. 60. If I look to the Company’s written statement, at page 4, I got 
that the Company is paying at present 105 per cent, for the first Rs. 100, 51 £ 
per cent, for the second Rs. 100, and 20 per cent, for the rest with the 
minimum of Rs. 63 in respect of establishments Nos. 1 and 2. lor the 
subordinate staff, viz., the chaprasis and peons, etc., the minimum is Rs. oi 
per month. So far as the gang labourers are concerned, they are paid 
Rs. 1-5-4 as dearness allowance per day. If the claim of the Union and 
the existing conditions of dearness allowance are compared side by side, 
it WH appear that the existing dearness allowance is in some respect better 
than the dearness allowance claimed. So there is no question of any 
interference by the Tribunal concerning dearness allowance in the present 
case. But in respect of gang labourers as I have put them m the grade 
of the coopers, and as they have been placed on par with permanent 
employees, they should he given the same dearness allowance as coopers. 
This also applied to the Muster Gang Sirdars. This will mean a little 
increment in their dearness allowance which I award. But 1 do not give 
it with retrospective effect. I may add generally that the present award 
will not cut down any higher dearness allowance if enjoyed at present. 

Issue No. 5. — House allowance. 

The Labour Union claims house allowance at the rate of Its 10 per 
month per head. The Company resists the claim on the ground that it is 
included in the pay. There is no gainsaying that the cost of housing has 
been taken into reckoning in arriving at the pay. But nevertheless where 
the houses are not available near the place of work . or where JJe how*. 
erBn if available, have exorbitant rates of rent the Tribunal grants house 
allowance just to soften the rigour involved. But m the 
localities where these men are employed have not been proved to be such 
iThere no house is available or the rents obtaining are very high. In the 
• absence of that I am not prepared to grant any house allowance. Beude » 

’ cSromrient have intervened in the matter, and there is a housing scheme 
JJLh is being introduced for industria! empioyees. . Und ® r , ^ ® 

Government will give subsidy to the extent of one-third, and also give a 
8JSSS to the extent of another one-third, while the Company will be 
Jaouired to contribute only to the remaining one-third of the total cost of 
for such housing. In a place like Calcutta or its suburbs lands are 
tftt wily available for housing purpose. However, the <>>mpany cmi 11 t 
M Hiked to undertake ambitious housing scheme all at onoe. Besides, in 
rAsethis Bird & Co. is merely the handling agents for supply 
of la&Nirto Messrs. Balrner Lawrie A Co. and Messrs. MacNeill A Barry, Ltd. 



MM THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JUNE 80, 1955 [Past 1 


So in their case the housing scheme must wait beoause the nature of tlie 
work is not such as ensures a certain fixed volume of work to be done by 
a fixed number of men. So the present Company cannot be saddled with 
the liability to pay house allowance in lieu of providing quarters.* So I 
give no direction in this respect. 

Issue No. 6« — Bonus. 

The Labour Union claims bonus at the rate of two months’ basic wage 
before the Puj&h. The Company resists the claim. The Mazdoor Union 
does not press this demand. The Labour Union has merely made the 
demand and left. It is not said whether the Company had been granting 
bonus in the past or whether the bonus is claimed for the first time hero. 
It does not call for the balance sheets of the Company just to ascertain the 
profits. No evidence has been led just to show whether the Company 1 h 
making profits, and, if so, the extent thereof. Even it has not been said 
for which year the bonus has been claimed. So it is only a half-hearted 
claim which the Tribunal cannot entertain. In that view of the matter 1 
reject the claim. 


Issue No. 7.— Working hours. 

The Labour Union depends on the charter of demands for its claim. 
Therein I find that the working hours cannot exceed 8 hours a day, and 
44 hours in a week. In the compromise petition with the Mazdoor Union 
I get that the working hours are the same as laid down by the port 
authorities. In the written statement of the Company at page G I fin.l 

that the normal working hours are 8 hours per day. So there is no dispute 

on this head. I dispose of the issue without any direction. 

Issue No. 8. — Overtime* 

Regarding overtime, the Labour Union wants that the rate should he 
double the usual rate for each hour in excess of 8 hours. Part of an hout 
should be reckoned as an hour. In the compromise petition with the 
Mazdoor Union I find that overtime pay is given for work in excess of 8 
hours in a day. This is given at the rate of as. 1-8 p. per man per hour. 
This should be increased by 25 per cent., as. 1-8 p. per hour is certainly 

very small. At page 7 of "the Company’s written statement I get tin* 

different overtime rates in the case of different classes of employees, during 
day and night. The night overtime is higher. Day overtime, as 1 find, 
is at the rate .of 1$ time of the usual pay rate. This, I think, is adequate. 
But what I award in the present case is that this will continue up to 48 
hours’ work in a week. But in excess of that the overtime rate would he 
double the usual rate. This is on the line as provided under the Factories 
Act. I see no reason why that rate should not be followed in the present 
case. 

Regarding the Muster Gang labourers, the overtime rate is not mention- 
ed. As I have placed them in the Coopers’ rank, so far as their pay* is 
concerned, they will get the same overtime as coopers. The Muster Gang 
Sirdars will get overtime according to the above method on their pay rate. 
This is prospective. The issue is thus disposed of. ^ 

Issue No. 8.— Extra pay for woighing and over-piling. 

Extra rate for weighing arises in oase of Sirdars’ men. I have already 
ruled that Sirdars’ men are Sub-contractors’ employes®), and they are not 
attracted by the present case. I do not think I am called -upon to give any 
finding regarding this issue. So this issue is disposed of without any 
direction. *

necessary to provide for further medical aid. v To make the Company 
liable to meet the expenses of treatment obtained from outside dootors 
would put the Company in a very uncomfortable position. It cannot, for

Issue No. 13. — Provident Fund and Gratuity. 

The Labour Union wants membership of the Provident Fund to be 
made open to all employees drawing Bs. 30 or above per month. It 
further claims contribution to the Provident Fund on each side at the rate 
of 81 per cent, of the basic salary. The Union also demands for gratuity 
at tne rate of one month’s pay for every year of service. The Company 
has not met this claim. I have not been supplied with any evidence about 
the existing Provident Fund, if at all, or the existing gratuity. The 
Union also does not appear to be serious on this point. It places no 
evidence which can be depended on in this respect. I do not understand 
whether these are sought to be introduced for the first time, or whether the 
claim is merely an improvement on the existing system. To establish this 
claim, it is necessary just to have the balance sheets of the Company, or, 
in the absence of tnat, direct evidence about the financial condition of the 
Company and its soundness. But there is no Buch evidence placed before 
me. So in the present state of things I cannot adjudicate upon this matter. 
I leave the issue without any direction as both sides have treated it only 
summarily. • . 


Issue No. 14^-Contrict system end Miege. 

The Labour Union wants to abolish this system of contract labour. 
The Company merely denied the claim. I have considered the evidence on 
the point. I am satisfied that howsoever much we may condemn this 
contradt Bystem academically from the point of view of labour, it cannot 
be abrogated all at- once. If it is an evil, it is a necessary evil. Just us 
the WftTtftgin g Agency in the case of companies cannot be abolished 
altogether all at once, so the Tribunals even emphatically inveighing 
ag ains t the system of Bub-contract have left it there. So I also cannot 
accept the Union’s claim that the contractors’ labour system should be 
stopped at once. I call upon the Company to reduce the employment of 
contractors’ labour and to absorb them gradually in its permanent strength 
so that ih coprse of time the contract labour system may be done away 
with. 

In the present case I have found that contractors’ men have been 
serving here for a' good number of years. They are not getting amenities 
they should otherwise have got in consideration of their length of service, 
had they been in the Company’s employ. But the Tribunals are helpless 
here, howsoever much convinced they are of their grievances, to ameliorate 
the conditions of service of these employees because any direction given on 
the Company in this respect may not be legally binding on the contractors. 
If it was a case where the contractors were directly impleaded, then relief 
could have been given against the contractors legally. But in a case like 
the present one, the Tribunals are not competent to grant relief to these 
Sirdars’ men unless the lanr is so amended, or the form of the case is 
different. So. I am unable to grant any relief under the present issue. 

Regarding the bhaga system also, my finding* is the same. I an 
unable to grant any relief because it is a matter of the subcontractqjs.
